ASEAN

Philippine Energy Secretary Sharon Garin says the ADB and World Bank have 'indicated their interest in financing' regional power grid connections, which could require hundreds of billions of dollars in investment

items: All 11 ASEAN countries have signed an Enhanced Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on the ASEAN Power Grid, aiming for an interconnected electricity network to facilitate cross-border electricity trade.

The agreement focuses on infrastructure planning, policy development, and financing, with significant potential benefits for the Philippines, including improved electricity reliability and reduced reliance on fossil fuels.

Challenges include the need for substantial investments in infrastructure and the integration of power markets, with ASEAN targeting fully integrated operations by 2045, although no firm construction timetable has been established.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Southeast Asian nations have long dreamed of an interconnected electricity network. Now, they are one step closer after all 11 ASEAN countries completed the signing of a power grid agreement that could eventually allow them to buy and sell electricity across borders.
The Enhanced Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on the ASEAN Power Grid officially entered into force upon completion of its signing on Sunday, November 15, during the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila.

According to ASEAN, the agreement “covers cooperation on infrastructure planning, institutional arrangements, policy and regulatory development, and access to financing, including for overland transmission lines and subsea power cables.” (Watch ADB’s brief explainer video below:

The agreement builds on discussions during the 48th ASEAN Summit in Cebu last May, when leaders pushed for greater regional energy connectivity, particularly through submarine power cables connecting the region’s island economies. This continued during the ASEAN energy ministers’ meeting in Manila last October, when all member countries at the time reached a consensus on the agreement.
With all ASEAN countries now manifesting their support for an interconnected grid, the proposal now moves down to the more detailed technical, legal, and financial levels of discussion.

blocks.caption: Rappler Recap: Myanmar, South China Sea among issues as 49th ASEAN Summit opens

blocks.text: For the Philippines, the benefits could be significant. Connecting to neighboring countries could allow the country to import electricity when domestic supplies are tight. Beyond improving reliability, it could also help move the Philippines’ away from expensive and dirty fossil fuel generation. (READ: Solar for whom? What Philippines can learn from Pakistan’s rooftop boom)
But connecting the grids will be neither cheap nor easy.

The Philippines itself operates three major electricity grids, Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao, which are now interconnected but still face transmission constraints. It was only in 2023 that the P52-billion Mindanao-Visayas Interconnection Project was energized, allowing electricity to flow between the two regions.

Even this year, the Visayas and Mindanao grids have repeatedly been placed under yellow and red alerts, with parts of the Visayas experiencing rotational power outages. These shortages were caused mainly by power plant outages, compounded by transmission constraints that capped the amount of electricity the Visayas could import from Luzon.
Connecting the Philippines to the rest of ASEAN would no doubt require another major investment in submarine cables, alongside improvements to domestic transmission infrastructure.

The costs could be substantial. According to the International Energy Agency, ASEAN would need around $27 billion in investment in cross-border power interconnections from 2025 to 2040, on top of more than $300 billion needed to expand and modernize domestic electricity grids. ASEAN’s own estimate is even higher, at $764 billion covering both power generation and transmission through 2045, assuming high adoption of renewable energy.

The regional bloc knows this well, which is why its enhanced MOU encourages pooling resources among governments, the private sector, and financial institutions to finance power grid projects. This is complemented by the ASEAN Power Grid Financing Initiative, which brings together ASEAN, the Asian Development Bank, and the World Bank to help prepare projects and mobilize funding.

Energy Undersecretary Felix William Fuentebella said that investors will view the signing of all ASEAN members in the enhanced MOU as a strong positive sign, which could unlock “big amounts of investments” and pave the way for more detailed feasibility studies on interconnections. Energy Secretary Garin also said that the ADB, World Bank, and other development-focused financial institutions have “indicated their interest in financing this” depending on the project proposal.

blocks.caption: ASEAN leaders sign new power grid deal. What’s next for Philippines?

blocks.text: Another major challenge could be power market integration, which ASEAN said would follow a “voluntary, stepwise approach” that takes into account policies, laws, and regulations of the participating countries.

“It will be by steps, voluntary – because we won’t be forcing any country that will not participate,” Garin told Rappler in a press conference on Tuesday, November 17. “But with the signature of everyone in the enhanced MOU, that’s a clear indication already of their participation.”
ASEAN is targeting fully integrated regional electricity grid operations by 2045, although individual connections could be developed earlier.

However, for now, no firm construction timetable has been set, with ASEAN acknowledging that “further development of technical, regulatory and commercial frameworks will be essential to translate this foundation into bankable investments.”

On November 15, the Philippines’ Department of Energy also separately signed a two-year research agreement with the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia, which includes technical studies supporting the Philippines’ participation in the regional grid. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: 'Europe needs to wake up' to realise defence costs if Ukraine fails, Danish minister says
Danish defence minister Jeppe Bruus has warned that “Europe needs to wake up” as “the price, if Ukraine falls, will be lot higher than the amount we are now delivering for Ukraine.”

blocks.caption: Denmark's defence minister Jeppe Bruus Photograph: Ida Marie Odgaard/Reuters

blocks.text: “Ukraine has the most efficient and also modern army in all of Europe. We are gaining a lot of advantages [from] the cooperation with the Ukrainians,” he said.
But he added that “the cost of Ukraine losing will be a lot higher” than any current aid given to Kyiv.
Germany to contribute $300m for US air defence systems for Ukraine ahead of 'exceptionally difficult winter', Pistorius say

German defence minister Boris Pistorius has warned that Ukraine is facing “an exceptionally difficult winter” amid intensifying Russian attacks on critical infrastructure as he confirmed Germany will fund a new package of air defence systems for Kyiv.

blocks.caption: Germany's defence minister Boris Pistorius speaks with the media as he arrives for a meeting of EU defense ministers at the European Council building in Brussels. Photograph: Virginia Mayo/AP

blocks.text: “Ukraine is facing an exceptionally difficult winter as Russia is doing everything in its power - and will continue to do so – to destroy Ukraine’s water, electricity and energy infrastructure,” he said.
Pistorius said that Russia was “intensifying its aerial assaults because its if failing to make progress on the battlefields.”
“For us, as nations supporting Ukraine, this means one thing clearly: we must continue to provide effective and rapid support for Ukraine’s air defence,” he said.
Germany will contribute $300m for another round of defensive weapons purchases from the US, with Norway also expected to join.

“Supporting Ukraine is not an act of charity. It is about far more than solidarity or assisting a nation under attack; it is about the security of Europe – and, by extension, about stopping Putin and keeping him in check.”
During the Ukraine defence contact group, which Pistorius co-chairs, the EU ministers will be joined by the US undersecretary of defence, Elbridge Colby.
“This is important, as we have several matters to discuss – for instance, the upcoming Force Posture Review, as well as cooperation on defence equipment and various other topics.”
Morning opening: Ukraine hits crucial bridge linking Russia and Crimea

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin.

blocks.caption: Gallen section of Kerch Bridge after it was hit by Ukrainian drones. Photograph: Ukrainska Pravda

blocks.text: Photos suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means that traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.
But Russian officials, quoted by Reuters, insisted that damage was only minor, and would be quick to sort out.

“We have already gathered together the resources, designers, and builders ‌for repair work. We are sorting out logistics issues with the regional leadership,” Russian deputy prime minister Marat Khusnullin wrote on Telegram.
The bridge has in the past been a key supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine ​and is widely viewed as one of Russian president Vladimir Putin’s signature infrastructure projects.
The overnight strike followed ‌an intensification of ​Russian attacks in the ​past few months on bridges in Ukraine, including in the capital Kyiv.
Elsewhere, EU defence ministers are meeting in Brussels this morning for their latest discussions on Ukraine, followed by the Ukraine defence contact group.
Meanwhile, Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting Finland’s influential Alexander Stubb, two days before a major meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin.
They will no doubt offer their reaction to today’s events in Ukraine. I will bring you all the latest.
It’s Tuesday, 17 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Communications watchdog leadership reversed findings of draft report into ABC Four Corners program, FoI documents reveal
articles.summary: Documents show draft Acma reports backed reporting of Gold Walkley award-winning journalist Mark Willacy about Australian War Memorial

blocks.text: An investigation by staff of the Australian Media and Communications Authority (Acma) cleared an ABC Four Corners program over its War Memorial reporting – only for the draft report findings to be reversed by the regulator’s leadership, freedom of information documents reveal.

Internal correspondence shows the 11th hour backflip forced a “retrofit” of the report which initially said: “Staff are of the preliminary view that the program did not breach the impartiality provision of the [ABC] code [of conduct] with respect to this allegation.”

In September the ABC’s managing director, Hugh Marks, rebuked the Acma after its finding was published, arguing its criticism of the program about the redevelopment of the Australian War Memorial was unfair and could have a chilling impact on investigative journalism in Australia.
“It also unfairly impugns the integrity of the reporter and fails to acknowledge the great efforts made by the program team to ensure impartiality,” the ABC said.

The Australian War Memorial initially complained to the ABC, but its concerns were dismissed by the broadcaster’s independent ombudsman and the chair of the memorial’s council, Kim Beazley, made a formal complaint to Acma which found in its favour.

According to the FOI, first reported by the ABC’s Media Watch, the Acma board’s decision to go against the recommendation prompted a staffer to reply: “In trying to retrofit the additional arguments into the existing report, there are probably a few places where we’ve ended up repeating some points and could tighten the report up”.

The Acma board had passed on feedback during the investigation that they weren’t quite sure the draft report “captures the vibe… that this reporting skirted a fine line” and that they can be “a bit critical”. Most of the documents revealed by the FOI appear to accept the investigation’s findings but encourage more critical language.
An Acma spokesperson said the FOI documents “include informal exchanges between colleagues” and should not be viewed in isolation.
Notes from an internal meeting in January include: “Are the concerns bad enough to be a breach? Probably not.”
Another note says: “On balance there’s not a breach but ABC could have done more to make it clearer”.

But in March 2026 notes from a board meeting say the members of the authority “found that the ABC breached the impartiality provision of the ABC Code of Practice 2024 in relation to [the episode Sacrifice]”.

The FOI documents reveal several draft reports written by specialised regulatory staff backed the reporting of Gold Walkley award-winning journalist Mark Willacy, including that “impartiality does not require that every perspective receives equal time, or that every facet of every issue is presented”.

“Although the ordinary reasonable viewer may consider the program was critical about how the [redevelopment] project was conducted, there is no evidence that the program was partial to critics of the project”, the draft report said.
Announcing the finding in September, Acma chair Nerida O’Loughlin said the ABC must present contentious issues with due impartiality and provide audiences with sufficient context.

“We found that the cumulative effect of the program’s framing, its use of strong and emotive language and its selection and differing treatment of interviewees unduly favoured critics of the redevelopment,” O’Loughlin said.
A former member of the authority told the Guardian there is often debate between authority members and staff over contentious issues but reversing an investigation finding was “pretty rare”.
Acma said investigations are “a collective and consultative process” and are ultimately decided by the six authority [board] members.

“The Acma stands by its decision that the Four Corners ‘Sacrifice’ program did not comply with the ABC’s own impartiality standards, a spokesman said. “The Authority reached its decision after considering the program, the original complaint, the ABC’s submissions and the analysis and advice developed during the investigation,” they said.
The ABC declined to comment on the FOI report and referred to its original statement.
“The ABC stands behind the team, the processes that were followed and the program as broadcast,” the statement said.

articles.title: PNP: No formal report yet on alleged threat reported by Sara Duterte's camp
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) said Tuesday it has not received any formal report regarding an alleged threat against a former household helper of Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 4:32pm
The Philippine National Police (PNP) said Tuesday it has not received any formal report regarding an alleged threat against a former household helper of Vice President Sara Duterte.

PNP spokesperson Police Brigadier General Allen Rae Co was asked about the claims of Duterte's lawyer Paolo Panelo that the household staff asked the vice president for help as she was allegedly being held against her will and was being forced to sign a document.
"Have they reported it to us? To the Philippine National Police? As of this time, we have received no reports that they have reported it to us," Co said at a press briefing.
Co pointed out that the PNP could not initiate an investigation based solely on social media posts containing unverified allegations.
He encouraged the vice president or anyone with information about the alleged threat to report the matter directly to the PNP.

According to a Facebook post by Atty. Paolo Panelo, Duterte's spokesperson, the vice president received a message at 11:19 p.m. on Monday "from what appeared to be the account of a former household staff member" asking for help and rescue in Manila.

The sender claimed to be under the custody or control of certain individuals who allegedly threatened their life. The former staff member also said they were being forced to sign a document but refused to do so.
Panelo said the person's whereabouts remain unknown and their safety and well-being have yet to be verified.

Panelo expressed concern that the incident could be part of what he described as a campaign by the Marcos administration to allegedly harass and coerce individuals into becoming false witnesses against Duterte amid her impeachment trial.
For its part, Malacañang said authorities should investigate the matter to determine the truth behind the Duterte camp's claims.

Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro shrugged off Panelo's statement that the alleged incident may be part of the administration's supposed campaign against Marcos, saying the President was busy with the ongoing 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: China taps US AI models to train homegrown rivals as chip curbs bite
articles.summary: China's use of distillation could undercut the effectiveness of US curbs on the sale of advanced chips to China, as its developers can build AI capabilities by drawing on those of their American…

blocks.text: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE. An AI sign is seen at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai, China on July 6, 2023.
Aly Song/Reuters

China's use of distillation could undercut the effectiveness of US curbs on the sale of advanced chips to China, as its developers can build AI capabilities by drawing on those of their American rivals

items: Chinese entities are increasingly using distillation techniques to leverage output from American AI models, aiming to enhance their domestic AI capabilities amid tightening US restrictions on chip access.

Research indicates this practice has moved from academic settings to mainstream industrial applications, with Chinese companies automating processes and training smaller models based on American outputs.

The growing use of distillation raises geopolitical tensions, as US officials express concerns over potential intellectual property theft and the effectiveness of US chip export controls, while Chinese developers seek clarity on the legality of their practices.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

BEIJING, China – Chinese entities are adopting increasingly sophisticated ways to use output from leading American AI models to train domestic rivals, documents show, as China aims to broaden its AI strategy and offset tightening US curbs on its access to chips.

A Reuters review of more than 300 Chinese academic papers, patents, corporate disclosures, recruitment notices and government documents reveals how the practice — known as distillation — has expanded beyond academic experiments into mainstream industrial use in China.

The records describe Chinese researchers using US models to produce answers to questions, build computer code, and find solutions to difficult problems, with Chinese companies then developing software to automate the process and specialist workers preparing material for training smaller domestic models.
The documents also show that Beijing is encouraging distillation to make AI cheaper and easier to deploy across China’s powerful manufacturing sector.

Distillation is not illegal and is prevalent in other parts of the world. While the process cannot reproduce a leading model’s full capabilities or eliminate the need for advanced computing power, it can help developers preserve selected skills in smaller systems that cost less to operate, potentially reducing their reliance on American technology.

China’s broadening use of distillation could undercut the effectiveness of US curbs on the sale of advanced chips to China, as its developers can build AI capabilities by drawing on those of their American rivals. Washington said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to such chips from companies like Nvidia.

Distillation is also a source of friction between the world’s two biggest economies ahead of the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, where US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are expected to meet.
US authorities publicly accused Chinese companies in September of aggressive, targeted distillation of American AI models on an industrial scale.

And at meetings in Chengdu in July, US Commerce Department officials raised concerns with Chinese regulators about developers collecting output from leading American AI models, warning that some activities could amount to intellectual-property theft, three people familiar with the discussions said.

Chinese officials defended distillation as a standard AI-development technique and said they were open to acting where the conduct constituted IP theft, but made no concrete commitments, according to a US official familiar with the previously unreported exchange.
The US Commerce Department and China’s Cyberspace Administration did not respond to requests for comment.
Distillation involves a powerful ‘teacher’ model generating answers or demonstrating how to complete tasks, which developers use to train a smaller ‘student’ system.

For Chinese developers facing constraints on computing power, the attraction is in making one expensive query do repeated work, according to a former Alibaba Group engineer who spoke on condition of anonymity. An American model can generate the answer to a difficult question once, allowing a Chinese team to retain useful examples and train a local system around them.

In a November 2024 paper, Shanghai Jiao Tong University researchers described selecting about 5,000 answers from OpenAI’s o1 model, translating them using GPT-4o mini and assembling 10,750 bilingual training examples to further train Alibaba’s Qwen2.5-72B model.
The researchers also cautioned that excessive reliance on distillation could stifle original innovation, leaving developers dependent on breakthroughs made by more advanced model providers.
The project illustrated how American model output can become reusable data, allowing developers to improve domestic systems without repeatedly consulting the original provider.

Alibaba researchers described a more systematic approach in an April 2025 paper, using OpenAI’s GPT-4 and GPT-4o to generate training material in languages other than Chinese, then refining and scoring responses before training smaller Qwen models.

In a February 2026 paper, researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Chinese food-delivery company Meituan described using GPT-4o to generate plans for coordinating AI agents working together on programming problems, helping train a smaller model to organise such tasks.
Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Alibaba and Meituan did not respond to requests for comment.

Among leading American AI companies, OpenAI’s terms restrict using its output to develop competing models, subject to exceptions, while Anthropic similarly restricts training competing systems without permission.

A US official familiar with the July Chengdu regulatory discussions said Washington believes industrial-scale distillation is the main reason Chinese AI models have narrowed the gap with their American rivals.
Two people familiar with Chinese developers’ operations disputed that assessment, saying distillation was only one factor alongside advances in engineering, algorithms, data and model design.
Chinese government documents do not instruct companies to distil American models but encourage distillation as part of Beijing’s push to spread AI across the world’s second-largest economy.

A national AI+Manufacturing policy package published by eight Chinese government agencies in January includes guidance supporting model training, fine-tuning and distillation for industrial applications. Shanghai and Shenzhen have also encouraged techniques to reduce computing requirements.
The policies reflect Beijing’s ambition to deploy smaller, cheaper AI systems across industries.

Concerned by distillation’s growing geopolitical sensitivities, Chinese AI developers have in recent months asked Beijing’s industry regulator for guidance on the boundaries between ordinary use of foreign models and organised collection of output for training, according to one person familiar with the discussions.
China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology did not respond to a request for comment. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Waitrose is to expand its digital broadcasting portfolio after this year’s Christmas ad launch with Keira Knightley attracted more that 2 million viewers.

“There are not many brands that would command an appointment of you for six minutes on ITV to launch their Christmas ad and have 2.3 million people show up to watch,” said the supermarket’s chief executive, Tom Denyard.

Showing the Guardian around Waitrose’s latest shop which opened in the wealthy Greater Manchester neighbourhood of Hale Barns last week, he said the company was looking at more digital ideas. “We would be daft not to think about that as an opportunity,” he said.

Waitrose is already a serious digital player with the Dish podcast, hosted by the DJ Nick Grimshaw and the chef Angela Hartnett, which has been downloaded more than 1.3bn times. It says its social media following has risen 8% year on year and fans spent more than 1m hours watching its YouTube channel in the last 12 months, double the previous year.

It launched a weekly recipe and tutorials series, Let’s Cook, this summer and has taken Dish live, selling more than 2,000 tickets for an event at the Royal Opera House. It also has a growing presence on TikTok with 128,000 followers.
Denyard said: “Waitrose as a brand punches well above its weight in food culture. We have the fastest growing channel for food in the UK.”
He said the retailer was thinking carefully about how to ensure it kept the trust it had gained from food fans. “We want to do it in a way that’s right for the community that we’re part of.”

Denyard, who joined Waitrose in January after four years leading Tesco’s online business, wants to link Waitrose stores and the digital world more closely with a host of ideas including AI assistants for staff and shoppers.

Staff across the chain are now equipped with handheld gadgets that give them access to AI-assisted information. The Rosie system, which began trials last year and is now in most shops, can help staff provide advice on suitable wines for different meals, and where in store to find products.

Denyard says the introduction of electronic pricing labels in almost all its shops over the past year will, from this week, also help staff, including those picking shelves for online orders, to find products. Rosie will indicate product locations with a flashing light on the electronic shelf label.
The system is said to have freed up thousands of hours of staff time, amid pressure to cut costs as a result of higher minimum wages and tax.
After opening two supermarkets this year, its first in eight years, Waitrose is to open as many as six new outlets of various sizes in 2027 as part of a £1bn investment plan.

Despite industry chatter about consolidation, Denyard says Waitrose is not looking to buy a rival chain. But in the event of a widely expected move by the UK’s second biggest supermarket chain, Sainsbury’s, to buy up either Asda or Morrisons, or any attempts by rivals to downsize, Waitrose will be waiting in the wings to pick up store locations.
“We will remain acquisitive and we are keen to make sure that we’re at the table taking those opportunities,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

Next year’s plans include a supermarket in Oakham, Rutland, and three convenience shops in Bedminster inBristol, Chalk Farm in London and Springstead Village in Cambridge, as well as refurbishing 29 existing branches.

Denyard says he is keen for more larger supermarkets, such as those recently opened in Hale Barns and Cricklewood in north London, where the company can show off its full foodie credentials with fresh food counters, something removed by most rivals.

Waitrose, which has more than 300 supermarkets, is introducing meat, fish and sushi counters, on-site bakeries and fine wine sections in more stores. It is also using pop-ups, such as a mini cheese tasting table in Hale Barns.
Denyard says counters are “a core part of our offer” as the foodies Waitrose wants to attract “really want to shop them”.

Those foodies are also being courted with an ever-expanding own-label range, particularly at the premium end with Waitrose No.1. Sales of the luxury own brand are growing by more than 10% year on year despite the squeeze on household budgets, as many buy ready meals instead of takeaways and dining out.
Denyard says there is “lots of headroom” to expand the range and that own-label is a key part of what makes Waitrose distinctive.

After a difficult period, when sales were hit by IT problems that led to gaps on shelves, Waitrose is holding market share, according to the latest figures from the market analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. It is coming under pressure from Marks & Spencer, however, which has a higher share of the grocery market by some measures after opening a number of new food-led outlets.

Denyard nonetheless says Waitrose is “resilient and competitive in the market”. “Customers have a repertoire of places that they go for different missions and fulfil different needs across the course of a given week or month,” he said. “Our job is to make sure in that mix we are brilliantly differentiated and give food lovers more reasons to come to Waitrose, and we feel like we’re getting well down the path.”

The Philippine National Police (PNP) said Tuesday that it has not monitored any major security threats ahead of the arrival of United States President Donald Trump for the 49th ASEAN Summit.
At a press briefing, PNP spokesperson Police Brigadier General Allen Rae Co said the security situation remained generally peaceful despite tensions between cops and protesters.

articles.title: Japan sends up jets after alleged Russian incursion of its airspace
articles.summary: Taiwan and South Korea also responded to Russian military aircraft detected near their airspaces.

blocks.text: Japan says it launched fighter jets and "strongly" protested after two suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace early on Tuesday.
South Korea also says it deployed fighter jets, while Taiwan says it "responded" to Russian military aircraft detected in their respective air defence identification zones.
These are unofficial buffer areas beyond territorial airspace where governments identify approaching aircraft for security purposes. Moscow has yet to comment.
The alleged incursions are a reminder of Russia's military power ahead of the Apec economic summit in China this week, which Vladimir Putin will attend alongside US President Donald Trump.

Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft, off the south-western Okinoshima island, were a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and "completely unacceptable".
The last such incursion was in 2024, when a Russian military patrol plane entered Japanese airspace off Rebun island, Hokkaido.
Taiwan says its military "responded accordingly" after two Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone, also on Tuesday.

South Korea says it sent up jets after an unspecified number of Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan. The aircraft departed without violating South Korean airspace, authorities said.
It is unclear if the three neighbours were responding to the same or different aircraft.
The East China Sea contains self-declared, overlapping air defence identification zones between China, Taiwan, Japan and South Korea.
Foreign military aircraft are expected, but not legally required, to notify governments before entering such air defence identification zones.
Tensions are flaring between Japan and Russia, which are locked in a decades-old territorial dispute over a cluster of islands in the Pacific Ocean.
For months, Moscow has been ratcheting up the pressure on Tokyo.

In August, Putin paid his first visit to one of these islands, prompting sharp rebuke from Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. In October, Russia detained a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.

articles.title: Ukraine critically damages Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia
articles.summary:
Photos of bridge, built after 2014 annexation and viewed by Ukraine as illegal, suggest massive steel arch has fallen into water

Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking…
articles.byline: Luke Harding and Dan Sabbagh in Kyiv

blocks.text: Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin.

Footage showed a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile seconds before it hit the road and railway crossing, followed by an explosion. The strike follows an earlier attack on Monday that targeted an arch across its central section.
Russian forces struck ⁠two major bridges in Kyiv that straddle the Dnipro River late on Monday, along with some other critical infrastructure, amid drone ⁠and missile attacks ​across Ukraine.

Ukraine has declared that the Kerch bridge, built eight years ago after Vladimir Putin’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and known officially as the Crimean Bridge, is illegal. It has repeatedly attempted to destroy it, with a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone strike the following year.

blocks.caption: A screengrab of footage of a Ukrainian missile approaching the Kerch bridge in Crimea. Photograph: supplied

blocks.text: The latest drone and missile barrage appears to have succeeded, after months in which Ukrainian unmanned systems forces have systematically knocked out the peninsula’s multi-layered air defences.

The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the bridge, which was temporarily closed on Monday, was no longer usable. “The enemy has once again attacked the Crimean Bridge. At the moment, traffic has been suspended,” he posted.
He added on Telegram: “We ask residents and visitors in Crimea to refrain from traveling toward the bridge and to take these restrictions into account when planning their routes.”

Photos on Tuesday suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means that traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.

blocks.caption: A screengrab showing the moment when a Ukrainian missile hit the Kerch bridge. Photograph: supplied

blocks.text: The debris appears to have blocked the main navigable route beneath the bridge, used by maritime traffic from the Sea of Azov and the ports of Berdiansk and Mariupol. The channel is 120 metres wide and 8.3 metres deep. Submerged steel struts could prevent large vessels from passing until the debris is removed.

Ukrainian observers were gleeful at the bridge’s long-awaited destruction. They pointed out that Ukraine’s armed forces could hit the bridge again to prevent repair work from being carried out. Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to the defence ministry in Kyiv, wrote: “In response to your many questions. Yes, the bridge is fucked.”

In Kyiv, loud explosions could be heard as Russian forces struck two bridges over the Dnipro River. The mayor of the Ukrainian capital, Vitali Klitschko, wrote on Telegram that according to “preliminary information, there have been hits on the north and south bridges in ⁠the capital”. There were water and power cuts in parts of the city, he added later.
Russian forces launched a ​series of attacks on bridges crossing ‌the river earlier this ‌month and in October.
A Russian missile attack had injured three people ‌in the region of Cherkasy and also targeted Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-biggest city, local officials said on Telegram.

Russia’s defence ministry claimed ⁠on ⁠Tuesday its ​forces had ⁠carried out a massive ⁠overnight strike ​on ‌Ukrainian ‌military-industrial facilities, ‌transport infrastructure in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia and the ‌Cherkasy and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
The ministry ​said the strikes had also ⁠targeted energy facilities, ​port infrastructure ​and ​vessels ​used ‌by ​Ukraine’s armed ​forces.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said earlier on Monday that intelligence showed Russia’s military was planning strikes for Monday evening and throughout Tuesday.
Russian defence ministry data from Monday showed that an overnight Ukrainian drone barrage on was the biggest since the start of full-scale war in 2022.

Zelenskyy also said on Monday ⁠that Ukraine had held new online talks with the US presidential envoys ​Steve Witkoff and ​Jared Kushner, as well as European ​representatives, on the prospects of ending the war with Russia.

Kushner ​said progress had been ‌made toward an ​agreement, though important ​challenges remain to end the war that Russia started by invading Ukraine in February 2022. Moscow annexed the Black Sea Crimea peninsula in 2014.

articles.title: More than 200 protesters still in police custody after stalled inquest
articles.summary: An inquest delay has left arrested ASEAN protesters in custody.

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 3:42pm

Protesters clash with police officers during a demonstration that coincides with the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Leaders' Summit and Related Summits in Manila on November 15, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta. Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — Hundreds of protesters arrested during an anti-Pax Silica demonstration in Muntinlupa City remained in police custody on Tuesday, November 17, after inquest proceedings failed to proceed the previous day, prolonging their detention without formal charges filed in court.
The protesters were arrested Sunday, November 15, during a demonstration opposing the US-led Pax Silica initiative and the visit of President Donald Trump for the 49th ASEAN Summit.

They were taken to Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City, where they remained as of Tuesday. Protest organizers estimated that nearly 300 people were arrested, while police reported more than 200 are still in custody.

Jesus Monasterial, deputy secretary-general of the Katipunan ng mga Samahang Magbubukid sa Timog Katagalugan, told ABS-CBN's "TV Patrol" that Monday's inquest proceedings fell through because the prosecutor failed to arrive.
Inquest are when a prosecutor determines whether a person arrested without a warrant should face criminal charges.
Monasterial said the delay left protesters in custody for more than 30 hours without formal charges filed against them.

He also said authorities had asked some detainees to sign waivers under Article 125 of the Revised Penal Code, which sets time limits for delivering people arrested without warrants to the proper judicial authorities.
Under Article 125, the limits are 12 hours for offenses punishable by light penalties, 18 hours for correctional penalties and 36 hours for afflictive or capital penalties.
A waiver may allow a detainee to remain in custody beyond the applicable period while seeking a preliminary investigation, but it must be voluntary and executed with the assistance of counsel.
The National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO), meanwhile, denied allegations that it had deprived those in its custody of legal assistance, food and other basic necessities.
UP students, campus journalists detained
At least 50 students from the University of the Philippines system were among those arrested during the Muntinlupa protest, according to reports from university units and student publications.
UP Diliman called for the immediate release of 10 of its students on Monday, November 16. Among them was a staff member of the Philippine Collegian, the university's official student publication.
The Collegian reported that a preliminary bail amount of P30,000 had been set for the staff member's release.
At UP Los Baños (UPLB), various colleges confirmed that 44 students were in detention.
The detainees included 10 staff members of UPLB Perspective, the campus' official student publication.

UPLB's Standing Committee on National Issues and the Promotion and Protection of Academic Freedom and Human Rights said police had informed detainees that they would face complaints for illegal assembly and public disturbance after allegedly refusing orders to stop their protest.
The specific offenses to be pursued and whether criminal cases have been filed in court remain unconfirmed.
DFA declines comment. Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro declined to comment Monday on the arrests during the ASEAN Summit.
At a press conference Monday, she said the discussions among regional leaders had focused on regional matters rather than domestic issues.
The summit has drawn protests against several initiatives, including the US-led Pax Silica framework, which aims to secure semiconductor and artificial intelligence supply chains.

articles.title: Supreme Court 'recalibrates' damages for criminal raps
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has increased the amounts of civil damages awarded to victims in criminal cases, introducing a recalibrated compensation framework designed to ensure consistency and reflect the…

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 3:34pm
The main building of the Philippine Supreme Court in Manila.
Philstar.com / Martin Ramos
Trigger warning: Mentions of rape, abuse

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court (SC) has increased the amounts of civil damages awarded to victims in criminal cases, introducing a recalibrated compensation framework designed to ensure consistency and reflect the gravity of criminal offenses.

In a statement on Tuesday, November 17, the Supreme Court said that civil damages are not merely incidental relief in criminal cases, but essential expressions of the law's recognition of victims' suffering and society's condemnation of criminal acts.

"They are essential expressions of the law's recognition of the harm suffered by victims and society's condemnation of criminal conduct. Through the updated guidelines, the Court seeks to ensure that monetary awards remain consistent, proportionate to the gravity of the offense, and responsive to the realities of victims," the Supreme Court's statement said.
The recalibration is based on a decision in the case of People of the Philippines vs Flores, penned by Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh.

In this case, the high tribunal ordered that all future awards for civil indemnity ex delicto, moral damages, exemplary damages, and temperate damages in criminal proceedings must conform to the updated amounts set in its decision.

Under the revised guidelines, the high court established specific amounts for temperate damages to address financial losses that were incurred by victims or their families but cannot be proven with exact documentary evidence.
The Supreme Court explained that these standardized figures account for ordinary and necessary expenses stemming from death or injury while providing a consistent basis for compensation.

"The court explained that these amounts recognize the ordinary and necessary expenses to account for the actual economic burden arising from death or injury, while providing a consistent basis for compensation, when exact expenditures cannot be established through documentary evidence," the Supreme Court's statement read.
The Court also adjusted the awards for crimes resulting in death, noting that the loss of life warrants the highest compensation ranges because it is permanent and irreversible.

In setting the benchmarks, the High Court calibrated higher amounts for intentional killings compared to deaths resulting from negligence — a distinction reflecting the greater legal gravity and culpability of intentional criminal acts, rather than placing a different value on human life.
The case

Applying the updated framework to the Supreme Court case of People of the Philippines vs Flores, the High Court raised the civil awards granted to a child victim who was only six years old when the crimes were committed.
For cases of qualified rape of a minor, the Supreme Court increased civil indemnity ex delicto, moral damages, and exemplary damages from P100,000 to P325,000 each.
For acts of lasciviousness cases, the corresponding awards were raised from P50,000 to P175,000 each.
The monetary awards will earn a legal interest of six percent per annum from the finality of the decision until fully paid.

Additionally, the high court mandated that trial courts direct the Department of Social Welfare and Development to refer the child victim, with her guardian's consent, to an appropriate rape crisis center for support and assistance.

articles.title: India has been named a ‘destination of the year’ for 2027 – here are insiders’ tips on travelling beyond the tropes
articles.summary:
As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here

The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to…

blocks.text: The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.

India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.

So when, last week, Travel + Leisure named India its destination of the year for 2027, I found myself considering what it means that the country holds such multitudes. The magazine’s recognition will undoubtedly add to its growing appeal as a travel destination. But expectations built around India can differ from the experience of being there, particularly for women.

My own experiences of travelling in India largely surround my work as a journalist, often visiting places that would never make it into a travel guide. I remember the towering chinar tree outside the home of a woman in Kashmir whose son had been killed in an encounter with the security forces; the rolling hills of Odisha, where we travelled to meet a guerrilla fighter; the tiny hut in Chhattisgarh where, after a 13-hour journey, our team found a meal of rice and lentils. These scenes have stayed in my mind, for their landscapes as much as for the stories and circumstances.

Ultimately, such experiences were far more illuminating than those from a conventional travel itinerary, and taught me to navigate uncertainty and embrace discomfort. For this week’s newsletter, I spoke to three women about the journeys in India that stayed with them and what travelling here has meant to them.
‘The only sounds you hear are of nature’

blocks.caption: Memorable … the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh. Photograph: Sumit Kumar/Getty Images

blocks.text: One of the most memorable journeys for travel writer Shivya Nath was a trek through the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh, with a crew of local women.

Trekking has always been a male-dominated industry and Nath, author of the book Rootless and Restless, was struck by the personal journeys of the women leading the expedition. (She travelled with an organisation which trains women to become guides, overcoming social and family restrictions.) “For some of the women, spending even two nights away from home required negotiating with their families,” she told me.

The route wound through dense forests in the Great Himalayan national park, across ancient bridges, over gushing, undammed rivers, accompanied by the soundtrack of birdsong. “The only sounds you hear are of nature,” she recalled. Along the way, they stopped to forage lingri, a seasonal wild fern used in regional cooking, which they later prepared at a riverside camp they set up for the night.

The following morning, the group hiked to a waterfall, standing together on a large rock in the middle of the cascading water. Being with “just a group of women who love being in the outdoors, was a really powerful feeling for me”, she said.

For Afsha Sethi, a corporate leadership professional from Bengaluru who has travelled extensively in India, one of her most cherished travel experiences is an unlikely one. As part of an extracurricular project when she was in high school, students were paired with a local community through an NGO. She spent a week shadowing a farming family growing rice and areca nut in Karkolli, in northern Karnataka.
Walks through lush forests with waterfalls were a daily routine. “We would come back with leeches on our legs, and then put salt to get rid of them,” she recalled.

The trip also brought her into contact with something she had not encountered before. When her roommate told the host family about getting her period, their sleeping arrangements were shifted to the courtyard. “It turned out to be a great experience, because the weather was very nice and [we were] looking at the stars and just chatting late into the night,” she said. It reminded her that travelling through India can mean encountering different social conventions.
‘The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it’

blocks.caption: Overtourism is a real risk in places like Goa. Photograph: Pavel Laputskov/Getty Images/iStockphoto

blocks.text: The travel boom in India is led by domestic travellers. The country recorded almost 2.95bn domestic tourist visits in 2024, a jump of 17.5% from the previous year, according to recent government data. Overall, India ranks 31st in the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index 2026, up eight spots since 2024.
Women accounted for 43% of foreign arrivals, an interesting counterpoint to India’s reputation as a challenging destination for female travellers.

But the boom raises questions about what happens to the places being discovered. “Social media has definitely accelerated the over-tourism problem,” says Nath. “I think one of the most basic things travellers can do is to avoid geotagging locations.” She suggests choosing community-owned tourism initiatives that allow local people to benefit directly from visitors.

Nayanika Gaffino, a mother and recreational athlete who has also clocked up the miles around the country, has seen this happen first-hand in Goa, where she lives. “The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it … even though it doesn’t have the capacity to handle so many people,” she says, adding there are beaches her family now avoids because of this.

Travelling with girls, Gaffino also has to consider practicalities such as hygiene and access to clean public toilets and safety. As such, she gravitates towards boutique properties that are accustomed to hosting families with children.

Nath acknowledges that solo travel can require extra vigilance. On solo trips, she prefers family-run homestays or guesthouses where someone is aware that she is on her own and can watch out for her. At the same time, she adds, India can be an intensely hospitable place where people generously invite you for tea or a meal.

Discovering a place, she says, should also include finding ways to preserve the very qualities that led you to it in the first place. The journeys the women described involved seeing a side of India that differed from their own expectations. This is what makes al-Qazwini’s understanding of wonder relevant for me. To approach something with wonder is not to be impressed by just beauty or uniqueness but to have a curiosity about what it might show us – its possibilities and its limitations.
after newsletter promotion
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: The Congress party, led Rahul Gandhi, says one-third of delegates at its summit in Hyderabad at the weekend were denied entry to India. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Politics | More than one-third of the international delegates – about 115 people – expected to attend the Congress party’s Bharat summit over the weekend were denied entry to India or had their visas cancelled, according to the Wire. Congress described this as an attempt to stifle voices of criticism, while the foreign ministry said that visa-related decisions are “sovereign functions” but did not share further details.

Lawsuit | The US state department has served summons in a civil lawsuit brought by Khalistani separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannu against national security adviser Ajit Doval and former research and analysis wing, Samant Goel, according to the Hindu. The foreign ministry described the lawsuit as “frivolous”.

Culture | A 50-year-old Navaratri festival at Wesleyan University, in Connecticut, has made it an unlikely home for Carnatic music and dance traditions. Although such festivals take place at cities around the world, few institutions have become as significant a platform for Indian music and dance.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: A screenshot from I Am 20, an inventive documentary short film from 1967. Photograph: YouTube

blocks.text: Shaunak Sen, director of the Academy Award-nominated All That Breathes, recommends: “If you find yourself in the oft-trodden window of wanting to watch something for an hour after dinner, but feel drowned in the mediocre flotsam of the big streamers, I have a suggestion watch the strangely inventive short films of the artist-bureaucrat SNS Sastry from the 1960s and 70s [on YouTube]. Unlike the regular pedantic state films of the time, Sastry somehow created avant garde, surreal, even funny films, funded by the Films Division of India. I Am 20, which interviewed young adults born in the year of India’s independence, is an inquiry into a certain national zeitgeist. Between the candour of the participants and the sharpness of their complaints, one can scarcely believe this was made under the aegis of the government.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: Post-Diwali pollution near President’s House in New Delhi. Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPA

blocks.text: Firecrackers were responsible for most of Delhi’s fine particulate matter of PM 2.5 – about 71% – in the hours after Diwali celebrations, according to a first-of-its-kind assessment by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. The national capital reported its most-polluted Diwali since 2021, data from the Central Pollution Control Board showed.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: In We Were Here, humans are trying to take AIs’ jobs. Photograph: Sunshine Motion Pictures

blocks.text: AI anxiety is everywhere. Pranav Bhasin’s comedy We Were Here has brought that to screens in a short film that is making an impression internationally. Bhasin’s mockumentary is about three retired men in a small Indian town who, persuaded that artificial intelligence is taking over human jobs, fight back by impersonating household appliances. One becomes a dish antenna, another a vehicle’s reverse camera and a third a microwave. The situation becomes more complicated when one of their children takes a job at an AI company. “Do you want artificial intelligence?” “No, I have real one,” goes one caustic exchange.
The New Yorker released the film on YouTube and it’s eligible for Oscars consideration after winning at the Palm Springs International ShortFest.
Get in touch

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

articles.title: UK unemployment unexpectedly eases to 4.6%, as government prepares to release Milburn report
articles.summary: Wage growth falls to to 3.5% in September, as ministers examine how best to get young people into work

blocks.text: The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government prepares to release a major report on the youth jobs crisis.
The unemployment rate was 4.6% in September, dipping from 4.7% in August, according to the Office for National Statistics. City economists had expected it to remain at 4.7%.
However, wage growth fell to 3.5%, excluding bonuses, in the latest official figures for the three months to the end of September, down from 3.7% in the three months to August.

With inflation also at 3.5% and expected to rise for a fourth consecutive month to 3.7% when figures are released on Wednesday, the average worker faces a fall in real wages growth to zero or even into negative territory.

The figures highlighted how difficult it will be for ministers to improve living standards as they consider the findings of a key report by the former health secretary Alan Milburn examining how to get young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) back into work, released later on Tuesday.

The jobs market has proved difficult for analysts and politicians to assess in recent years. It has been called weak after a dramatic slide in the number of vacancies, which illustrates the reticence of companies to hire new staff.
However, employment has proved resilient, with unemployment falling between July and August from 4.9% to 4.7%, indicating that few employers were ready to cut large numbers of staff.
after newsletter promotion
Ministers are known to be concerned that some large employers, including several banks, have said they intend to use artificial intelligence to reduce their staffing levels.

Economists are divided over whether AI will enhance productivity across all major sectors of the economy – after signs it has boosted GDP – or lead to improvements in certain industries, such as healthcare.

Employer groups have complained that Labour’s increase in national insurance payments, a higher minimum wage and changes to employee rights have increased costs, leading to a fall in the number of advertised vacancies.
The Bank of England increased interests rates earlier this month after a rise in the consumer prices index to 3.5% in September.

It has said that its own surveys showed employers did not expect to increase pay beyond 3.5% to 4% next year, despite the higher level of inflation, and also reported little change looking ahead in their own prices.

However, a growing number of the Bank’s policymakers believe the prospect of high oil and energy prices next year as the Iran war drags on will push inflation towards 5% and force employers to offer higher pay, which will be passed on in higher retail prices.

articles.title: Canada, China agree to ease tariffs amid trade rows with US
articles.summary: The Canadian and Chinese leaders have vowed closer cooperation as both nations seek to reduce reliance on the US. Canada's government said it had agreed to further reduce tariffs on a range of…

image.caption: Carney (L) and Xi held talks ahead of the APEC summit in ShenzhenImage: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Talks between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen have produced deals to further reduce tariffs, Ottawa said on Tuesday.

The agreements reflect a growing rapprochement between the two countries after years of strained relations, thanks totrade tensions with Washington leading both Canada and China to seek to reduce dependence on the US.

At the talks, Carney hailed "greater predictability and stability" in ‌relations with China, while Xi said the cooperation between his country and Canada would "benefit not only our two countries but also Asia-Pacific and the world."
Carney said Canada had already made faster-than-expected progress toward its goal of boosting exports to China "by 50% by the end of this decade."
What have China and Canada agreed on?
According to a statement from the Canadian government, China is to reduce tariffs on Canadian pork, fish and seafood.
In exchange, Canada will prolong the current tariff exemptions for Chinese steel and aluminum for another two years.
The two leaders also agreed to cooperate more closely on economic and financial matters, and to work together in the fields of education and environmental protection.
Canada is too reliant on the United States, Carney tells DW
Growing China-Canada rapprochement
Xi and Carney already declared their intention to enhance bilateral ties during talks in Beijing in January.
There, they struck a deal that foresaw a reduction in tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, while Chinese electric vehicles gained easier access to the Canadian market.
Critics in Canada have, however, pointed out what they see as dangers to the country's security and values through the closer ties to Beijing.
Among other things, Canadian intelligence believes that China interfered in at least two federal elections, something Beijing denies.

articles.title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
articles.summary:
New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores

Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros…

blocks.text: Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.

But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market. Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1m), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest.

Anthropic’s millionaire factory promises to expand the group of tech buyers, who range from senior staff at major AI labs to founders who have sold their startups, with budgets that range from £2m to £40m, Eccles says.

blocks.caption: San Francisco, where tech wealth has driven up demand for already scarce housing. Photograph: Josh Edelson/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Tech’s wave of wealth has already reshaped Silicon Valley – notably in San Francisco – driving up demand for already scarce housing as young entrepreneurs and engineers became millionaires overnight. Now, that money is washing up on British shores too.

Anthropic, which employs about 5,000 people worldwide, has more than 200 employees in the UK. The company, founded in San Francisco in 2021, has announced plans to expand its presence in London, with a new office that is capable of accommodating up to 800 people.

The company’s UK filings show that it spent £24.1m employing an average of 43 staff in 2024 alone – a mean average of £560,000 per person. Job listings this year have advertised base salaries of up to £630,000 before stock options for research engineers.

Salaries across Britain’s AI sector are flying: OpenAI’s staff in London each received £2.3m on average last year – about 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings. That puts them on par with partners at top law firms such as Linklaters and Clifford Chance, and ahead of some bankers in the City.

UK-based investors in these companies are also watching the value of their stakes grow at breakneck speed. Alex Gerko, the billionaire founder of the trading firm XTX and an early investor in Anthropic via the venture arms of the business, is expected to make hundreds of millions of pounds in paper gains when the company joins the stock market this week.

blocks.caption: Google’s headquarters in King’s Cross in London. Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta are all a stone’s throw away. Photograph: Nathaniel Noir/Alamy

blocks.text: The flush of technology cash is already evident in London’s commercial property market. First, a wave of startups led to Shoreditch being nicknamed Silicon Roundabout, before tech firms began expanding across the capital. Now, US AI firms are expanding at pace in the UK, clustering tightly inside the King’s Cross “knowledge quarter” where Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta all work a stone’s throw from each other.

They have followed in the footsteps of Demis Hassabis, a totemic figure in AI’s breakthrough era who co-founded DeepMind in 2010 and sold it to Google for £400m four years later. He was one of the first to set up in the north London enclave. Isomorphic Labs, his AI drug discovery startup that is also now owned by the Google parent Alphabet, is in the area.

The AI gold rush is already being felt at the highest end of London’s housing market. Although tech bosses may be younger than the sector’s traditional client base, agents report that interest – while spread across London – includes plenty of familiar wealthy haunts.

In February, the Times reported that Igor Babuschkin, the billionaire co-founder of Elon Musk’s AI venture xAI, had bought a £57m penthouse overlooking Hyde Park, in one of the biggest deals in the city this year.

Meanwhile, Providence House, the Reform UK treasurer Nick Candy’s former mansion on the grounds of the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London, was reportedly sold for £270m to the founder of the quantitative investment firm Quadrature Capital, Suneil Setiya. Aidan Devane, the chief executive of the firm, attributed its success partly to its proximity to AI labs in the city, telling the Financial Times: “We are probably in the golden age of London quant.”

Tech wealth, increasingly generated by gains in the AI sector, “has become a force at the very top of the prime central London market”, according to the super-prime estate agent Beauchamp Estates, which has a portfolio including a £42m sub-penthouse overlooking Hyde Park.

Jeremy Gee, a managing director at Beauchamp, says inquiries from tech and AI buyers have risen noticeably over the past year. “Some are international buyers, principally from the US, but a growing number are based here in London,” he says, adding that many have amassed their fortunes with remarkable speed.

“They tend to be younger, they move quickly and they are very clear about what they want. Location and quality matter most and they will pay a premium for something genuinely special,” he says. “London offers culture, history, world-class schools and a growing AI community of its own.”

blocks.caption: Providence House, formerly known as Gordon House, photographed in 2015. It was reportedly sold this year to Suneil Setiya of Quadrature Capital. Photograph: logorman/Mola/RBKC

blocks.text: Even the traditional bastions of old British money are adapting. According to Shona Baijal, the managing director of wealth at Coutts, the private bank long associated with the British aristocracy, the tech and AI sectors are increasingly a source of new clients. One of the key challenges, she says, is helping young entrepreneurs who are coming into vast amounts of wealth very quickly.

“A lot of people feel overwhelmed,” she says. “We have to discuss the emotional aspects of what it means to come into wealth. We might say: you’ve come into the money, but do not rush to do anything.”
Coutts found last month that eight out of 10 properties in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods – such as Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge – now sell below asking price.
But sellers and property agents hoping the AI industry may ride to London’s rescue face a glaring problem: much of these new AI fortunes remains on paper.

blocks.caption: Tech and AI multimillionaires are very clear on what they want, says a super-prime estate agent: ‘Location and quality matter most.’  Photograph: Fenton Whelan

blocks.text: At founder level, many are “paper rich, cash poor”, Baijal says – meaning until they sell their businesses or their shares vest, their wealth is largely theoretical.

At the same time, Britain’s wider economy is growing more reliant on the sector’s momentum. Last week, official figures showed that the UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, its fastest expansion in two and a half years, almost entirely due to strong and widespread growth in services, led by the IT sector. Separate analysis by Bloomberg found that roughly a quarter of UK economic growth this year had been powered by AI.

That dependence makes the prospect of an AI bubble bursting all the more dangerous. There have been months of warnings over the valuations of AI companies, and there has been a groundswell of public opposition to datacentre construction and worries around AI safety.

Investors were reminded again of the fragility of the AI trade last week after a scandal involving extramarital affairs and an alleged Chinese spy sent shares in one of the most valuable AI companies in the US, the chip designer Nvidia, tumbling.

Other market indicators have been flashing warning lights. This year one popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE, or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings, ratio – rose to its highest level since 2000, showing that the US stock market was unusually highly valued compared with its profits. That was before the Anthropic’s blockbuster debut.

For now, the AI boom’s physical footprint is unmistakable. In San Francisco, the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 a month, up more than 25% from last year and nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.

Meanwhile in London, the transformation of King’s Cross from a railway goods yard once notorious for criminal activity into an international hub for tech and AI is well under way. Whether this new class of wealth is permanent, or a temporary flash in a historic tech bubble, is yet to be seen.

articles.title: Popular websites subverted in bid to steal crypto, target iPhone users
articles.summary: Malicious JavaScript was aimed at visitors to the websites of 178 organizations across various sectors through Optimizely, a website optimization platform, according to researcher Scott Helme

blocks.text: Malicious JavaScript was aimed at visitors to the websites of 178 organizations across various sectors through Optimizely, a website optimization platform, according to researcher Scott Helme

Some of the world’s most visited websites, including those belonging to Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce, and IKEA, were subverted in an effort to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones, a security researcher said on Monday, November 16.
Malicious JavaScript was aimed at visitors to the websites of 178 organizations across various sectors through Optimizely, a website optimization platform, according to researcher Scott Helme.

The scripts attempted to replace cryptocurrency payment addresses with the attacker’s wallet, skim card numbers as users entered credit card details, steal cookies and screenshots, and plant exploit code on iOS devices.
Cybersecurity firm HudsonRock also said it had found evidence that the sites had served malicious code to their visitors.
Reuters could not immediately ascertain whether the code was successfully used in each case, or the extent of any resulting hacks.
Salesforce said it was investigating unauthorized Optimizely script changes, and had disabled them as a precaution.
Equifax also investigated the issue and ceased using Optimizely. The company said it did not find evidence of any compromise to its systems.
Optimizely, Apple, Zoom, HSBC, CNN and IKEA did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Former Vatican envoy to the Philippines passes away
articles.summary: Former apostolic nuncio to the Philippines Archbishop Antonio Franco has died on November 15, 2026, CBCP News reported.

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 2:51pm
Former apostolic nuncio to the Philippines Archbishop Antonio Franco has died on November 15, 2026, CBCP News reported.
Franco was the diplomatic representative of the Vatican to the Philippines from 1999 to 2006. He was 89.
The announcement was made by Bishop Giuseppe Mazzafaro of Cerreto Sannita-Telese-Sant’Agata de’ Goti, who also expressed his condolences to the family and those who shared his priestly ministry.
CBCP News reported that Franco died at Rummo Hospital in Benevento, where he had been admitted a few days earlier.
The Italian diplomat spent seven years in the Philippines, from 1999 to 2006, before he was assigned to the Middle East.

"His tenure coincided with the 2001 EDSA II People Power uprising and the reorganization of the Archdiocese of Manila, which resulted in the creation of new dioceses in the capital region," the report stated.

Franco was born in Puglianello, Italy, on March 24, 1937 and was ordained a priest for the Diocese of Cerreto Sannita-Telese-Sant’Agata de’ Goti on July 10, 1960 and entered the Vatican diplomatic service in 1972 and served in Bolivia, Iran and France, and at the Holy See’s permanent mission to the United Nations in New York.

Franco was the first Vatican representative to the country following its independence from the Soviet Union. He was also apostolic nuncio to Israel and Cyprus and apostolic delegate to Jerusalem and Palestine.
Franco retired from diplomatic service in August 2012.

CBCP News also reported that Franco’s remains arrived Nov. 16 at the Parish of St. James the Apostle in Puglianello, where a wake held. A funeral Mass is scheduled for Tuesday at the Church of St. Alphonsus Maria de’ Liguori in Telese Terme. — BAP, GMA News
