articles.title: ‘Disgusted by it’: body of Melbourne Cup race horse found dumped in Sydney skip bin
articles.summary:
So You Are placed eighth in race just two weeks ago and was put down after a severe bout of colic

The body of a horse that placed eighth in the Melbourne Cup two weeks ago and recently fell…

blocks.text: The body of a horse that placed eighth in the Melbourne Cup two weeks ago and recently fell ill has been found dumped in skip bin in Sydney.
The horse So You Are, a five year old Gelding, was put down after it suffered from a severe bout from colic and was taken to hospital on Monday for surgery.
The same day, Gregg Jowett posted to his personal social media account a video that showed a dead horse inside skip bin in Sydney.
“I’m at the tip. It’s a fucking horse. They tipped a horse in the fucking bin at the tip,” he can be heard saying in the video.
“[I’m] quite shocked about that; that’s not normal. Please let me know if I’m wrong, but that’s not normal.”
Jowett later told Guardian Australia he didn’t know when he found the horse that it was So You Are, or a horse that had competed in the Melbourne Cup.
“I’m just disgusted by it,” he said.
The horse’s trainer, Bjorn Baker, said the handling of So You Are’s remains had compounded an already devastating loss.
“Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the apparent handling of So You Are’s remains,” he said in a statement.
“He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death.”
“I understand the hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances, and I expect a full explanation of what occurred.”
“My thoughts remain with [So You are breeders] the Ramsey family, and with all my staff, for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss.”
More to come …

articles.title: Hundreds arrested in anti-Trump protests in Philippines amid anger over Iran war and AI pact
articles.summary: Organisers say up to 10,000 people could join the next round of demonstrations ahead of the US president’s arrival in Manila for the Asean summit

blocks.text: Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as authorities braced for more protests ahead of the US president’s arrival in the city for a leaders’ summit.

Organisers claim as many as 10,000 people will join protests against Trump in the Philippine capital on Tuesday, when he will attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds are expected to try to walk to the summit site.
Authorities have arrested nearly 300 people in widespread protests in held in the days leading up to the summit, with large parts of the capital closed off and tight security in place.

Some burned effigies of Trump and faced off with police officers armed with batons and shields. Slogans on placards called the American leader the world’s “number one terrorist” in protests held on Monday.

Demonstrators angry at the cost-of-living and energy shock caused by the Iran war, and the new US-led Pax Silica initiative on AI and critical minerals, tried to reach the summit at the Philippine International Convention Center on Monday, but were blocked by police.

Pax Silica has sparked tensions in the Philippines over plans to build a tech hub outside Manila that critics say will affect water and energy supplies, and displace members of the Ayta Indigenous community.
Large sections of central Manila were closed to the public as part of the security cordon, and public holidays instituted for the Asean summit.

Trump will meet with the leaders of Australia, Japan and India on Tuesday night before heading to Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. There he will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and hold trilateral talks with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.

The backlash against Trump follows the ouster of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, and allegations members of the US administration, including the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, knew about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump’s delegation was expected to include businessman Elon Musk.

Protest leader Renato Reyes blamed the arrests in Manila on the heavy handed response of the government on the president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr., calling Monday the largest single day of police arrests since Marcos came to office in 2022.
“It is really crazy that the Philippine government is rolling out the red carpet for someone who has been so flatly rejected by the American people,” Reyes said.
“Trump started a war that devastated the global economy and pushed oil prices in the Philippines to historic highs. It has caused untold suffering on the Filipino people.
“So yes, Trump will have to pay for his crimes and he will have to be answerable, not just to the American people, but to the people of the world.”

blocks.caption: Indigenous communities and other groups protest in Manila on Monday.  Photograph: Nathaniel Soriano/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The Philippine national police said some officers were injured during confrontations with demonstrators opposed to the summit, including when objects were allegedly thrown at officers.
Pax Silica will include a technology hub planned at New Clark City in Tarlac, about 120km from Manila.

Intended to bolster western stocks of AI technology and reduce “excessive dependencies” on single source supply chains, including from China, Pax Silica will provide chips and critical minerals to 25 participating signatory governments.
Amnesty Philippines said demonstrations should not be forcibly or violently dispersed.
“Reports of arrests during the protests demand immediate scrutiny,” director Ritz Lee Santos III said.
“Authorities must explain the specific grounds for each arrest and any continued detention. Anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights must be released immediately.”

The initiative aims to strengthen government-to-government and industry-academia collaborations under the following pillars:

articles.title: Malacañang calls for probe into alleged coercion of VP Sara Duterte's ex-staff
articles.summary: Malacañang said Tuesday authorities should investigate the claims of the camp of Vice President Sara Duterte that her former household help was allegedly coerced to sign a document.

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 2:29pm
Malacañang said Tuesday authorities should investigate the claims of the camp of Vice President Sara Duterte that her former household help was allegedly coerced to sign a document.
“Ang pag-iimbestiga sa nasabing kwento kung may katotohanan ay nararapat lamang,” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said in a statement.
(It’s only fitting to investigate the claims to determine if there is any truth to it.)

Atty. Paolo Panelo, spokesperson for Duterte, said that the Vice President received a message "from what appeared to be the account of a former household staff member" at 11:19 pm on Monday, November 16.
He said the message contained “a desperate plea for help and rescue” in Manila.

“The sender claimed to be in the custody or under the control of certain individuals who allegedly told them about a threat to their life. The former staff member further narrated that they were being forced to sign a document, which they had refused to execute,” Panelo said.

He said the Vice President’s camp is deeply concerned that the alleged incident may be part of a supposed “relentless campaign by the Marcos administration, utilizing state institutions like the NBI, against the Vice President.”
Castro, for Malacañang’s part, shrugged off the allegation, saying the President is currently busy with the ASEAN Summit.

“Buhos ang oras ng Pangulo sa pagtatrabaho para sa ikakaunlad ng bansa at sa pagpapatibay ng magandang ugnayan sa mga member states ng ASEAN at mga dialogue partners. Pagpapaayos ng ekonomiya, solusyon sa usaping enerhiya, teknolohiya, agrikultura, at edukasyon ang tinututukan ng ating Pangulo,” she said.

(The President is dedicating his time to the nation’s development and strengthening positive relations with ASEAN member-states and dialogue partners. He is focusing on improving the economy, as well as addressing issues related to energy, technology, agriculture, and education.)
Castro also stressed that Marcos does not resort to doing such tactics.

“Hindi po gawain sa panahon ngayon ang gumawa ng intriga at magplanta ng ebidensya kung saan sanay at hasa ang Duterte administration at ito naman ay inamin noon pa ni dating Pangulong Duterte sa harapan ng media,” she added.

(The administration does not stir up such allegations or plant evidence—tactics in which the Duterte administration is well-versed and highly skilled, as former President Duterte himself previously admitted before the media.) —KG, GMA News

articles.title: US presses UN agency over Taiwan flight restrictions, China hits back
articles.summary: The fight over Taiwan's use of international airspace underscores growing tensions between Washington and Beijing over China's efforts to restrict the island's room to operate internationally, from…

blocks.text: LAI CHING-TE. Taiwan President Lai Ching-te speaks at the annual congress of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party in Taipei, Taiwan, July 19, 2026.
Ann Wang/Reuters

The fight over Taiwan's use of international airspace underscores growing tensions between Washington and Beijing over China's efforts to restrict the island's room to operate internationally, from its participation in global bodies to its diplomatic ties and overseas travel by senior officials

items: The US is urging the UN aviation agency to oppose flight restrictions imposed by Mauritius and Seychelles on Taiwan, reigniting tensions with China over the island's international engagement.
China criticized the US proposal, claiming it misuses the Taiwan issue for political gain and asserting that Taiwan is an integral part of China.
Taiwan's government expressed gratitude to the US and allies for their support, emphasizing that China's actions threaten international aviation safety and order.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

The US is asking the UN aviation agency to push back against flight restrictions involving Taiwan, reigniting its long-running dispute with China over Beijing’s efforts to limit the island’s international engagement.

In a paper submitted for the November session of the International Civil Aviation Organization’s governing council, Washington challenged the decision by Mauritius and Seychelles to revoke permission for an aircraft carrying Taiwan President Lai Ching-te to cross portions of international airspace they manage during a planned trip to Africa in April.

The US wants the ICAO Council to reaffirm that countries responsible for managing air traffic over the high seas do not have sovereignty over that airspace and cannot use that role for political purposes. Such actions could “set a dangerous precedent” by encouraging similar disruptions or political pressure on other countries, the paper said.
China hit back at the US proposal, accusing Washington of using the Taiwan issue for political purposes and wasting international resources.

The fight over Taiwan’s use of international airspace underscores growing tensions between Washington and Beijing over China’s efforts to restrict the island’s room to operate internationally, from its participation in global bodies to its diplomatic ties and overseas travel by senior officials.

The US document “selectively and one-sidedly cites” principles including freedom of overflight over the high seas and, “under the pretext of safeguarding freedom of navigation,” smears other countries and presumes sovereign states were at fault, China’s foreign ministry said in a statement to Reuters.

“There is only one China in the world, and Taiwan is an inalienable part of China’s territory,” it added. “China urges the countries concerned to stop using the Taiwan issue for political manipulation.”
Taiwan’s foreign ministry said it thanked the US and other like-minded countries for their previous concern about the issue.

The ministry will continue to work with allied countries to keep explaining to ICAO and the international community that “China’s actions undermine the international civil aviation order and flight safety,” it stated.
The governments of Mauritius and Seychelles did not respond to requests for comment.
Taiwan is not a member of the United Nations or its agencies due to opposition from Beijing, which considers the democratically governed island part of its territory.
Taiwan rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims and says China has no right to represent the island internationally.

Taiwan’s government said Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar revoked permission for Lai’s aircraft to fly through airspace they manage on the way to Eswatini, one of only 12 countries with formal diplomatic ties to Chinese-claimed Taiwan.

Lai said China had used economic “coercion” to secure their cooperation, which Beijing denied. Lai eventually traveled to Eswatini the following month aboard the Eswatini king’s private aircraft, announcing the trip only after arriving.
The US paper, seen by Reuters, focuses on Mauritius and Seychelles and does not mention Madagascar.

According to the paper, Taiwan’s China Airlines had received permits for the charter flight to cross portions of the two countries’ flight information regions, or FIRs, over the high seas. Both countries revoked the permits days before departure without citing safety or operational concerns, it said.

The distinction between sovereign airspace and FIRs is central to the dispute. Countries have sovereignty over airspace above their territory and territorial waters, but the FIRs they manage can extend far beyond those boundaries over international waters.
Countries provide air traffic services in those areas for safety and operational purposes but do not gain sovereignty over them, according to the US paper.

Washington has asked the ICAO Council to express concern over the withdrawn permits and have the agency’s secretary-general seek written explanations from Mauritius and Seychelles. It also wants ICAO to determine whether any remedies are needed to ensure their compliance with international aviation rules.

The State Department expressed concern in April, saying responsibility for managing international airspace beyond a country’s sovereign territory was “solely to ensure aviation safety, not to serve as a political tool for Beijing.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: David Jones: what went wrong and what happens next? Five takeaways from first creditors meeting
articles.summary:
Upmarket retailer, which recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year, has total debt over $400m including $11m owed to staff

  • Get our

blocks.text: Upmarket retailer David Jones owed hundreds of millions of dollars when it collapsed into administration, after accelerating financial losses and reputational damage threatened its ability to stock shelves for Christmas.

About 500 creditors attended its first meeting on Tuesday, where administrators McGrathNicol started to break down who is owed what, when those left out of pocket will know where they stand, and what ultimately went wrong.
Here are five things we learned.
How much is owed?
David Jones collapsed early this month owing in excess of $400m to an assortment of creditors, including $180m of debts to trade creditors, mainly consisting of the brands that stocked its shelves.
There are also outstanding employee entitlements, such as annual and long service leave, worth about $11m, and about $33m in unredeemed gift cards, which the retailer is still accepting.

The rest is owed to large secured creditors, led by the retailer’s main financier, Hilco, which has a controlling hand over the current process and even has its own representatives in the 19 stores marked for closure.
Taken together, the debts are well over $400m, but that total is almost certain to climb as landlords tally up their losses.
On top of unpaid rent up to the appointment of administrators, shopping centre owners will also claim for broken leases after the chain’s receivers moved to close half of its 38-store network.
How much will creditors get back?

What, if any, money suppliers get back hinges on whether a buyer steps in and how much they are willing to pay, or whether the chain ends up liquidated, as well as how much cash David Jones can bring in through the crucial Christmas trading period.
Because product suppliers sit near the bottom of the creditor priority list, they won’t receive any money until secured lenders and employees are paid out.
Given the size of the outstanding debts, and poor financial state of the department chain, many suppliers are bracing for a near total loss of outstanding amounts.
Shaun Fraser, a founding partner at McGrathNicol, told creditors there were “too many variables” to indicate how much, if any, suppliers would receive.
“We haven’t yet got to a point where we’re engaged enough with bidders to have a sense of what value might be there,” Fraser said.
“We haven’t reached a point in the sale process where people are talking value or price.”
How are creditors feeling?
Out of pocket suppliers are particularly frustrated, though the modern practice of holding meetings online kept any real anger contained behind muted microphones.
There were questions over whether there had been preferential treatment to some suppliers, and if the retailer had been trading insolvent before the appointment of administrators.
McGrathNicol said it would investigate when the company might have been insolvent, and if preferential payments were made.
One brand representative said they had also repeatedly asked for stock lists and weekly sales figures without response.
after newsletter promotion
What went wrong?
The administrators provided updated financials at the meeting that showed the poor state of affairs at David Jones.
The 188-year-old retailer recorded a net loss of $228m in 2025-26, before losing a further $69m in the first four months of the new financial year leading up to the administration.
Creditors were told that the funding pressures it was facing, coupled with reputational damage, was affecting its ability to get stock for the Christmas trading period.
David Jones ultimately got tipped into administration when negotiations with its main landlord, Westfield owner Scentre Group, broke down.

The retailer’s private equity owner, Anchorage Capital, wanted to radically reduce store numbers – something that is now happening during receivership – to rid the network of underperforming suburban stores.
The directors of David Jones listed several causes of the retailer’s problems, including everything from cost-of-living pressures and soft luxury demand to fierce online competition.
Fraser said there was also “clearly a business model problem” with the retailer.
What happens next?

Under a dual appointment, receivers FTI Consulting have taken day-to-day control of the business while administrators McGrathNicol hunt for a buyer, having called for “non-binding indicative offers” for the retailer by the end of the month.

That will trigger a process that could see formal bids lodged either late this year or early in 2027, giving some clarity to employees and suppliers ahead of the next creditors’ meeting, due by March.
The road ahead is, however, complicated by the breakdown in relations between Anchorage and the Westfield owner, which is threatening the retailer’s ability to operate at any of its complexes.

The Scentre Group chief executive, Elliott Rusanow, told Guardian Australia the landlord now had a “unique opportunity to facilitate the entry and growth of businesses that are more relevant to customers today and into the future”.
“That is the opportunity we will pursue at each of the 17 destinations with a David Jones store,” Rusanow said.

articles.title: Aboriginal mother allegedly kicked off a bus in regional NSW because her baby was crying
articles.summary:
The NSW transport department says passenger safety is its ‘highest priority’ and the driver is no longer employed by the operator

  • Get our

blocks.text: Transport for NSW is investigating allegations that a young Aboriginal mother and her family were told to leave a bus and left by the side of a regional highway because her 22-month-old child was crying.

Wiradjuri woman Kaneesha Lee Williams was travelling home from Sydney to the Riverina town of Darlington Point, 155km west of Wagga Wagga, with her young daughter, Audria, and her mother, Tamara, on Sunday.
They had been in Sydney for a family birthday and had caught the train from Sydney to Wagga Wagga, before transferring to a regional bus operated by NSW TrainLink, with tickets to Hay.
But about 15 minutes into the journey, on Coolamon Road, Williams alleges, the driver pulled over and told her and her family to disembark because her daughter was crying.
“We got on the road and my daughter Audria started getting a little bit restless so I sat her on my lap and put her to sleep because she was crying and stuff,” Williams said.
She said her daughter had just begun to settle when the driver pulled over.
“I thought, ‘why did we stop for?’ I didn’t think he was coming up to me. Then he walked up to me and he said, ‘I can’t drive this bus while that baby is crying, you’re gonna have to get off’.
“I just looked at him and I looked at my daughter and my eyes started swelling up into tears.”
She said the driver gave her no warning. “We weren’t aggressive or anything, we were more in shock … Are you really gonna kick a little baby off the bus for crying?

“She’s 22 months old, she’s overtired, overstimulated and doesn’t want to be on the bus … We had little food, no water. He didn’t even ask if we were able to get a lift or anything, he just kicked us straight off.”

Williams said they were deposited on the side of the road with low phone battery and no alternative transport arrangements. The driver did not offer to make alternative arrangements or ask if they had anyone to pick them up, she alleges. They eventually found somewhere to charge their phones to contact family, who drove more than two hours to pick them up.

Teenager Alexis Longdon, who was sitting three seats back on the opposite side of the aisle, told Guardian Australia she saw Williams and her family being asked to get off the bus, and was confused when they then left without them.

“We were just outside of Wagga and the bus driver stopped the bus and said: ‘can you get off the bus and calm her down please’, because apparently it was creating an unsafe environment for the driver,” the 14-year-old said. “And then she got off the bus and I guess she couldn’t calm her baby down, we waited five minutes maybe and then he got on the bus and left.

Williams then wrote a formal complaint to the NSW transport minister demanding an independent investigation into the incident, including an examination of all relevant CCTV, and asking whether the driver’s actions complied with TrainLink and the transport department’s policies and standards.
The letter, seen by Guardian Australia, also asked whether this would have happened to a non-Aboriginal family.
after newsletter promotion

On Tuesday, the NSW minister for regional transport, Jenny Aitchison, said her office had reached out to Williams to offer support and that the “alleged behaviour of this driver was completely unacceptable”.

“It’s extremely disappointing that a mother and her young child were treated so poorly on a service that they had every right to use,” Aitchison said in a statement to Guardian Australia. “It’s not the service we accept from our bus drivers.
“I hope to speak to the family soon and reiterate my concern about this incident and apologise for what happened to them.
“I’m advised the bus driver is no longer employed by the coach operator.”
A Transport for NSW spokesperson said the incident was being investigated.

“Transport for NSW is aware of an incident involving passengers travelling on a NSW TrainLink coach service operated by Dyson between Wagga Wagga and Mildura on Sunday,” they said in a statement. “Transport for NSW takes the concerns raised extremely seriously.
“The operator is investigating the incident and Transport for NSW has requested updates as those enquiries progress.
“Passenger safety is our highest priority and we expect all operators and their employees to uphold the highest standards of safety and professionalism when interacting with passengers.”
Dyson was contacted for comment.

articles.summary: The quote card attributes a call for mass action to lawyer Sheila Sison, Vice President Sara Duterte's lead counsel, but she did not make such a statement, contrary to the claim

blocks.text: Claim: Lawyer Sheila Sison, lead defense counsel in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, called for “People Power” during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit to expose corruption and humiliate President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Why we fact-checked this: A video was posted on November 14 by the Facebook page Jay Halago Near, a day before the Philippines began hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit.
Its thumbnail carries a quote attributed to Sison, which says, “People Power sa ASEAN Summit! Para malaman ng mundo ang korapsyon sa Pinas, ipapahiya natin si PBBM!”
(People Power at the ASEAN Summit! So the world will know about corruption in the Philippines, we will humiliate [President Bongbong Marcos]!)
The graphic has a “PH News Update” label and the word “Korapsyon? (Corruption?)” beside a photo of Marcos.

The post’s caption reads: “People Power sa ASEAN Summit? Panawagan laban sa korapsyon, umani ng atensyon! Dapat bang gawing pagkakataon ang ASEAN Summit para iparinig ang hinaing ng taumbayan? Kayo, anong opinyon ninyo?”
(People Power at the ASEAN Summit? A call against corruption draws attention! Should the ASEAN Summit be used to air the people’s grievances? What is your opinion?)
As of writing, the video has 93,000 views, 5,900 reactions, 1,700 comments, and 758 shares.
The facts: No news report or public statement shows Sison urging the public to gather for a “people power” movement during the ASEAN Summit.
Sison is lead defense counsel in Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial, and her recent public remarks concern the case.

On November 10, she raised concerns before the impeachment court over statements that private prosecutors made to the media. On November 12, she asked the court to cancel the November 13 session. None of these accounts mentions the ASEAN Summit or any call for mass action.

Protest amid ASEAN: Protests did take place during the summit, but Sison did not lead them, and they were not a People Power call to humiliate Marcos over government corruption. On November 15, the summit’s opening day, police clashed with activists at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila as they attempted to march toward the summit venue.

Groups under Bagong Alyansang Makabayan and the All Workers Unity coalition were protesting antiworker policies, the arrival of US President Donald Trump, and the proposed Pax Silica hub in New Clark City.

Police said the groups lacked a permit to assemble outside the Freedom Park. Nearly 300 arrests were made in Muntinlupa alone following the protests. (READ: Lawmakers, groups slam November 15 arrests: Where is maximum tolerance?)
The Palace has previously urged protesters not to “tarnish” the country’s reputation during the summit.
The Philippines, ASEAN chair for 2026, is hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from November 15 to 17. (LIVE UPDATES: 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila)

Impeachment trial: Meanwhile, Duterte’s impeachment trial continues. By the end of its 43rd day on November 12, the trial examined two major credit card purchases by the Vice President’s husband, Manases Carpio, in Japan and Malaysia, with witnesses explaining the expenses as shared dining and purchases for basketball players.
Rappler has fact-checked similar claims related to the impeachment trial.

items: FACT CHECK: Marcos not impeached, replaced by Sara Duterte
FACT CHECK: No new SC decision stopping VP Sara’s impeachment trial
FACT CHECK: No SC order dismissing ongoing impeachment proceedings vs VP Sara

blocks.text: – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: European-made pesticides named in 1,605 poisoning reports in Brazil last year
articles.summary:
About a third of cases involved chemicals banned for use on EU farms, according to investigation by Unearthed and Public Eye

Pesticides sold by European chemical companies were named in…

blocks.text: Pesticides sold by European chemical companies were named in more than 1,600 poisoning reports in Brazil last year, an investigation has found.

About a third of the cases involved chemicals banned from use on farms in the EU because of the risks they pose to people and the environment. But European companies are not banned from manufacturing these chemicals, as long as they export them overseas to countries where they are legally allowed to be used.

Analysis of Brazilian health ministry data by Unearthed and Public Eye in a report published on Tuesday found that of 2,857 poisoning reports that named an identifiable agricultural product, 1,605 named brands sold by European pesticide companies.

Farm workers in Brazil have described their flesh rotting, skin burning, difficulty breathing and vomiting after using the chemicals at work, according to the report. A small number have died accidentally or killed themselves by drinking the pesticides.

Under Brazilian law, reports must be submitted by healthcare professionals to Brazil’s national disease notification system in all suspected pesticide poisoning cases. These reports can be marked “confirmed” poisoning or “exposure” only by the doctor or nurse who saw the patient.

blocks.caption: A worker in protective gear rinses gloves under water near a pesticide warning sign in Brazil. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: Clinicians sometimes record cases as exposure when they lack the training or support to confirm a diagnosis, but are presented with a patient who says they have been exposed to pesticides or present symptoms of pesticide poisoning. Laboratory confirmation is rare, so recording a diagnosis of “confirmed” poisoning usually depends on clinical judgment.
Experts say clinicians can be reluctant to confirm cases because of a lack of training or support. A brand being named in a poisoning report is not proof that it caused poisoning or death.

“The insufficient training of healthcare professionals to recognise and manage these cases is a major limiting factor,” said Vanda Garibotti, a public health biologist at the State Centre for Health Surveillance in Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil.
High staff turnover and a lack of institutional support meant poisoning cases were rarely confirmed through laboratory tests and often relied on clinical judgment, Garibotti added.

In more than 6,700 medical reports involving agricultural pesticides last year, 2,857 named an identifiable product. Of those, 1,420 were classified as confirmed poisonings. A further 1,108 were classified as exposures; for the remainder the classification was unknown or other diagnoses.

Some of the products are made in Britain. Reglone is the most frequently cited UK-made weedkiller. It contains diquat, a chemical that was banned in the UK in 2020 after experts concluded it posed a high risk to people living near fields where it was sprayed. Diquat is also found in other pesticides.

Despite the usage ban, Reglone is still manufactured by the Swiss-headquartered pesticides company Syngenta at its factory in Huddersfield for export to countries with more permissive regulations, including Brazil.

blocks.caption: A mass is held in honour of Nelson Castoldi in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: Nelson Castoldi died last year after accidentally ingesting Reglone on his family farm in Rio Grande do Sul. To save money, his family had bought the weedkiller in bulk, decanting a single litre into an empty cola bottle to avoid hauling a heavy 20-litre canister into the fields.

Working under the scorching sun, Castoldi mistook the black chemical for a soft drink and took a sip. Though he spat it out immediately, the chemical caused his kidneys to fail before attacking his lungs. He died two days later.

“We fell apart,” Ivan Castoldi said of his father’s death. “Four months after our father passed away, our mother also passed away. She cried day and night. She became depressive and had a stroke. She was left alone.
“That poison, Reglone, should be banned in Brazil,” he added. “Not because of what happened to us, but because of its toxicity.”
The Brazilian health ministry recorded 75 cases involving diquat last year, compared with 36 over the five years from 2018 to 2022.

The investigation found Reglone was specifically named in 44 reports, including four deaths. Of those cases, 26 were classified as confirmed poisonings and the rest were classified as exposure, unknown, or adverse reaction.
Dormex, a pesticide manufactured in Germany by Alzchem and distributed in Brazil by the German chemical company BASF, is another product workers said injured them or made them ill.

blocks.caption: Sidnei Souza de Oliveira, 49, suffered a severe injury after a jug of Dormex spilled on his leg while he was filling a sprayer. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: Sidnei Souza de Oliveira, 49, suffered a severe injury after a jug of Dormex spilled on his leg while he was filling a sprayer. The handle broke as he was transferring the chemical into the tank. At first, his leg turned red, and he continued spraying.

He carried on working for four days before going to hospital. “After 15 days, my leg was black. Chunks of flesh were falling off,” Oliveira said. A doctor said the injury was serious and had to remove dead tissue to stop it spreading towards the bone.

Oliveira said the protective trousers supplied by his employer were thin and allowed the chemical to seep through. He said he had been afraid of losing his job if he stayed away from work for too long.

Dormex contains cyanamide, which was banned from use in the EU in 2008 because of concerns about its effects on human health, particularly among farm workers spraying the chemical. Analysis shows the Brazilian health ministry database recorded 17 confirmed poisonings involving Dormex last year.

Finale, a BASF product identified in the investigation, contains glufosinate, which was banned in the EU in 2018. Roundup – a glyphosate-based weedkiller manufactured by the German chemical company Bayer – was frequently cited in Brazilian poisoning reports, including 12 deaths.

Across all the poisoning reports identified by the investigation as involving products sold by European companies, there were 32 reported deaths. Of these cases, 31 were classified as confirmed poisonings, and 26 were recorded as suicides.

Syngenta products were cited 425 times in the poisoning reports, and BASF 179 times. The company figures are not mutually exclusive: some poisoning reports named products sold by more than one manufacturer.
Nina Schrank, a senior campaigner at Greenpeace UK, said the findings were a “deadly double standard”.

“If a pesticide is too dangerous to use in Britain, it should be too dangerous to export. Ministers must stop allowing Britain to be part of a production line for toxic chemicals that are putting lives at risk overseas.”

blocks.caption: Empty pesticide containers in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: The EU’s pesticide approval system requires chemicals to meet strict standards for human and animal health and the environment. Diquat has been banned on EU and UK farms since 2019 and 2020 respectively, after experts concluded it posed a high risk to workers, people living nearby and birds. Cyanamide was withdrawn after an assessment found exposure among agricultural operators could exceed safe levels. Glufosinate, meanwhile, is classified in the EU as toxic to reproduction, meaning it can harm fertility or the development of unborn children.

Suicide prevention is also a factor. A 2020 study found national bans on highly hazardous pesticides could be a cost-effective intervention for reducing the number of people who kill themselves in countries with a high burden of suicides attributable to pesticides.

A Syngenta spokesperson said almost half the Brazilian cases attributed to the company were not classified as confirmed poisonings, adding: “Public Eye and Unearthed are aware of this but have explicitly chosen to disregard the dataset’s final classification.” The company accused the investigation of disregarding the dataset’s final classifications and identified “numerous other inconsistencies” that it said raised “serious concerns” that the evidence was “being selectively interpreted to support a predetermined conclusion”.
“There are real people behind these statistics. Every genuine case of poisoning matters, and every family affected deserves our concern,” the spokesperson added.

Syngenta said Brazil had its own “robust regulatory system” and that products banned in Europe could still be independently assessed and legally registered in the country, citing differences in crops, growing conditions and pest pressures. It said it trained 95,000 people in Brazil in the safe use of its products in 2025, including through free online courses.

blocks.caption: Pesticide are sprayed in an apple orchard in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: Bayer said its products were safe when used according to label instructions, citing what it described as rigorous testing and assessments by global health authorities. The company said it took pesticide poisoning seriously but questioned the reliability of the data, arguing that products and circumstances of exposure had not been independently verified, some chemicals may have been incorrectly identified and symptoms such as headaches and skin irritation could have other causes.
It said “Roundup” was “widely used as a generic term” that could refer to weedkillers made by other manufacturers or counterfeit products.

The company said it provided training on the safe handling and use of pesticides, including protective equipment, and that its programmes reached more than 4 million people globally in 2025. It also argued that a pesticide being banned in the EU did not necessarily mean it was unsafe, saying other countries had robust regulatory systems that took account of local agricultural conditions.

It added: “While the data presented helps to provide information on broad trends of exposure, the data has limitations and warrants caution when drawing conclusions, particularly when looking at individual cases.”
BASF said it was deeply concerned by reports of poisoning that might be linked to its products, adding that it took all such incidents seriously.

A spokesperson said publicly available information suggested some incidents might have involved the intentional ingestion of crop protection products, describing such acts as “deliberate misuse” of products intended exclusively for agricultural use.

BASF said it had global and local procedures to assess and investigate incidents potentially involving its products, and worked with authorities and experts where appropriate to understand cases and identify ways to prevent similar incidents. It said it invested in education and training to promote the safe handling and use of its products, with initiatives in Brazil reaching more than 14,475 participants in 2025.
The company said it was confident in the safety of its products when used in accordance with label instructions and applicable regulatory standards.

It added that Brazilian law required crop protection products to be handled and applied only by authorised and properly trained individuals, and said it took its responsibility for ensuring their safe use seriously.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
articles.summary: Efforts to recover bodies after a “double-tap” attack in southern Ukraine are being hampered by continuing Russian strikes, officials say.

blocks.text: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images
ByMerlyn Thomas BBC Verify correspondent and Paul BrownBBC Verify
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.

Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.
Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there have been multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.
The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged.
"Due to the threat of repeated shelling, emergency workers are constantly forced to periodically suspend work and retreat to a safe place," it added.
The DSNS said the death toll had risen to at least 72 people making it one of the deadliest single incidents since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Emergency service vehicles have also been targeted

blocks.text: Image source, DSNS
Emergency service vehicles have also been targeted

Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".

He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.

BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.

blocks.caption: Emergency services workers leave a rubble filled area in Ukraine

blocks.text: Bodies are still to be recovered from the rubble, Oleksiy said. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead."
BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.

blocks.caption: Map of southern and eastern Ukraine showing areas under Russian military control and the location of Komyshuvakha, a village on the southern front line in Zaporizhzhia region. Russian-controlled territory is shaded pink, with limited Russian control shown by red hatching and claimed Russian contr…

blocks.text: A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.

While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.
Fears of second strike heard on police radios

Local people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.
Video shows moments between deadly Russian attacks on village in Ukraine
Bodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.
Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.

blocks.caption: Satellite image showing the site of the Komyshuvakha attack in Ukraine. White annotations highlight a large rectangular compound and surrounding buildings. A white dot marks the reported impact point inside the compound, while brackets indicate access points on the western side of the site. Two n…

blocks.text: The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.
Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.

Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.

blocks.caption: The crater was identified by experts as consistent with a 3,000kg bomb

blocks.text: Image source, Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Trevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures.
His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The remnants of the wing from a glide bomb guidance kit

blocks.text: Image source, SBU
The remnants of the wing from a glide bomb guidance kit

Ball and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.
International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.

Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".

Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.
Additional reporting by Margaryta Maliukova, BBC Monitoring

articles.title: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says
articles.summary: The reported strikes come a day after Ukraine launched its largest recorded drone attack on Russia since the start of the war, according to Moscow.

blocks.text: Two major bridges in the Ukrainian capital have reportedly been struck in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The missiles hit Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges spanning the Dnipro River, Klitschko said, adding that water and power supplies had been disrupted.
Meanwhile, Ukraine struck the landmark Kerch Bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea killing two people, the region's Moscow-installed governor said.

President Volodymyr Zelensky had earlier warned that Moscow might launch further strikes on the country on Monday night, after Ukrainian, US and European officials held further talks aimed at ending the years-long conflict.
Those online talks, attended by US envoy Jared Kushner and US special envoy Steve Witkoff, came after Russia said it recorded the largest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began.
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems".
"Some areas are experiencing disruptions to water and heating supplies", he added.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services have been damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Residents of Kyiv typically shelter in the city's underground stations during air raids.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv. An estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Several of the capital's major bridges were also targeted by Russian drone strikes in October.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials.
Separately, the Ukrainian military struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea for a second consecutive day, the region's Moscow-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov said on Telegram.
Traffic across the bridge had been suspended, he added.
The landmark bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014.

Russian President Vladimir Putin inaugurated the bridge to great fanfare in 2018. The severity of the latest strike on Kerch Bridge is still unclear, though it is protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.

Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said.
The latest round of tit-for-tat strikes came after US, Ukrainian and European officials held talks on ways to facilitate "direct engagement" between Russia and Europe to end the war.

Following Monday's meeting, US envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, said the US was committed to providing Ukraine with a "strong, credible security guarantees", as well as a path towards EU membership.
He added that Nato "will remain a critical pillar of European security", and that preparations are underway for a further multilateral meeting "in the near future".
In an address on Monday evening, Zelensky said that the meeting was "difficult", adding that more needed to be done to support Ukraine's defence against Russian ballistic missile strikes.

Zelensky said that Europe was represented for the first time by the full delegation that will participate in negotiations with Moscow - including the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, the EU and Nato.
The Ukrainian president has long called for European delegates to be included in any peace talks, which he argues is necessary because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
He also said that Moscow is receiving "dozens of missiles per month" from North Korea.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials said that the final death toll from a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian village of Kamyshuvakha earlier this month had reached 72.
Four people are still considered missing after the bombing, which Ukrainian officials say is one of the deadliest individual attacks since the start of the war in 2022.

Footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, showed residents going to an underground shelter after the initial attack on 2 November. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit.
Ukrainian police said of those killed were police officers, "staff of the gymnasium, utility workers and medical personnel".

Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title: Mongolian President Khurelsukh to resign amid corruption allegations
articles.summary: Khurelsukh has said he will step down over accusations that he profited from a government railway project, but said he had been "falsely accused."

image.caption: Khurelsukh Ukhnaa belongs to the center-left Mongolian People's Party [FILE: October 22, 2026]Image: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa said Tuesday that he would resign after the opposition Democratic Party accused him of profiting from a government railway project.
At a press conference, Khurelsukh said he was being "falsely accused and defamed" but would resign in order to "restore my good name."
He has pledged to cooperate with investigators.
Before the resignation takes effect, it must first be accepted by parliament, the State Great Khural.
Khurelsukh, from the Mongolian People's Party, has been president since 2021.
But infighting has caused disruption in the party, with three prime ministers taking office in just nine months.
Khurelsukh paid a state visit to Germany from October 19 to 22 this year.

articles.title: [Ask the Tax Whiz] As PH growth slumps, what will Marcos’ economic reshuffle do?
articles.summary: The question is how the Marcos administration will demonstrate that the leadership changes in BIR, Customs, BCDA, and PEZA actually improve economic performance

blocks.text: With foreign direct investment falling 19.2% and ASEAN leaders gathering in Manila, the reshuffle of key economic agencies raises a timely question: Will new leadership strengthen reforms and investor confidence—or disrupt progress when the economy can least afford it?
Global investors are not surprised when governments change agency heads. They worry when the rules, services, and reforms they depend on change with them.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has every right to reshuffle his economic team. New appointments may bring fresh ideas. But presidential prerogative answers who has the authority—not what economic problem the reshuffle is meant to solve.
And the timing deserves explanation.

Philippine growth slowed to 2.1% in the third quarter, its weakest non-pandemic pace since 2009. Net foreign direct investment fell 19.2% to $4.77 billion in January–August. Meanwhile, Manila is hosting ASEAN leaders, presenting the Philippines as a destination for global capital.
If there is a moment to demonstrate regulatory stability, this is it.

Under Director General Tereso “Theo” Panga, the Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA) approved a record ₱315.5 billion in investments by November 10; January–October approvals rose 76.6%. Under Joshua Bingcang, the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) recorded ₱145.46 billion in approved investments in the first nine months, up 142.5%.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] Clark’s billions demand public accounting

blocks.text: Approvals are commitments, not realized FDI. Still, they are investment pipelines worth converting into factories, exports, and jobs.

Having joined Panga on investment missions across Asia, Europe, and Australia, I witnessed his reform-driven leadership firsthand. PEZA’s one-stop-shop services and signature red-carpet treatment extend beyond registration, supporting locators through regulatory compliance and investor aftercare while addressing VAT refunds, unpredictable tax audits, and costly delays.
That is how investor confidence is earned—one problem resolved at a time.
Our proposal to modernize PEZA’s charter would institutionalize these services through integrated digital permits, enforceable processing deadlines, and effective investor grievance resolution.
Investment promotion attracts capital. Investor aftercare keeps it.
So why move Bingcang to PEZA and Panga to the Toll Regulatory Board? Was an exchange between PEZA and BCDA considered? What measurable improvements would justify the chosen arrangement?
At Customs, Ariel Nepomuceno’s bureau collected ₱853.66 billion in January–October, ₱7.14 billion above target. During his tenure, it reported ₱50.93 billion in seizures of illicit goods.

blocks.caption: Customs chief takes BCDA helm amid controversial Pax Silica

blocks.text: Seizures are not recovered revenues, nor do collection figures prove corruption has disappeared. But these results deserve evaluation alongside ongoing modernization reforms.

I joined Nepomuceno at the Ease of Doing Business Economic Briefing, International IT-BPM Summit, and industry dialogues. I witnessed how he addressed complaints about bureaucratic delays, corruption risks, and cross-border compliance costs. He acknowledged institutional shortcomings while consistently pursuing practical improvements through digitalization, transparency, and stakeholder engagement.
When I proposed an independent, digitally integrated National Revenue Authority combining BIR and Customs, he welcomed constructive dialogue.

Such reform could integrate revenue intelligence, institutionalize AI-assisted risk-based enforcement, strengthen anti-smuggling efforts, and protect compliant taxpayers from unnecessary costs and arbitrary audits.

Why reassign Nepomuceno to BCDA while moving BIR Commissioner Charlito Mendoza to Customs when both revenue agencies were implementing modernization programs? How will their successors preserve institutional progress?
New BIR Commissioner Rolando Ligon Jr. faces equally consequential questions.
Will BIR pursue unexplained wealth involving politically exposed persons, including politicians and political dynasties, where evidence warrants investigation?

Will it clarify the collection status of the longstanding Marcos estate-tax assessment, including available legal remedies and disputed prescription issues? (READ: [ANALYSIS] The estate tax liability of the Marcos Estate)
Tax enforcement should never depend on a taxpayer’s surname, wealth, or political connections.
Malacañang assures the public that reforms will continue. I welcome that assurance.

But Finance Secretary Frederick Go and Trade Secretary Cristina Roque should go further: explain the reshuffle’s strategic rationale and establish measurable targets for investment realization, customs clearance, VAT refunds, revenue integrity, and taxpayer services.
With global minimum tax rules reshaping investment incentives, efficient administration matters even more.
I am not suggesting that performing officials must remain indefinitely—or that their successors cannot deliver better results.
The question is how the administration will demonstrate that these leadership changes actually improve economic performance.
If officials serve at the President’s pleasure, economic policy must still serve the public interest.

Ultimately, the world will judge the Philippines not by who occupies government offices, but by whether doing business becomes easier, taxes are collected fairly, and investment commitments become real jobs. – Rappler.com

Mon Abrea, CPA, MBA, MPA (Harvard) is a global tax policy expert and Chief Tax Advisor of Asian Consulting Group (ACGlobal), an international tax and investment advisory firm. He advises governments, multinational enterprises, and international organizations on tax policy, investment competitiveness, and fiscal reform. He is the author of Reimagining the World Without Corruption and Why Invest in the Philippines? CREATE MORE Edition, and has represented the Philippines in policy dialogues at the OECD, World Bank, and other international forums.

articles.title: Protests to greet Trump in Manila over Pax Silica
articles.summary: The protesters are opposing the US-led initiative that seeks to secure supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors through partnerships with other countries

blocks.text: PROTEST. Militants gather at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila on November 15, 2026, to protest the proposed Pax Silica initiative and US President Donald Trump’s visit to the 49th ASEAN Summit.
Rappler
The protesters are opposing the US-led initiative that seeks to secure supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors through partnerships with other countries
MANILA, Philippines – US President Donald Trump’s arrival in Manila on Tuesday, November 17, is expected to draw protests, with activists preparing to march against the US-led Pax Silica.

Protesters have been holding a campout at Liwasang Bonifacio since Sunday, November 15. They plan to march to the Philippine International Convention Center, the venue of the ASEAN-US Special Summit which Trump will attend, ahead of the US leader’s arrival.
The protesters are opposing Pax Silica, a US-led initiative that seeks to secure supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors through partnerships with other countries.
Trump is expected to arrive in the Philippines at 5:30 pm. He will conduct a state visit before leaving the country on Wednesday, November 18.
On Wednesday, when Trump will be in Malacañang for activities related to his state visit, protesters are expected to converge in Liwasang Bonifacio and march to Mendiola, near Malacañang.
Roads leading to Ayala Bridge and Recto Avenue toward Mendiola Peace Arch are closed to both motorists and pedestrians. Fences and barriers have been installed around the area.
Activists have warned that Pax Silica could put indigenous communities and farming areas at risk, particularly amid growing demand for minerals used in advanced technologies.
The Philippine National Police has deployed around 20,000 personnel across summit venues and nearby areas.

Security forces faced protesters on the summit’s opening day on Sunday, when police arrested around 300 people in Manila and Muntinlupa. The arrests drew condemnation from lawmakers and various groups. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Woman whose baby died after free birth didn’t know she was pregnant with twins, NSW inquest hears
articles.summary:
Inquest continues into deaths of four babies born in free births or home births in northern rivers

  • Get our

blocks.text: A northern rivers mother whose baby died after a free birth did not know she was having twins until she was in labour after having no pregnancy scans, the New South Wales coroner’s court has heard.

The inquest will examine the deaths of four babies born in free births or home births who died in the northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024. It will consider whether the care was reasonable in the circumstances and whether care by an unregistered support worker was reasonable and appropriate before, during and after the birth. Free births are when a person gives birth without a registered health professional present.

Both of the twins died – one was stillborn and most likely died in the womb before he was born, and one died after the birth, the inquest heard. Only Baby D, who was born alive, is included in the inquest – coroner’s courts can not examine the death of a stillborn baby.
The inquest heard on Tuesday that the mother – who cannot be named for legal reasons – had decided to do a “sovereign birth”, where a woman gives birth at home on her own.

The mother had three to four sessions with Sita Tara Kali, a self-described birth keeper, before the birth, according to a statement the mother gave to police that was read to the inquest. She was paid a fee of $4,100, the inquest heard.
Kali, who is expected to give evidence at a later date, was involved in the care of two of the four babies included in the inquest. She is not facing criminal charges.”

The mother said in the police statement that her sessions with Kali before the birth were “mostly bodywork”. She said: “I didn’t get anything much out of the system in terms of birth preparation, a few books. Nothing of the quality she offered me.”

blocks.caption: Self-described birth keeper Sita Tara Kali, also known as Mumma Sita. Photograph: gofundme.com

blocks.text: She said she felt “vibrant” and “healthy” during the pregnancy and the birth was “amazing”.
The mother only realised she was having another baby after giving birth to the first baby.
She said Kali advised them to ring an ambulance immediately, according to the police statement.
Sgt David Greenway told the inquest on Tuesday that when he arrived at the family’s house in 2024, he found one of the newborn twins had died. The other baby was on its way to hospital, he said.
The second twin, referred to as Baby D, did not survive.
Greenway said the parents were in shock and had not known they were expecting twins.
after newsletter promotion
Greenway told the inquest that Kali was present at the house and said to him: “I’m the birth keeper, so I support women that want to free birth.”

“I am not medically trained. And there is a big need because a lot of women don’t want to go to the hospital, and they can’t afford midwives. I’m not doing anything illegal. I know my rights,” Greenway recalled her saying.
“When people are choosing to be in their sovereignty, it is up to them what they choose to do,” Kali said, according to Greenway.

Dr Alison Teate, the president of the Australian College of Midwives, told the inquest on Tuesday if there are two twins and one placenta, they are at a higher risk category than if there are two placentas.
“The level of surveillance goes up significantly. It would be appointments every fortnight, from 20 weeks,” she said.

“Our decision to not systemize our birth was very prominent. We decided to not have scans and try to birth as holistically and spiritually as possible. Which would mean that we would have a home birth out of the system with a doula who is incredibly experienced.”
The inquest continues.

articles.title: PH envoy Romualdez: US won't initiate Pax Silica talks during ASEAN meetings
articles.summary: United States President Donald Trump will not discuss the US-led Pax Silica initiative during his bilateral meeting with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. and other meetings amid the ongoing…

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 1:33pm

United States President Donald Trump will not discuss the US-led Pax Silica initiative during his bilateral meeting with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. and other meetings amid the ongoing 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, Philippine Ambassador to the US Jose Manuel Romualdez said.
Romualdez, in a Super Radyo dzBB interview, said the US has given the Philippines time to determine the fine print and coverage of the Pax Silica.

“Ang US ang nagsabi sa atin na hindi muna natin pag-usapan 'yan dahil dapat ayusin muna kung anong agreement na puwede natin pasukan, kung ano 'yung hinihingi nila, at kung ano 'yung puwede sa atin,” Romualdez said.
(The US told us that it will not be discussed yet because there is a need to check first the agreement that will be entered into, what they were asking from us, and what is acceptable to us.)
“President Marcos wants the process to be transparent,” he added.

A House bill establishing an economic zone for the Pax Silica initiative has been filed, but the measure is yet to be comprehensively discussed amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte and ongoing deliberations on the proposed P7.2 trillion national budget for 2027.

The bill provides that the Advanced Industries Zone will serve as “the country's national platform for strategic technology, advanced manufacturing, and innovation, under a dedicated authority empowered to attract investment and deliver government services efficiently.”

In return for competitive incentives, the bill states that enterprises or locators in the Advanced Industries Zone must create jobs for Filipinos, train Filipino workers, and transfer skills and know-how, so that Filipinos will not only assemble these technologies but ultimately design, build, and manage them later on.

Over 200 individuals, however, were arrested over the weekend due to protests against Trump and Pax Silica, mainly due to concerns raised by the indigenous people that they will be displaced from their ancestral domain.
The authors of the bill establishing the ecozone earlier said that the initiative will only cover the government’s patrimonial land.
Romualdez said protests and questions about the initiative are proof that sealing the Pax Silica deal is not something that can be rushed.
“It would be better if we are not doing this in haste,” he said.
The main issue for the Trump-Marcos meeting, Romualdez said, remains the completion of the Code of Conduct on the South China Sea between ASEAN and China.
The US supports freedom of navigation in the area in accordance with international law and has an existing mutual defense treaty with the Philippines since 1952.
“That Code of Conduct is the priority, and our future in the digital world,” Romualdez added. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: PNP tightens ASEAN Summit security following tensions at protests
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday said tighter security measures will be implemented for the Association of Southeast Asia Nations (ASEAN) Summit 2026 due to tensions during recent…

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 1:20pm

The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday said tighter security measures will be implemented for the Association of Southeast Asia Nations (ASEAN) Summit 2026 due to tensions during recent protests.

PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. ordered commanders to address identified security vulnerabilities, strengthen intelligence-sharing, and ensure that all security units remain prepared for the remaining summit activities.

"We cannot afford complacency when the security and credibility of our country are at stake. I have directed all commanders to close security gaps without delay, and keep our forces fully coordinated," he said in a statement.
"The success of the ASEAN Summit rests not only on our ability to prevent threats but also on our capability to protect people while upholding their rights," he added.
Some 23,000 government personnel, comprised of about 20,000 cops and 3,000 force multipliers, have been deployed to secure the 49th ASEAN Summit, the PNP said.
The National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO), Police Regional Offices 3 and 4A, and Camp Crame-based units have also been placed under full alert status from November 13 to 19.
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. has directed to maintain a safe, peaceful, and orderly environment throughout the summit, according to the PNP.
Nartatez said the police force would remain vigilant and professional while respecting the rights of the public.
"A successful summit must be measured not only by the security of our guests but also by the safety and dignity of our people," he said.
Over 200 protesters were arrested in Sucat, Muntinlupa during a protest caravan and were brought to Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City as ASEAN Summit 2026 opened on Sunday. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte's former staff being held, forced to sign document, says VP camp
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte has received information about her former household help allegedly being held against their will and being forced to sign a document, Atty. Paolo Panelo said Tuesday.
articles.byline: LLANESCA T. PANTI, GISELLE OMBAY, GMA News

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 1:15pm
Vice President Sara Duterte has received information about her former household help allegedly being held against their will and being forced to sign a document, Atty. Paolo Panelo said Tuesday.

In a Facebook post, Panelo, Duterte's spokesperson, said the Vice President received a message "from what appeared to be the account of a former household staff member" at 11:19 pm on Monday, November 16.

“The message contained a desperate plea for help and rescue in Manila. The sender claimed to be in the custody or under the control of certain individuals who allegedly told them about a threat to their life. The former staff member further narrated that they were being forced to sign a document, which they had refused to execute,” he said.

He added the incident is similar to what happened to Duterte's former media officer, Jefry Tupas, who earlier accused the National Bureau of Investigation of forcing him to come to Manila after being told that there is a threat to his life.

NBI chief Melvin Matibag earlier said that Tupas was the source of information about threats to his security. Tupas disputed this saying NBI agents were the ones who went to his home in North Cotabato in September.
Panelo said the whereabouts of the former household staff member remain unknown, "and their safety and well-being have yet to be independently verified."

"We are deeply concerned that this incident may be part of what we believe to be a relentless campaign by the Marcos administration, utilizing state institutions like the NBI, against the Vice President,” he added.
Probe needed
Malacañang, on the other hand, said that such claims should be investigated to determine its accuracy.
“Ang pag-iimbestiga sa nasabing kwento kung may katotohanan ay nararapat lamang,” Palace Press Officer Usec. Claire Castro said in a statement.
(It’s only fitting to investigate the claims to determine if there is any truth to it.)
Regardless, Castro emphasized that the President is currently busy with the ASEAN Summit.

“Buhos ang oras ng Pangulo sa pagtatrabaho para sa ikakaunlad ng bansa at sa pagpapatibay ng magandang ugnayan sa mga member states ng ASEAN at mga dialogue partners. Pagpapaayos ng ekonomiya, solusyon sa usaping enerhiya, teknolohiya, agrikultura, at edukasyon ang tinututukan ng ating Pangulo,” she said.

(The President is dedicating his time to the nation’s development and strengthening positive relations with ASEAN member-states and dialogue partners. He is focusing on improving the economy, as well as addressing issues related to energy, technology, agriculture, and education.)
Castro also stressed that Marcos does not resort to doing such.

“Hindi po gawain sa panahon ngayon ang gumawa ng intriga at magplanta ng ebidensya kung saan sanay at hasa ang Duterte administration at ito naman ay inamin noon pa ni dating Pangulong Duterte sa harapan ng media,” she added.

(The administration does not stir up such allegations or plant evidence—tactics in which the Duterte administration is well-versed and highly skilled, as former President Duterte himself previously admitted before the media.)
GMA News Online has reached out to the NBI for comment and will publish it as soon as it becomes available.
The Vice President’s impeachment trial is ongoing, with the defense panel presenting its witnesses and evidence.

Duterte is accused of betrayal of public trust and culpable violation of the Constitution for allegedly amassing P817 million to P1.5 billion worth of unexplained wealth due to non-declaration of assets and non-divestment in businesses despite a Constitutional ban. —AOL, GMA News
