articles.title: Asylum seekers on final ‘one in, one out’ UK-France flight feel they are being ‘punished’
articles.summary:
Many of those onboard are being deported for second time after fleeing threats from people smugglers in France

Many of the asylum seekers on Tuesday’s final “one in, one out” deportation…

blocks.text: Many of the asylum seekers on Tuesday’s final “one in, one out” deportation flight are people who returned to the UK fleeing threats from smugglers after they were already forcibly returned to France.
Hundreds of asylum seekers who were sent back to France are thought to have returned to the UK, citing threats from smugglers who said their families still owed them money for the Channel crossing.

Asylum seekers who spoke to the Guardian described being punched, beaten or raped by the smugglers. Some said smugglers had caught them while they slept on the streets and forced them to work for them in conditions of modern slavery in a migrant camp in Calais, cleaning the smugglers’ tents and carrying water or firewood.
The charity Medical Justice, which has provided support to people detained for one in, one out, called the pilot scheme “a disaster”.

The one in, one out scheme involved forcibly returning hundreds of people who had travelled to the UK on small boats to France in exchange for bringing a similar number from northern France to the UK to claim asylum.

blocks.caption: Asylum seekers who were forcibly sent back to France said they had been threatened by smugglers who said they still owed them money for the Channel crossing. Photograph: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto/Getty Images

blocks.text: One asylum seeker with a ticket for Tuesday’s flight said he was captured by the smugglers after being returned to France by the Home Office earlier this year. He said he was a political dissident in Iran, and believed he would be executed if he was returned there.
“I came back to the UK a second time because the smugglers caught me in France,” he said. “I was sleeping on the streets in Paris because France did not accept my asylum case.

“Many of the people who have tickets for Tuesday’s flight are people like me, who came back to the UK a second time. I believe those of us who came back to the UK a second time are being punished by being sent back to France a second time. I believe that 100%.”
He said that although the Home Office stated that sufficient lawyers were available for asylum seekers detained for France, he and others had struggled to access good quality legal advice.

“Friends paid privately for a lawyer for me. The lawyer promised me that 24 hours before the flight, they would challenge my removal, but he has done nothing,” he said. “They do not even answer the phone although I have tried to call them 10 times.
“My mind is broken. I am scared that when I am returned to France on Tuesday, the smugglers will catch me and kill me.

“When the guards came to take me to the plane for France last time, three or four of them surrounded me and made me feel like a criminal. I have committed no crime apart from coming to UK to claim asylum.
“When I slept on the street last time the weather was warmer in France. Now it is too cold to sleep outside. I don’t know what I’m going to do.”
after newsletter promotion
A second asylum seeker with a ticket for the flight, who also returned to the UK after being sent back to France, said he knew of dozens of people due to fly on Tuesday.
“All of us have bad solicitors who are not helping us,” he said. “One in, one out finished on 1 October. I do not understand why the Home Office wants to continue sending us to France.”

blocks.caption: One person who said he would be deported back to France on the last one in, one out flight said he feared being captured by smugglers who he had fled from. Photograph: Kiran Ridley/Getty Images

blocks.text: John Tuckett, the independent chief inspector of borders and immigration, said in a report published last week that it was not known how the Home Office would measure the success or failure of the one in, one out scheme, despite it being given the highest operational priority, with regular updates supplied to ministers and 10 Downing Street.

He cited a ministerial submission which stated that the aim of the scheme was to demonstrate that dangerous journeys on small boats were not a viable option for entry into the UK, with the aim of undermining the organised immigration crime model. Since the scheme ended on 1 October, 4,786 people have crossed the Channel in 69 small boats, according to government data.
A Medical Justice spokesperson said: “One in, one out has been a disaster, causing avoidable suffering to a vulnerable group and it has failed in the Home Office’s stated objective.
“The Home Office must start to learn lessons and put an end to dangerous detention conditions.”

Seema Syeda, of the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants, said: “The UK government has forced people fleeing war, climate breakdown and persecution to take murderous and traumatising journeys across the Channel, only to treat them with brutality once they have arrived here, retraumatising them with detention and deportation.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “We welcome the inspector’s recognition of the strong operational delivery of the UK-France pilot, which successfully demonstrated that a returns arrangement of this kind can work.
“The message was clear: if you returned to the UK after being transferred to France under the pilot, you would be sent back.

“The pilot has now concluded and we are taking forward lessons learned as part of wider efforts to strengthen returns. Any future operational decisions, including on evaluation and reporting, will be considered in the usual way.”

articles.title: Invest in international rail services to boost UK-EU reset, Burnham urged
articles.summary:
Campaigners call for reopening of high-speed Eurostar stations and new infrastructure for London St Pancras

Britain should throw its weight behind international rail services to reset the…

blocks.text: Britain should throw its weight behind international rail services to reset the UK-EU relationship, transport campaigners have urged the prime minister.

A coalition of groups has called on Andy Burnham to commit to reopening high-speed stations for Eurostar and other services in Kent, and to support new infrastructure for passengers at London St Pancras and for rail freight.
The call came alongside research showing that annual rail passenger numbers through the Channel tunnel could more than double in five years and hit 28 million by 2040.

The report said that planned increases in services and routes, including competition to Eurostar from new operators and significant investment in rolling stock, should drive demand for international rail travel, but that the government needed to help realise the potential.

A letter to Burnham from the Campaign for Better Transport, co-signed by sustainable transport groups and train operators, said the numbers would come “only if a strategy is put in place and the barriers to growth are unlocked”. The campaigners urged him to tackle high fares and border delays and invest in more depot and station capacity.

Ben Plowden, the chief executive of the Campaign for Better Transport, said: “The Channel tunnel is one of Britain’s greatest, underused transport assets. Improving our international rail network would give people a genuine alternative to flying, making international travel more affordable and accessible, and delivering major benefits for the economy and the environment.”

According to research by the Transport and Environment (T&E) thinktank, three times as many Britons support expanding international rail rather than airports. Labour has approved expansion at London’s Stansted, Luton and Gatwick airports, although, significantly, Burnham has not expressed support for Heathrow’s third runway.
Georgia Whitaker, a rail campaigns manager at T&E, said: “If the EU and UK want to get back on track, ensuring the Channel tunnel is no longer half-used is a no-brainer.”

Gareth Williams, the general secretary of Eurostar, said: “The UK needs a big picture plan to unleash international rail growth. There is a real opportunity to deliver economic benefits through rail and to provide low-carbon connections, including direct routes as far afield as Germany and Switzerland. To get there, there’s a need to be ambitious about infrastructure investment – particularly in stations and depots that are fit for the future.”

The letter calls on Burnham to open Stratford International station in east London as a second gateway into the capital, something the government committed to providing funding for in the autumn budget.

It also urged him to commit to reopening international services at Ashford and Ebbsfleet International stations. The letter is signed by Eurostar, despite the current cross-Channel operator having deemed the Kent stations commercially unviable.

A strategic approach to international rail should mean more investment, the report said, but it also pointed to “proportionate and efficient border and security arrangements”, better connections and integrated ticketing.
The campaigners also suggested levying more taxes on aviation to reflect the climate impact of short-haul flying compared with rail.
A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We also want to see a thriving, competitive international rail market that gives passengers more choice and supports economic growth.

“That’s why we’re supporting industry and local partners to deliver international services at Stratford International, Ebbsfleet and Ashford, and are exploring options for new international rail depot capacity.”

articles.title: Serbia’s Student List candidates to be sworn in as MPs after election triumph
articles.summary:
Inaugural parliamentary session comes as ousted populist Aleksandar Vučić threatens mass protests of his own

Candidates for Serbia’s Student List, the grassroots movement of political…

blocks.text: Candidates for Serbia’s Student List, the grassroots movement of political outsiders that pulled off a spectacular victory in last month’s elections over the party of the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić, are to be sworn in as MPs as they begin the process of forming a government.

The 140 candidates – among them academics, lawyers, scientists and the odd actor – will be sworn in on Tuesday during the inaugural session of the new parliament, bringing 14 years of rule by Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) to an end.

A caretaker government under the outgoing prime minister, Ðjuro Macut, will remain in office until MPs approve the Student List’s choice of a cabinet. For now, its makeup – including the identity of a future prime minister – remains unclear.

Sarah El Sarag, a human rights lawyer and MP-elect, said the wider student movement continued to be active in the process of selecting the cabinet, along with the candidates themselves. “We are there because of them,” she said of the students. “All the time, we are doing it together.”

blocks.caption: Student List supporters celebrate after Aleksandar Vučić concedes defeat in Serbia’s parliamentary election on 26 October. Photograph: Uros Arsic/Reuters

blocks.text: Parliamentary planning sessions had helped prepare the candidates, she said. “We have been having meetings and exercises for the parliament almost every day, because none of us are professional politicians. We are lawyers, doctors, professors – and it is the first time for us to do this kind of job.”

The sessions reflect the Student List’s efforts to pre-empt sceptics who question whether a group of candidates with no political experience is equipped to govern. Members of the movement that selected El Sarag and her fellow MPs-elect have reiterated that all are experts in their professional or academic fields and are better qualified than many of the people who served as ministers or MPs under Vučić.

El Sarag said her colleagues had a good idea of what to expect from Tuesday’s opening session. “People who have had some experience of politics have been making some simulated exercises for us,” she said.
She would not divulge the identity of the candidate for speaker – who will become Serbia’s acting president – let alone the name of the next prime minister.
after newsletter promotion

Vučić is not accepting his new role as leader of the opposition meekly. Since the election, he has accused the Student List of instituting a regime of “naked terror” by directing “submissive prosecutors and police” to carry out unlawful detentions.

Police and prosecutors have made a series of arrests of people with links to the SNS. Last week, prosecutors targeted the owners of a well-connected construction company over a project on the site of the once-famous Hotel Jugoslavija, which was hit during the 1999 Nato airstrikes on Belgrade.

That followed the arrest of the owner of Alta Bank, which held the concession for processing bill payments on behalf of Serbia’s state-owned electricity company. Others facing charges include senior police officers accused of abuse of office, and people suspected of vote rigging and violence during the elections.
After the two years of protests which culminated in the SNS’s defeat at the ballot box, Vučić is threatening major protests of his own.
Raša Nedeljkov, the programme director of the Serbian election and democracy monitor CRTA, said the first disruptions could come during parliament’s inaugural session.

“We can expect a lot of sabotage, a lot of obstruction, a lot of circus-creating atmosphere,” he said. “If we see such scenes in parliament – including some kind of physical obstruction – that’s something which would not surprise me.”

In such an atmosphere, speed may be of the essence, he said. MPs must approve a new cabinet within 90 days of the national assembly’s inaugural session but will be motivated to name a PM well before that deadline.

articles.title: Marcos calls for open sea lanes to ensure global energy security
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has called for keeping sea lanes open to ensure the continued flow of global energy supplies during the 4th Asia Zero-Emission Community (AZEC) Summit on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 12:42pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has called for keeping sea lanes open to ensure the continued flow of global energy supplies during the 4th Asia Zero-Emission Community (AZEC) Summit on Tuesday.
He also emphasized the need for enhanced information-sharing among oil-producing and oil-consuming countries, saying stockpiling alone would not be enough to ensure energy security.
"Stockpiling is not enough. Sustainable and enduring energy security demands that oil-consuming and oil-producing nations act in unison," Marcos said in his opening remarks.
"We must deepen information sharing and practical storage arrangements, as well as commit to upholding international law to keep sea lanes open and maintain fair, transparent markets," he added.
The summit is co-chaired by Marcos and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
In her opening remarks, Takaichi said Japan was proposing initiatives to strengthen cooperation on oil stockpiling and power grids.
Takaichi also announced that Japan would establish the Asia Oil Security Task Force, a framework for cooperation on oil procurement during emergencies.

The task force will work with the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia (ERIA) to strengthen regional energy security, including through information-sharing and oil stockpiling.

The initiative is envisioned as an Asian counterpart to the IEA, which is headquartered in Paris and is establishing a new base in Tokyo. The ERIA, based in Jakarta, is expected to serve as the task force's secretariat.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Duterte camp urged to file report over alleged coercion of ex-staffer
articles.summary: This was after a post by lawyer Paolo Panelo, one of the legal counsels of the Vice President, saying that the Vice President received a message from what appeared to be the account of a former…

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 12:40pm
NBI director Melvin Matibag
The STAR / Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag urged the camp of Vice President Sara Duterte to file reports over alleged coercion of her former staff to sign a document.

This was after a post by lawyer Paolo Panelo, one of the legal counsels of the Vice President, noted that the vice president received a message from what appeared to be the account of a former household staff member containing a "desperate plea for help and rescue in Manila."
“They have to file a formal report. If they feel the urgency, dapat go through (the) legal process,” Matibag said in a message to Philstar.com.

According to Panelo, the sender claimed to be under the custody or control of certain individuals who allegedly warned of a threat to the former staffer's life and tried to force them to sign a document, which they refused to execute.
Panelo added that the individual's whereabouts and safety remain unverified.

Duterte’s lawyer also drew parallels between the alleged incident and that of Jefry Tupas, claiming that NBI agents had previously told Tupas on Sept. 29, 2026, of threats to his life before attempting to bring him to Manila.

“We are deeply concerned that this incident may be part of what we believe to be a relentless campaign by the Marcos administration, utilizing state institutions like the NBI, against the vice president,” Panelo said.

In a separate Facebook post, the vice president’s brother, Rep. Paolo Duterte (Davao City 1st District), condemned the alleged actions as a tactic to intimidate and pressure individuals into signing documents and acting as witnesses to fabricate a case against the Vice President.

“If your case is strong, then prove it in court. Stop intimidating people. Do not force anyone to become a witness through intimidation, coercion, or threats,” the vice president’s brother said in a Facebook post.

Aside from the impeachment trial, Duterte is also facing a grave threat charge before a Quezon City Regional Trial Court over her threats in October and November 2024 press conferences against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Marcos and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.

The NBI is also investigating alleged irregularities in the properties of the vice president and her husband, Manases Carpio, which are indicated in their Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth.

articles.title: ASEAN Plus Three: Marcos calls for urgent action amid economic pressures
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Tuesday underscored the urgent need for the ASEAN member-states, as well as China, Japan, and Republic of Korea to put their collective strength to work…

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 12:07pm

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., China Minister of Agriculture and Rural Affairs Zhang Zhu, and Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong prepare to pose for a group picture during the 29th ASEAN Plus Three Summit, part of the 49th ASEAN Summit, on November 17, 2026 in Manila, Philippines. Ezra Acayan/Pool via REUTERS

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Tuesday underscored the urgent need for the ASEAN member-states, as well as China, Japan, and Republic of Korea to put their collective strength to work to respond to current global economic challenges.

Marcos made the call during the 29th ASEAN Plus Three (APT) Summit, which was also attended by Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, and Chinese Agriculture Minister Zhang Zhu.

“A disruption thousands of miles away can reach households across East and Southeast Asia through the price of rice, the cost of energy, or the loss of a day's income. Our peoples feel the effects of the global economy in palpable and immediate ways,” Marcos said.
“The benefits of regional cooperation, in turn, should be just as tangible and reach our peoples with the same urgency,” he added.
Marcos also noted that APT has served as one of East Asia's most important platforms for stability, resilience, and shared prosperity for nearly three decades now.
He said that this regional cooperation connects the markets, industries, technology, and investment of ASEAN member-states with China, Japan, and the Republic of Korea.
“Acting together, we can give our peoples greater security today and greater confidence for tomorrow,” Marcos said.
“With ASEAN at its center, the partnership gives us a platform to act on our common stake in a stable, connected region that sustains growth and opportunity for all,” he added.

ASEAN leaders are set to adopt on Tuesday two ASEAN Plus Three Leaders’ statements---one on maritime trade and logistics connectivity, and another on strengthening energy and food security resilience amid external shocks and supply chain disruptions. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Bishop laments ASEAN protest arrests on World Day of the Poor
articles.summary: "Poverty is not a crime," a bishop says, noting the irony of arrests of those raising concerns about communities and livelihoods.

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 11:56am

Protesters clash with police officers during a demonstration that coincides with the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Leaders' Summit and Related Summits in Manila on Nov. 15, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — The Catholic Church was observing the World Day of the Poor when hundreds of Filipinos were arrested during the ASEAN summit protests on Sunday, November 15, San Carlos Bishop Gerardo Alminaza said.

The bishop pointed to the irony on Tuesday, saying the arrests came as protesters were raising concerns about their rights, livelihoods and communities, underscoring the need to protect the voices of marginalized Filipinos.

"Poverty is not a crime. Peaceful protest is not a crime. Demanding justice is not a crime," Alminaza said in a statement Tuesday, November 17. "The poor deserve a seat at the table and a meaningful voice in decisions that shape their future."
More than 300 people were reportedly arrested during demonstrations across Metro Manila as Southeast Asian leaders gathered for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.

Alminaza urged the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) and other independent bodies to investigate reports of police abuse during the November 15 protests, including incidents involving journalists and a reported arrest on church property.
He also called on authorities to preserve evidence, allow independent access to detainees and hold personnel accountable for any violations.

"Authorities have a responsibility to protect public safety. That responsibility must be exercised with restraint and respect for human dignity. Allegations against particular individuals must be examined fairly; they must never become a blanket justification for punishing peaceful dissent," Alminaza said.
The bishop demanded the immediate release of those detained solely for exercising their right to peaceful assembly and the withdrawal of charges based only on such activities.

"I call for the immediate release of all those detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights, and for the withdrawal of charges based solely on such exercise. Every person in custody must have prompt access to legal counsel, family members and necessary medical care. Children must receive appropriate care, protection and assistance, with their best interests given priority," he said.

The Philippine National Police has defended its handling of the demonstrations, saying officers exercised maximum tolerance and that arrests were made in response to alleged obstruction of public roads and refusals to comply with authorities.

articles.title: Trump to kick off Asia trip with Quad talks in Manila ahead of China visit
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump flies into the Philippines on Tuesday at the tail end of a Southeast Asian summit, where he could face protests ahead of the first meeting in two years of the leaders of the…

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 11:39am

US President Donald Trump flies into the Philippines on Tuesday at the tail end of a Southeast Asian summit, where he could face protests ahead of the first meeting in two years of the leaders of the Quad group of Indo-Pacific countries.

Trump's Asia trip, which also includes the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen and a much-anticipated trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, comes after his Republican Party's defeat in midterm elections and spy allegations that could complicate a fragile trade-war truce between the US and China.

There could be protests in Manila against Trump's visit, after days of demonstrations that have included the burning of effigies of the president and calls for an end to the Middle East war and the scrapping of the US-led Pax Silica initiative.

The meeting of the Quad – the US, Japan, Australia and India – will be Trump's first and takes place two years after the last gathering of the group, which his predecessor Joe Biden regarded as a signature foreign policy initiative.

It comes just ahead of the APEC gathering hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping, who has previously objected to the Quad as an effort to encircle Beijing. Quad members have said the grouping is not directed against any one country.
Quad meeting the 'best possible signal'

At the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations on Monday, Chinese Premier Li Qiang hailed what he called "truly extraordinary" economic achievements of China and ASEAN in the face of global trade restrictions, expressing Beijing's commitment to free trade and the need to "stand united, ward off interference, and work together".

China is ASEAN's biggest trading partner and a key source of investment, but the biggest economies of the 11-member bloc – which has a combined GDP of more than $3.9 trillion – want to deepen ties with the United States despite protracted trade and diplomatic uncertainty under the Trump administration.
Former US Deputy Secretary of State Kurt Campbell credited Washington's top diplomat, Marco Rubio, with the timing and reconvening of the Quad, which he said had lost ambition under Trump.

"Part of what he (Rubio) is thinking is that this is probably the best possible signal if you're going to go into a trilateral meeting," said Campbell, co-founder of The Asia Group, referring to Thursday's US-China-Russia talks.
"The linchpin of everything that we do in Asia is the US-Japan relationship, and a perception that this is not at the top of the president's mind would concern me."

White House spokesperson Olivia Wales on Friday said that under Trump's leadership, the Quad had demonstrated it is "a partnership of action, tackling the region's toughest challenges and driving opportunities to ensure a free and open Indo-Pacific".
Trump to meet allies, ASEAN leaders

A Japanese foreign ministry official last week said it was expected that Quad leaders would try to show unity, with maritime security, export restrictions, critical-minerals supply-chain diversification and AI among potential discussion points.
Before Trump's late afternoon arrival, ASEAN will hold meetings on Tuesday with leaders of Japan, South Korea, China and India, ahead of the annual East Asia Summit.
Trump will skip the summit but will join a US-ASEAN "Special Summit" and will meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr on Wednesday. The Philippines is a US defense ally.

Trump is also expected to hold talks with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul on Tuesday, Thai media quoted the commerce minister as saying, with a joint statement to be issued on negotiations on a reciprocal trade agreement.
The US is Thailand's largest export market, accounting for 24% of its total shipments this year. The US designated Thailand as a major non-NATO ally in 2003. —Reuters

articles.title: Japan scrambles jets to counter suspected Russian aircraft
articles.summary: Japan said it lodged a "very stern protest" with Moscow after two suspected Russian aircraft violated Japanese airspace.

image.caption: Japan deployed jets to warn 'suspected Russian' aircraft that entered its airspace [Representative photo from September 2025]Image: Kurt Fairhurst/News Images/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Japan scrambled fighter jets in its airspace after two suspected Russian aircraft entered its territory on Tuesday morning, an incident that could further strain ties between the two countries.
Tokyo said it had lodged a "very stern protest" with Moscow after the incident.
Japan lodges protest against Russia over alleged airspace violation
The aircraft entered Japan's airspace near Okinoshima in southwestern Japan shortly after 4:00 a.m. local time Tuesday (1900 GMT Monday), Japanese ​Chief Cabinet ‌Secretary Minoru Kihara ‌said.

"The violation of our national airspace by Russian aircraft is not only a grave infringement of our country's sovereignty, but also a threat to our security and is completely unacceptable," Kihara said.
"We lodged a very stern protest with Russia through diplomatic channels and strongly demanded measures to prevent any recurrence," he said.
Japan had lodged a similar protest with Russia in 2024 after a Russian patrol plane entered its airspace three times, marking the first confirmed incursion since 2019.
Kihara said the aircraft travelled through the Tsushima Strait and went between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan before heading to the Pacific.
Strains increasing in Japan-Russia ties
Japan's relations with Moscow have soured over the past weeks after a Japanese journalist was arrested on spying allegations and after Russia seized four of Japan Tobacco's Russian assets.
Russia and Japan share a decades-old dispute over the status of a number of islands in the Pacific Ocean.
However, relations especially deteriorated further after Tokyo joined global sanctions against Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
South Korea says Russian aircraft entered defense zone

Tuesday's reported violation comes soon after South Korea said it too had deployed fighter jets and conducted tactical maneuvers after several Russian military aircraft entered its air defense zone in the early hours of Tuesday.
An air defense zone is not sovereign airspace but a buffer area in which countries identify approaching aircraft for security purposes.
Military aircraft are generally expected to notify the relevant country before entering its air defense zone, though this is not legally required.

articles.title: Vance says he will decide 'sometime next year' about 2028 US presidential run
articles.summary: The US vice-president tells Fox News that when he makes a decision to run or otherwise, he will "be all in on whatever that decision is".

blocks.text: US Vice-President JD Vance has said he will make a decision "sometime next year" about whether or not he will run for president in 2028.
In an interview with Fox News, Vance would not provide a timeline on making a determination, but signaled he is not in a hurry to make up his mind.
"I haven't made a decision. We'll figure it out sometime next year," Vance said. When pressed by host Laura Ingraham, he added: "When I make a decision, I'll be all in on whatever that decision is."
The comments came amid growing interest in Vance's next moves in the weeks since voters handed both President Donald Trump and Republicans a resounding defeat in the midterm elections.

People in Vance's orbit who have spoken to the BBC said the November elections did not change the timeline around his decision-making process for 2028. He is expected to run but allies believe he could wait several months to make a final decision.

Speculation about Vance's White House aspirations began the moment President Trump selected him as his 2024 running mate. The pick positioned Vance, who entered the White House as one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, as the most likely heir to Trump's Make America Great Again (Maga) movement.
But while serving in office, Vance has carefully avoided discussing his own political ambitions.

He kept that up during the midterms, when supporters frequently interrupted his campaign speeches to urge him to run in 2028. Vance's stock response was that Republicans needed to focus on the election at hand in November.
But with the midterms in the rearview mirror, and Republicans eager to move on from their 2026 drubbing, the next election at hand is now the 2028 presidential race.

Vance would likely jump to the top of the Republican primary field whenever he launches his bid, should he choose to run. But the contest is expected to be a competitive process with a large field of candidates.
Numerous other high-profile Republicans are rumoured to be interested in running or have said publicly that they are mulling a White House bid.
The list includes Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, outgoing Florida Governor and 2024 hopeful Ron DeSantis, and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, among others.
Trump has praised Vance and Rubio on several occasions, while also insisting that he is not sure who he will endorse in 2028 - or if he will weigh in at all.

The president's endorsement would be influential with the Maga base. But the midterms revealed widespread frustration with many of his second-term policies, complicating the path forward for potential candidates like Vance who are tied to Trump's agenda.

Vance blamed the midterm results on the war with Iran in a post-election social media post. In it, he also mapped out a plan for winning back Republican voters, which included ending the war and focusing on the economy.
The message was widely seen as a first step by Vance to distance himself from Trump ahead of a 2028 run.
In the Fox News interview, Vance reiterated his view that the war came with a "political cost", but said it has not damaged his relationship with Trump.
"There's no daylight" on the Iran war between Trump and senior administration officials including himself, Vance said.

He added that Trump would not let the conflict become a "forever war" and said the administration would not let the war, which was launched by the US and Israel in February 2026, even become "a two-year commitment".

Vance also discussed the nationwide air traffic outrage last week, which brought air travel across the US to a standstill for several hours. The vice-president called on lawmakers to fix the issue in the final weeks of the current congressional session.

He also touched on the scandal engulfing Nvidia, its former CEO Jensen Huang and its implications for US-China relations. Vance said there was still no "clarity" about the accuracy of reports that a woman with whom Huang reportedly had an affair with was indeed a Chinese spy.
"There is a lack of clarity about it. I don't know and [Trump] doesn't know whether this woman was a spy or not," Vance said.

articles.title: Dolores Huerta honored in ceremony at California state capitol
articles.summary:
Labor leader was remembered for her advocacy and co-founding union that would become United Farm Workers

California officials paid tribute to Dolores Huerta, one of the nation’s most…

blocks.text: California officials paid tribute to Dolores Huerta, one of the nation’s most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists, at a memorial ceremony Monday at the state capitol.

They remembered her as a relentless advocate for a more just and fair world. Huerta co-founded a union that became the United Farm Workers with César Chávez and made famous her rallying cry, “Sí, se puede!” – which translates to “Yes, it can be done!”
Huerta, 96, died of cancer at her home in Bakersfield, California, last month. A celebration of life, with an interfaith memorial service, will be held in her hometown on Friday.

Robert Rivas, the Democratic assembly speaker, had called Huerta a family friend and mentor. Rivas’ grandfather, Servando Flores, moved from Mexico to California in the 1960s and went on to organize fellow farmworkers alongside Huerta.

blocks.caption: People pay their respects to Dolores Huerta at the California state capitol. Photograph: Jose Luis Villegas/AP

blocks.text: “She is the mother of our Latino civil rights movement,” Rivas said. “Her place in the history of our state and nation is enduring.”

Rivas stood beside fellow Democrats Xavier Becerra, the governor-elect, Monique Limón, the senate president pro tempore, and Nancy Pelosi, the former US House speaker, in the Ccapitol rotunda as they spoke about Huerta during an invitation-only ceremony. There were performances of songs that included We Shall Overcome and Put a Little Love in Your Heart before the space was opened to the public.

“As we honor one of the towering figures of our time, we make her this solemn promise: the march goes on,” said Limón, who is serving as acting governor while Gavin Newsom, the governor, is out of state.

Before the event began, Huerta’s casket was transported to the capitol by a hearse adorned with flags reading “Sí, se puede!” Hundreds of people, including union leaders, politicians and members of the public, followed behind, many with marigolds in hand.

blocks.caption: Maria Helena Chavez, daughter of Dolores Huerta and Richard Chavez, is comforted by her husband Rafael Rodriguez. Photograph: Héctor Amezcua/Reuters

blocks.text: Huerta was born in New Mexico in 1930 and raised in California’s farm-rich San Joaquin valley. She became an elementary school teacher before turning her focus to the plight of farmworkers and teaming up with Chávez to create the National Farm Workers Association in 1962, which became United Farm Workers.

Then president Barack Obama, who borrowed her rallying cry for his campaign slogan, “Yes we can,” awarded her with the nation’s highest civilian honor, the Presidential Medal of Freedom, in 2012. Well into her 90s, Huerta was a familiar face at news conferences and rallies in Sacramento, where she advocated for the rights of workers, women, voters and others.
She revealed this year that she was sexually abused by Chávez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she kept for 60 years.

articles.title: Rio Tinto agrees to pay US$250m to begin repairing ‘devastation’ left by Panguna mine
articles.summary:
Bougainville cabinet minister says fund gives chance to find solutions to ‘huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation’

Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has…

blocks.text: Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has agreed to pay a quarter-of-a-billion dollars to begin the clean-up of the toxic Panguna mine site it abandoned more than three decades ago.

Panguna, once one of the world’s most profitable gold and copper mines, was shuttered in 1989 after violent protests over environmental damage and the inequitable division of the mine’s profits sparked a decade-long civil war on the Papua New Guinean island of Bougainville.
But the sprawling mine pit, once a mountain, remains a scar in the middle of the island, with vast pillars of rubble at risk of collapse, and polluted rivers running bright blue with toxins.

Rio Tinto was forced from the island and has never returned, but in recent years has been part of a detailed consultation process with landowners and government. It has now agreed to voluntarily contribute US$250m (A$370m) towards the remediation of the mine site.
Theonila Roka Matbob, a Panguna community leader, said the fund was a vital contribution towards repairing the “devastation left by the Panguna mine”.

“We have a lot of work still ahead of us, but the establishment of this fund gives us the chance to find solutions to the huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation.

“No amount of money will restore the damage caused to the environment in Panguna, but this sets a foundation for us to invest in addressing the environmental issues and invest in our children’s futures as well.”

blocks.caption: Bougainville minister Theonila Roka Matbob in her village of Mako ’Osi below the Panguna mine. Photograph: Mike Bowers/The Guardian

blocks.text: Roka Matbob said the most fundamental remediation was to improve “accessibility” for the people living around Panguna – “accessibility to clean drinking water that is safe and secure … and infrastructure, in bridges that makes people’s access to trade, to school, to health[care], much easier. This is one critical area that immediately needs attention.”

The president of Bougainville, Ishmael Toroama, seeking to become the world’s newest head of state at the forefront of a long-running independence movement on the island, said the money would make a “meaningful difference” to villages and communities that had suffered from the impacts of the mine’s pollution.

“This work will deliver benefits not only for people today, but for future generations. Continued engagement with our communities will be essential to ensuring the work responds to local priorities and delivers lasting outcomes.”

The Rio commitment has emerged from the Panguna Mine Legacy Impact Assessment consultation process, which was initiated in response to a human rights complaint brought by the Australian-based Human Rights Law Centre, with Roka Matbob as the lead complainant.
Keren Adams, the HRLC’s legal director, said establishing the fund had taken years of work.
“It is a testament to the courage and persistence of community leaders, and the willingness of all parties to engage in difficult but constructive dialogue,” she said.
“The significant funding contributed by Rio Tinto creates a real opportunity to now address an environmental disaster that has remained unresolved for decades.”

Mark Davies, Rio Tinto’s chief safety and technical officer, said the establishment of the fund was an “important milestone … intended to support the transition from the assessment to practical remedy implementation”.
“Community engagement is an important next step to identify priorities and we remain committed to working with communities to shape the activities supported by the fund.”
The quarter-of-a-billion dollars will not be sufficient to entirely remediate the mine site, but it is being seen as a major step towards rehabilitation.
The funding commitment for Panguna comes at an acutely sensitive time for the restive Bougainville island.

The mine has become inextricably linked with the Bougainville’s political future: restarting operations at Panguna – believed to still hold at least $60bn in unrealised reserves – is seen by many, including the president, as the fundamental financial basis for the island’s independent future. Indian miner Lloyds has been granted a 25-year large-scale mining lease, but any future mining is years from starting.
What caused the Bougainville civil war?
Bougainville, a group of islands off Papua New Guinea to the north of Australia, has been variously controlled by Britain, Germany, Japan, Australia and PNG.
It declared independence in 1975 as the Republic of North Solomons, but was absorbed into the newly independent PNG weeks later.
Its close ethnic ties and proximity to the Solomons archipelago means it has always sat uneasily with Port Moresby’s rule.
That discontent came to a violent head in 1988 after a long-running dispute over the lucrative Panguna copper and gold mine.
The mine, carved from a mountain in central Bougainville, was critically important to PNG, at one point generating more than 45% of the country's national export revenue.

Multinational Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly US$2bn from the mine over 17 years of operation. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands had been destroyed by it.
Under the leadership of a former mine worker, Francis Ona, disaffected Bougainvilleans ran a sabotage campaign which forced the mine’s closure in 1989.

The PNG Government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war that ran for a decade, and saw as many as 20,000 people die.
PNG later hired international mercenaries to end the conflict (the notorious Sandline affair), before a peace agreement was signed in 2001.
In a 2019 referendum, 97.7% of Bougainvilleans voted in favour of independence. Many argue that reopening Panguna mine will be key to the island’s economic future as an independent nation.

Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly $2bn from Panguna over 17 years of operation from 1972. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands were destroyed by it.

Disaffected landowners ran a sabotage campaign that forced Panguna’s closure in 1989. The PNG government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war – known as “the crisis” – that ran for a decade. Between 15,000 and 20,000 people were killed, roughly 10% of the island’s population.

A recent environmental impact assessment found the abandoned mine remains an acute threat to people’s lives, including from landslides, levee collapses and floods. Untouched, the river delta will stay polluted for a century.

The future of Bougainville’s independence campaign is now before the PNG parliament, which will decide whether or not to recognise a UN-backed independence referendum held on the island in 2019, in which 97.7% of voters were in favour of Bougainville seceding and becoming an independent country.
The PNG parliament, which heard lengthy and impassioned debate over Bougainville last month, appears almost certain to vote against recognising the referendum result.

But Toroama, who has staked his presidency on achieving political independence, has said, regardless of the parliament’s decision, Bougainville will enter a period of “self-government” from September next year, before seceding, breaking away from PNG as a fully fledged independent nation, by 2030.

articles.title: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
articles.summary: Pakistan's ex-prime minister, who has been in prison since August 2023, says he has been denied justice.

blocks.text: Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating.
"At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar.
Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health.

Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated.
Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage".
He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery.
"I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote.

He said that he is being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, where he is allowed neither visits by his family nor access to books and television, and that this has "taken a heavy toll" on his mental health.
He also claimed he had only seen his lawyers four times over the past year.
"I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he wrote.
Pakistan's parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed these claims, saying Khan is "provided with all facilities in prison, including food of his own choosing".
"[He] is currently the most well-accommodated prisoner in Pakistan," the minister told reporters.
Authorities also say Khan was taken to a government-run hospital for an eye injection a week ago, where doctors deemed him "clinically stable".
Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.

His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.
At least eight people died in the protests and the army were called in to quell the violence.
Even behind bars, Khan remains a force in Pakistani politics.

Thousands of his supporters took to the streets in early October in a dayslong march, demanding his release. Authorities later ordered a crackdown on protests and imposed a state of emergency in Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, insisting that Khan be given proper medical care.

articles.title: Fiona the hippo under veterinary care after eating hat at Cincinnati zoo
articles.summary:
Knit hat caught in ceiling fan and flung into enclosure eaten by Fiona, who is being closely monitored by zoo staff

The Cincinnati zoo says Fiona, its beloved hippo who became a global…

blocks.text: The Cincinnati zoo says Fiona, its beloved hippo who became a global celebrity after her premature birth nearly a decade ago, is undergoing veterinary care after swallowing a knit hat that got into her enclosure.
Zoo veterinarians and staff are monitoring Fiona and working to help her pass the hat, the zoo said in a statement Monday.
“Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self,” the zoo said. The zoo said she received fluids and an enema Sunday to help move things through her system.

The cap got into Fiona’s habitat after it was tossed into the air by a visitor and caught by a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows, said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.

“We probably couldn’t make [it] happen again if we tried,” zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley told Axios in a statement, emphasizing it was an accident. Fiona will be off the exhibit until she is in better health.
Fiona was born six weeks premature in January 2017, and her fight to survive grabbed international attention.
She initially could not stand on her own and weighed just 29lbs (13.2kg) at birth, 25lbs (11.3kg) less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
Fans followed her progress online, and she became so popular that books were written about her. She also inspired a line of beer, all sorts of clothing and an ice cream flavor.
One couple even got engaged in front of her exhibit, with Fiona getting into the picture while underwater in the background.

Other zoos contacted Fiona, showing concern for her health. Timothy, the hippo at the San Antonio zoo sent well wishes via Instagram. “I know you’ve got some amazing people looking after you. We’re sending lots of love from Texas to the most beautiful hippo in the world. Hope you’re feeling more like yourself soon!”
The zoo said in a social media post it will share more information as they get it, also reminding visitors to be careful when near habitats and to secure belongings.
“If something falls into a habitat, please notify a zoo staff member immediately,” the zoo said.

articles.title: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies about escape attempt during alleged kidnapping
articles.summary: Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski described how he tried to escape and how his alleged kidnappers ultimately released him during his continued testimony at their jury trial in Toronto on…

blocks.text: Toronto·New

Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski described how he tried to escape and how his alleged kidnappers ultimately released him during his continued testimony at their jury trial in Toronto on Monday.
Pleterski also recounted threats to his family, beating with golf clubs and his release
'Crypto King’ Aiden Pleterski testifies about alleged 3-day kidnapping ordeal
Pleterski, 27, testified that he was zip-tied and taped to a chair in a "run-down, old home" in the Niagara Region in Ontario on the third and final day of his alleged kidnapping in December 2022.

He also recounted having a COVID-19 mask duct-taped to his face, and more duct tape wrapped around his head and eyes, before he was left in the care of a couple he said told him they'd been paid $5,000 "in dope" to keep him there.
"'What if I can try and convince them I can give them money to let me go?'" Pleterski said in Ontario Superior Court, recounting his thinking at the time.
Pleterski testified this photo was taken of him while he was being held at a home in the Niagara Region during his alleged kidnapping December 2022. (Ontario Superior Court)

Pleterski testified he started telling the couple details from his bankruptcy proceeding, hoping they'd heard of his case, as well as the same "story" he'd told his alleged kidnappers about his former landlord, Sandeep Gupta, hiding money for him.

He said he offered to give the couple $50,000 to $100,000 to release him and would set them up in a hotel downtown Toronto for a few days. Pleterski told the court the couple agreed and rushed him out of the house.

But instead of leaving with them, Pleterski testified he was thrown back into the same Dodge Ram truck he'd been in and out of for three days with his alleged captors. Pleterski said they had a new plan to release him so he could get them money.
"Kid, you're going to go to Sandeep and you're going to get all your assets," Pleterski testified that someone identified as "Slime" told him.
"He said if I don't get money from Sandeep, he's going to kill my family."
"Slime" was the lead kidnapper, according to the Crown, but he is not part of this trial.

Two other men, Alfredo Paladino and Rakeem Henry, who Pleterski testified were also in the truck at that time and part of his kidnapping, are on trial for that and for allegedly extorting and assaulting him.

From left to right, Alfredo Paladino, Akil Heywood and Rakeem Henry are accused of kidnapping and extorting Pleterski in December 2022. (Evan Mitsui/CBC, Instagram/atlanticmastoronto, Evan Mitsui/CBC)

A third man, Akil Heywood, who allegedly invested more than $300,000 with Pleterski and lost a significant amount of it, is also accused of kidnapping and extortion. The Crown described him as the "driving force" behind the plan to kidnap Pleterski.
All three men have pleaded not guilty.
Pleterski was convicted of fraud last month in connection with more than $30 million he took from investors to trade on their behalf, but he has yet to be sentenced.
Released at the Ritz

During their drive back toward Toronto from the Niagara Region, Pleterski said Slime kept oscillating between the plan to let him go to get money from Gupta and giving Pleterski to other groups that wanted him.
"'If they were going to kill me, they would have done it, and if they kill me they won't get money out of me,'" said Pleterski about what he was thinking at the time.
"At this point I'm pleading with him to drop me off with Sandeep."
Pleterski demonstrates how he was grabbed by his alleged kidnappers during his testimony at their jury trial in Toronto last Friday. (Pam Davies/CBC)
Pleterski also testified that the truck stopped at a Walmart along the way. The jury was shown security footage of this.

At the big box store, Pleterski said Paladino purchased a SIM card, which was put in an old iPhone given to Pleterski with two numbers saved in it: one for "John Doe," to communicate with the alleged kidnappers, the other for Gupta.
From there, he said Slime "threw the phone at me" and told him "kid, if you don't do this, your family is going to get smoked."

items: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies he was beaten, tortured during alleged kidnapping
Crypto King's alleged kidnappers’ trial hears call Aiden Pleterski made to landlord asking for $3M

blocks.text: Pleterski said Slime, Paladino and Henry dropped him off across the street from the Ritz-Carlton in downtown Toronto, where Gupta was living. More security footage was played in court of Pleterski outside the hotel that night.

He phoned Gupta, who he said told him "teams of police" were looking for him. Soon after an officer found him in the lobby of the hotel while Pleterski said he was on the phone with his father telling him he was OK.
Failed meeting

Earlier Monday, Pleterski also described how he was coached to set up a meeting with Gupta at a Tim Hortons in Toronto the previous day, but his alleged captors bailed on the meeting and started heading toward London, Ont.
"When [we] started going toward the highway, my heart sunk a little bit," said Pleterski. "When Slime said there were police there, I felt very scared of what they were going to do to me."
Gupta, testified about the same calls and attempted meeting last week during his own testimony as the Crown's first witness.
Sandeep Gupta, Pleterski's former landlord, testified last week at the trial of three men accused of kidnapping Pleterski. (Pam Davies/CBC)

Pleterski testified about how in London, he was allegedly hit in the face with a pistol and beaten with golf clubs after his alleged kidnappers learned someone he'd convinced them to call had contacted Pleterski's family trying to get money.
When they left the city, Pleterski said his alleged kidnappers appeared to follow a Dodge Durango to the Niagara Region, eventually stopping at the house where Pleterski later tried to escape.

While being led into the house, Pletersi testified that he recognized the voice of another man, who he said was present earlier in his kidnapping when he was forced to record a confession video in the basement of a home in the Pickering area, east of Toronto.
Pleterski is expected to continue his testimony Tuesday morning.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nicole Brockbank is a reporter for CBC Toronto's Enterprise Unit. She digs up, researches and reports GTA-focused investigative and enterprise stories. nicole.brockbank@cbc.ca

articles.title: Volunteers back in Manitoba after grounding of U.S. flights set them on long road trip home
articles.summary: A group of Manitobans doing volunteer work are back home after Friday's closure of U.S. airspace forced them on a long journey across that country.

image.caption: Doug Brown, a former Winnipeg Blue Bombers player working for a health-care equipment company, was among a group of about 40 people who took a 28-hour bus trip on their way back from a volunteer journey to Central America. (Submitted by Doug Brown)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New
A group of Manitobans doing volunteer work are back home after Friday's closure of U.S. airspace forced them on a long journey across that country.
28-hour bus trip anything but comfortable for about 40 returning from Nicaragua, including former Blue Bomber
Doug Brown was returning from Nicaragua with about 40 other volunteers with Operation Walk Manitoba, a charity that provides surgical treatments to people in developing countries.

The former Winnipeg Blue Bombers player works for a medical device company. He was aboard a flight from Managua to Houston, Texas, when he learned U.S. authorities had grounded flights nationwide, causing tens of thousands of flight cancellations over the weekend.
"We were literally just about an hour and a half out of Houston, and we all found out via the internet," Brown said Monday.
"I thought it was some sort of AI-fabricated joke."
The nationwide stop, the longest in 25 years, was in place for about four hours Friday.
U.S. officials said a contractor was replacing a copper wire with fibre optic cable when an unknown issue triggered an air traffic control system outage.
Brown's plane landed in Houston, but the outage delayed a connecting flight that would take the cohort of volunteers he was with to Denver.

items: Winnipeg film producer, family resume trip to L.A. after 24-hour delay in Minneapolis
Winnipeg airport asks passengers to check flight status amid U.S. stoppage

blocks.text: With cancellations rolling over into Saturday morning, the charity chartered a bus driving the volunteers back to Winnipeg instead.
The trip was about 28 hours long, Brown said.
"First stop, we went to Walmart just so we could get supplies," he said.
He bought pillows, a blanket, electrolyte water and a couple of apples.
Two Americans would alternate driving the bus, one taking over while the other slept.
"We didn't stop for dinner. We didn't stop overnight. We just essentially stopped when the bus needed fuel," Brown said.
"When we finally got to Winnipeg…, I almost laid down on the ground," he said.
"We hadn't showered or whatever in 24 hours. I was able to brush my teeth twice, but [it was the] first time I've done that at truck stops, right?…. It was a different world."
Sense of perspective

A team of nearly 70 volunteers was in Nicaragua for more than a week as part of the mission, with medical professionals performing hip replacement surgery to patients with severe joint disease who can't access that kind of care in the Central American country.
Medical lead Eric Bohm was in a cohort that managed to avoid disruptions while getting back to Manitoba.
Eric Bohm welcomed the volunteers who were left stranded in Texas after the U.S. ground stop. (Submitted by Doug Brown)
Bohm said those who made it home as planned wanted to make the other volunteers feel special. He was there to receive them at the end of their trip in Winnipeg.
"I thought … these guys are going to be tired and hungry and a little bit bummed out," Bohm said.
"Let's try to welcome them back home with some posters and some people showing up and some gift bags.… Just remind them, you know, how much the people in Nicaragua appreciate what they're doing."

items: Canada-wide flight grounding unlikely, says aviation expert

blocks.text: Brown said he used to take a bus with the Bombers to Regina for the Labour Day Classic, but those trips were only about a quarter of the length of the 28-hour journey over the weekend.
He said nobody wanted anyone else to be in charge of the music. Everyone also wanted to avoid using the one tiny bathroom that was available.
At six feet eight inches tall, sitting in the bus was uncomfortable enough for the former professional athlete.
But Brown said the trip to Nicaragua gave him a sense of perspective.
"One of the surgeons on the bus ride said, you know, Nicaragua was one of the poorest nations in the entire Western Hemisphere.…
"This is still nothing compared to what the vast majority of those people go through on a daily basis."
Senior officials in U.S. President Donald Trump's administration blamed the grounding on aging air traffic control infrastructure and Congress underfunding.
With files from Meaghan Ketcheson

articles.title: Meta would 'consider' pulling services from Canada if lawful access bill passes as is
articles.summary: Representatives from Meta say the social media company would have to "consider" pulling encryption services from Canada if the government's proposed lawful access bill passes without further changes.

image.caption: Meta services include Facebook, Instagram and the encrypted messaging app WhatsApp. (Richard Drew/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Updated
Representatives from Meta say the social media company would have to "consider" pulling encryption services from Canada if the government's proposed lawful access bill passes without further changes.
Company says government amendments don't protect encrypted data
Bill C-22 would force tech companies to adapt their systems so they all have the ability to hand over information to investigators with a warrant.

The legislation is currently being studied in the Senate, where Meta representatives said the bill leaves encrypted information — meant only to be viewed by users sharing the information — vulnerable to malicious actors.

"Ultimately, the Canadian government would be enforcing and imposing a law that it is not technically feasible to comply with and still offer secure, end-to-end encrypted services to Canadians," Robyn Greene, Meta's director of privacy and public policy, told senators on the national security committee on Monday evening.
Meta services include Facebook, Instagram and the encrypted messaging app WhatsApp.

When asked if the legislation would mean the company would pull some of its services from Canada, Meta's head of public policy for Canada Rachel Curran said the company would have to "review all of our options."
But she said it is something the company would have to "consider."
Minister of Public Safety Gary Anandasangaree proposed amendments to the lawful access legislation, but critics say they don't go far enough. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Bill C-22 also grants the minister the authority to issue confidential ministerial orders to electronic service providers (ESPs) operating in Canada, requiring them to build surveillance and monitoring capabilities into their systems. Orders would first be reviewed by the intelligence commissioner — an independent quasi-judicial official.
Before the bill was sent to the Senate in June, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree brought in amendments that put limits on when companies would be required to decrypt information.

Another change reduces the length of time that tech companies would have to retain metadata to six months from up to a year, after cybersecurity experts warned that data would be an attractive target for hackers.

items: Privacy watchdog urges Senate to further amend Bill C-22
Liberals to amend police data interception bill following searing criticism

blocks.text: Curran told the Senate committee that the government's amendments don't go far enough to protect encrypted data.
"They have protected just the core and not the outside layers that are an integral part of the encryption process," she said.
Encrypted messaging service Signal has also consistently said it would withdraw from Canada if the bill passes.
"If we are forced to choose between betraying our users and leaving Canada, we will not compromise the security of Canadians," Signal vice-president Udbhav Tiwari told the Senate committee.
Tiwari called on the government to make further changes to the bill, including explicit assurances to protect encrypted data.
Tech giant Apple also said earlier this month that the amendments aren't enough.

"While we appreciate attempts to improve C-22, the bill could still undermine Apple's ability to offer the powerful privacy and security features our users expect from us, including encryption, even as AI and other evolving technologies provide hackers with new tools to exploit cybersecurity weaknesses," the company said in a statement.
Privacy watchdog calls for changes

The government has argued that the bill is needed to ensure law enforcement has the legal tools to prevent, investigate and respond to modern crime and protect Canadians. Still, the proposed legislation has faced consistent pushback and this is the second lawful access bill the government has introduced this session.
Earlier this month, Privacy Commissioner Philippe Dufresne urged the Senate committee to further amend the legislation to better protect the privacy of Canadians.

The bill would lower the legal threshold for law enforcement and intelligence bodies to access basic subscriber information — like names, addresses, telephone numbers, email addresses and account numbers — from "reasonable grounds to believe" down to "reasonable grounds to suspect" that an offence has been or will be committed.
Dufresne said the definition of subscriber information and who can be asked to hand it over remain overly broad relative to the lowered threshold required to access it.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.
With files from Catharine Tunney and The Canadian Press

articles.title: WATCH: Philippines sees no threat from AI, says Lazaro
articles.summary: The DFA chief's remarks come amid protests against Pax Silica, a US-led initiative involving semiconductor and AI supply chains.

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 8:32am

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines does not consider artificial intelligence a threat and is eager to explore its potential, Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro said Monday, November 16, as Southeast Asian leaders discussed a South Korean proposal for AI cooperation.

articles.title: Kidnap, child marriage and poverty: Why millions of Nigerian children can't go to school
articles.summary: BBC World Service launches programme in Hausa for out-of-school children in West Africa.

blocks.text: Kidnap, child marriage and poverty: Why millions of Nigerian children can't go to school

blocks.caption: Image caption, Hadiza left school at 13 to get married and now spends her time doing housework

blocks.text: Image source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBC
Hadiza left school at 13 to get married and now spends her time doing housework
ByMadina Maishanu
BBC AfricaReporting fromGoronyo
As she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school.
"Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says.
One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village.
"They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We had to run away. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says.

Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home. For a short while she went to school here, but soon met a young man and, at the age of 13, stopped going to classes and got married.
"It's tradition here that once a girl is married, her education ends," she explains.
Now she lives with her in-laws and helps look after the home.
Although Nigerian law prohibits marriage under the age of 18, it is not always enforced.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Hadiza practises writing on the ground to make sure she doesn't forget the English alphabet

blocks.text: Hadiza practises writing on the ground to make sure she doesn't forget the English alphabet

Hadiza is one of nearly 19 million children in Nigeria who are missing out on an education, according to estimates shared by Unesco in 2024. That's about one in four of the country's school-age children.

Against this backdrop, the BBC World Service has launched Dars Hausa, an educational programme in the main language spoken in northern Nigeria, as well as neighbouring Niger, Cameroon and elsewhere in West Africa.

It brings English, maths and science lessons to children across West Africa, via social media, local television partnerships and radio. Many people in the region get their news from the radio and nearly half of households in Nigeria have one, according to the charity Save the Children.
Dars means "lesson" in Pashto and Dari, and it was first launched in those languages in 2023 for Afghan children barred from attending school. An Arabic version followed in February 2025.
The reasons why so many Nigerian children are out of school are numerous and complex. Like Hadiza, 12-year-old Rukayya also lives in the displacement camp in Goronyo.

blocks.caption: Image caption, After Rukayya's father was killed, she gave up school to earn money instead

blocks.text: After Rukayya's father was killed, she gave up school to earn money instead
"It pains me to see other children studying and going to school while I cannot," she says.
As the eldest child, each day Rukayya goes out to gather firewood to sell and to beg so that her younger siblings can have something to eat.
"If my father was alive, I wouldn't have to go out and beg," she explains, saying some people mock her "but it doesn't stop me because it is our only way to survive."
Bandits killed her father about a year ago in front of her, she says, and her family fled from their home to the camp.

She and Hadiza are among 670,000 people in north-west and central Nigeria who have been forced from their homes by armed robbery and kidnappings, according to the International Organization for Migration.

items: Three Girls: Lessons in Limbo features the stories of Hadiza and Rukayya - you can watch the full film on YouTube, external

blocks.text: Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by criminal gangs, known in Nigeria as bandits, who steal, kill and kidnap.
The school that Hadiza once attended in Goronyo is the only one serving children in the camp and typically has about 50 students in each class.

One of the teachers, Kamilu Sulaiman Jakada, says that even though lessons are free, only a tiny portion of the children attend, and even then sporadically, because parents tell him that "it is the children that are the breadwinners" and they need to earn money to eat.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Armed gangs, poverty and lack of funding all have a huge impact on children's education, says teacher Kamilu Sulaiman Jakada

blocks.text: Armed gangs, poverty and lack of funding all have a huge impact on children's education, says teacher Kamilu Sulaiman Jakada
He says the school does not have enough teachers or classrooms, explaining that funding is inconsistent and often comes from individuals or organisations rather than the government.

The other challenge is the bandits. A gang once came to the school on motorbikes, shooting in the air, he says, and although no-one was hurt, many parents were scared and withdrew their children. That has been parents' reaction to attacks in some other parts of the country too.
Every Nigerian child is meant to get nine years of free, compulsory education - six in primary and three in secondary school. Responsibility is shared between federal, state and local governments.
But many schools are facing shortages and poorer families who cannot afford private education can struggle to pay for uniforms, books and transport.
The crisis has built up over decades, with successive governments struggling to address chronic underfunding and poor oversight of resources.
In addition, many children in the traditional Almajiri system, which provides Islamic education, are not taught subjects such as maths and science, and are considered by Unicef to be out of school.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Many of Nigeria's schools face shortages of teachers, classrooms and learning materials after years of underfunding and lack of oversight

blocks.text: Many of Nigeria's schools face shortages of teachers, classrooms and learning materials after years of underfunding and lack of oversight

Minister of State for Education Prof Suwaiba Sa'id believes the number of children out of school is lower than has been reported, but admits that with Nigeria's growing population "the proper investment, the proper oversight, has not been done… I will not mention the names, but we know of two states that did not recruit a single teacher for eight years".

She says that education is the government's "number-one priority" and initiatives such as Lumina are designed to help address "decades of neglect". Lumina aims to support one million girls by 2030, providing an accelerated learning programme for older girls who have missed years of formal education.
She also says that "the government is doing everything possible" to deal with bandits and that "we have seen children that should be at school but are engaged in this banditry".

In the meantime, it is children like Hadiza and Rukayya that the BBC World Service Dars Hausa programmes aim to help. Hadiza says she still has a dream to one day become a doctor "to help my fellow women".

Dars Hausa will air on BBC News Hausa radio on Sundays at 06:45 West Africa Time, with a repeat at 20:45. The programme will also be available via BBC News Hausa's digital platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, X and Instagram.
