articles.title: Germany beat Netherlands 5-0 to win Nations League group
articles.summary: Florian Wirtz scored twice as Germany cruised to a comfortable 5-0 win over the Netherlands to qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals on Monday.

image.caption: Flying high — Florian Wirtz and his teammates schooled neighbor and rival the Netherlands at Berlin Olympic Stadium in Monday's Nations League quarterfinalsImage: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany dominated neighbor and historic rival the Netherlands in their Nations League quarterfinal match-up at Berlin's Olympic Stadium on Monday evening.
It was the team's sixth game underhead coach Jürgen Klopp and the 50th ever between the two sides.

Germany's 5-0 shellacking of the Oranje was their most lopsided victory since 1959, when they won 7-0. In all, Germany have now won 19 of those matches, the Netherlands have won 12, and 18 ended in a draw.

Speaking to German broadcaster ARD after the game,attacking midfielder Florian Wirtz — who scored twice in the fixture — said: "We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second half."
Despite the loss, Xavi Hernandez's Dutch side will reach the final eight alongside Germany.
Prior to the match, Klopp had made it clear that he and his team were approaching Monday's showdown as a final after having lost to Greece 1-0 in his first home game in the job on September 27.
By night's end, Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck each scored once and Brajan Gruda scored once and added two assists on top of Wirtz's double.

Klopp has been high on Wirtz, who hascome under fire for not delivering at Liverpool since his arrival there in June 2025,and his bet seems to be paying off with the 23-year-old now scoring four goals in his last four games for Germany.

"We don't care who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," said Wirtz on Monday evening before adding: "We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team."

articles.title: Data centres in the U.S. put out more carbon emissions in a year than Denmark, says Harvard study
articles.summary: The 400 largest data centres in the United States put more heat-trapping gases into the atmosphere in one year than the entire nation of Denmark did, and that was before the artificial intelligence…

image.caption: In this aerial photo, an Amazon data centre is under construction Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in New Florence, Mo. A new study estimates that the massive electricity demands of hyperscale data centres in the U.S., combined with the fact that more than half of their electricity is generated through fossil

blocks.text: The 400 largest data centres in the United States put more heat-trapping gases into the atmosphere in one year than the entire nation of Denmark did, and that was before the artificial intelligence boom really got going, according to a Harvard University study published Monday.
Researchers found that more than half of the electricity powering hyperscale data centres in the U.S. was generated using fossil fuels, contributing to a significant increase in emissions.

The study results come as negotiators at the United Nations COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, which the U.S. skipped this year, launched a voluntary pledge Monday calling on companies and countries to power the world's data centres with clean energy and be more transparent about their power and water consumption and emissions.

"We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said Monday during the launch of the pledge. "Claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now, making climate disasters even worse."
As public opposition to data centres continues to mount, the political backlash has played out in U.S. elections and major local objections for new sites.

In Canada, plans for massive data centres have triggered protests in communities across the country, including this fall over a proposed data centre for AI giant Anthropic in Nova Scotia and a $52-billion data centre near Regina, Saskatchewan.
Inside the climate toll of data centres

Harvard researchers looked at 403 of the largest U.S. data centres between May 2024 and April 2025, using available data and modelling to analyze their electricity use and emissions. They estimated electricity used by the centres produced around 28.3 million tons (25.7 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide, according to the study in Monday's Nature Sustainability.
The Dave Johnson coal-fired power plant is silhouetted against the morning sun in Glenrock, Wyo. in this 2018 file photo. (J. David Ake/ The Associated Press)

More than half their 82 terawatt-hours of electricity use, enough to power nearly seven million homes for a year, came from fossil fuels, the primary cause of global warming, the researchers found. Coal, widely considered the most environmentally damaging fossil fuel, generated 15 per cent of the electricity used.

items: Protests across Nova Scotia oppose AI data centres
Why are there suddenly so many data centres planned in Canada? Your questions answered

blocks.text: The emissions estimate is two to three times higher than previous studies had shown, said Francesca Dominici, the study's senior author and a Harvard biostatistics professor.
Big emitters 'profiting' from the planet's destruction: UN chief

"It is the equivalent to the CO2 emission of an entire state like Michigan or a small European country," Dominici said, adding that plans for 2,000 more data centres make that quantity more worrisome for the future. "We are going backwards toward the goal of controlling CO2 emissions."

items: Canada presented itself as a global leader in methane reductions at COP31. But is Alberta holding it back?
Why data centre communities worry about water
Bell AI data centre expansion raises questions over power, water and local impact

blocks.text: Researchers noted that data centre construction has only expanded since the study period, meaning emissions from this industry are probably even higher now.

"What we're seeing is already striking, but it's only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry," lead author Gianluca Guidi, postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics, said in a press release.
Nova Scotians rally against planned $10B AI facility

Several outside experts in climate, energy and artificial intelligence said Monday's study reached realistic conclusions and that its use of modelling was reasonable because companies disclose little about their power consumption and pollution.

"We cannot manage environmental impacts effectively without reliable measurements and disclosure," said Fengqi You, a Cornell University energy systems scientist who wasn't involved in the study. "Ultimately, the environmental footprint of AI is not fixed. It depends on where we build data centres, how efficiently they operate, and how we supply their electricity."
'Selling us hope while hiding the harms'

The Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge, launched by COP31 host Turkey and the International Telecommunication Union, says data centres should use clean power and efficient energy and water systems.
Canada's new data centre guidelines lack teeth, critics say

The pledge says the environmental impacts of data centres should be assessed and disclosed, but it also calls for harnessing artificial intelligence to help address climate change, which some climate experts see as a contradiction given AI's growing environmental footprint.

items: 'The planet is not dying, it is being killed' - Thunberg at COP 31
Canada can't control climate change on its own, economist tells landmark trial
Canada's credibility on the line at COP31 as it defends fossil fuel expansion while trumpeting clean energy

blocks.text: The explosion of new and planned data centres has driven demand for new sources of power generation and contributed to some of the biggest tech companies missing their climate goals, according to a report by the advocacy group Climate Action Against Disinformation.

The report, published earlier this month, found that electricity consumption by Amazon, Microsoft and Google had risen 240 per cent between 2022 and 2025 amid the AI race. Its authors accused Big Tech of "greenwashing" AI by obscuring its current environmental impact behind claims of future climate gains.
Can AI save the planet before it wrecks it

Former U.S. vice-president and climate advocate Al Gore said that while it is essential for data centres to be powered by carbon-free energy, he is hopeful their computing power could help find new ways to fight climate change.

items: AI is increasingly being used to deal with climate change, but it has its own emissions problem

blocks.text: In an interview with The Associated Press, Gore cited research by prominent British economist and climate advocate Nicholas Stern, who predicted that by 2030 "we will see 6 to 9 per cent reduction in emissions of greenhouse gases because of the use of advanced AI in finding new ways to be far more efficient in the use of materials and energy."

Caleb Max, president of the National Artificial Intelligence Association, said, "AI will solve not only the energy usage issues that data centres face, but unlock numerous currently unknown advances in science and technology that will address climate change and make lives better for humanity. I respect the concerns about energy and water consumption from data centres, but the fears may be overblown."
But Climate Action Against Disinformation spokesman Philip Newell was skeptical.
"We have hope in one hand and then harms in the other," Newell said. "They're selling us hope while hiding the harms from us."

articles.title: United Airlines says ‘widespread’ system outage resolved
articles.summary:
Airline acknowledges ‘technology issue that delayed flight departures’ in latest high-profile outage to affect Americans

United ⁠Airlines said on ⁠Monday ⁠that it had resolved ⁠a widespread…

blocks.text: United ⁠Airlines said on ⁠Monday ⁠that it had resolved ⁠a widespread system ⁠outage, just three days after the Federal ⁠Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop on all US flights.

“We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures. While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” United said in a statement. “There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”

According to an internal memo from ​United’s pilots’ ‌union seen ‌by Reuters, a company-wide ‌web-based outage had affected multiple applications used by pilots, including crew communications. It said United was unable to provide final ‌aircraft weights for departing flights and advised pilots to ​follow airport station guidance on whether to leave their gates.

The United computer issue is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown to affect Americans in the last few days. On Friday, ageing equipment led to a temporary grounding of all commercial airplanes in the US for more than four hours, sparking travel chaos as thousands of flights were delayed or canceled.
The Trump administration said the rare ground stop stemmed from a fiber upgrade during routine maintenance that led to data flooding, which crashed a critical communication system.

And earlier on Monday, customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.

It also comes after a major outage by Microsoft that began on Thursday and lasted into the next day, which crippled a host of services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. The outage had serious repercussions for millions of people and organizations all over the world, including schools, hospitals, businesses, courts, banks, prisons, police forces and governments.

Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The office software giant did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, identifying in an initial report on Monday that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity sparked the outage.

articles.title: The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
articles.summary: From legal-tech to healthcare, dozens of Indian AI start-ups are solving uniquely Indian challenges.

blocks.text: In 2020, Sanjay Mandava flew down from Chicago to Chennai in southern India to resolve a personal land dispute.
Over the next few months, he was running around between government offices to access a dozen records that would conclusively prove that the property belonged to his family.
Just a sale deed dating back to when his parents bought the land was not enough. Authorities asked him to produce a string of other documents.

Frustrated by the experience, he built Landeed - an AI-led digital platform that enables users to aggregate fragmented, multi-source land-records, verify titles and conduct legal checks at the click of a few buttons, across 24 states in India.
He's solving a problem that is uniquely Indian.

"In the US or UK, when you purchase a property, the government verifies ownership. In India by contrast, we follow presumptive titling - the buyer is responsible for establishing ownership. A sale deed merely records the transaction - multiple other documents may be needed to prove title," Mandava told the BBC.
These include building certificates, property tax receipts and land survey maps among others.
The system is rife for misuse - property disputes account for a bulk of civil litigation cases in the country where some 80% of household wealth is held in real estate.
Landeed has mapped large swathes of India using geo-spatial technology and data from state land revenue departments, registration offices, survey records and municipal databases.
Using this, it has linked registered properties to their official land identification and survey numbers and ownership records.
An additional AI-layer can read these titles, extract information and spot inconsistencies within minutes - a process that takes lawyers and brokers several days.

With the largest repository of title data in the country, consisting of 1.8 billion documents, the app is now used by millions of individual and enterprise customers while doing real estate transactions.

The app is among a burgeoning list of Indian start-ups trying to address some of India's most complex challenges in sectors ranging from legal-tech to healthcare, infrastructure, education and agriculture using AI.

Unlike the US and China which have a global dominance in building frontier language models like ChatGPT, India's AI revolution is happening downstream in data centre infrastructure and consumer applications rather than in research.

Start-ups are solving issues for everything from pothole detection to tribal language translation to assisting overworked public-health professionals with medical tasks - often working with highly fragmented, multilingual datasets in extremely cost sensitive industries.
Bengaluru-based YouTube teacher Gaurav Sen's AI app detects potholes using a dash-cam, satellite-based navigation and an AI vision model to analyse images.
It then identifies civic officials responsible for fixing them and sends them this data. He got viral attention recently given how widespread the menace of potholes is across India's urban sprawls.
On last count, there are at least half a dozen other similar offerings that map and report road damage to authorities across the country.
"A municipal corporation can take the app and use it on public buses and taxis, to access real-time, updated data on road conditions," Sen told the BBC.
In Mumbai on India's western coast, Fractal Analytics - among the few Indian listed AI companies - has deployed its AI tool "Vaidya" in hospitals run by the local civic authority.

The app allows citizens to receive AI-generated, simplified summaries of their lab reports in multiple languages, identify nearby healthcare facilities based on their needs and gives doctors AI-guided pre-consultation support such as medical history and medication details of patients.

It also provides hospital administrators with a public health dashboard based on aggregated, anonymous insights from lab reports accessed through its tie-up with municipal hospitals, giving them crucial visibility into emerging infections or other disease trends.

This boom has led to a surge in funding for AI start-ups - up 265% year-on-year according to Inc42, external, a start-up information platform. They raised over $1bn in the first nine months of this year amid a relatively muted fundraising environment for the broader ecosystem.
Yet, these companies face an uphill task in commercialising their ideas and taking them beyond pilot.

"The cost of building in India is sometimes much higher than what Indian customers are willing to pay," Fractal's co-founder Srikanth Velamakanni told the BBC at his sprawling office overlooking Mumbai's film city.
"The computing power needed to run an AI model is the same whether it is built in India or the US - but American customers have a far bigger paying capacity than those here."
Indian AI founders are also being forced to build around scarcity, with availability of high quality chips at the right scale and price, a major impediment for many.
"I believe I am building one of the most impactful things for this country," says Mandava.
"But I am starved for GPUs [chips that perform millions of calculations and help train AI models]. I have a hellish time trying to acquire them," he says.
The country has promised its start-ups 38,000 GPUs through its government-led AI mission, external, but demand for this compute power is far greater than supply.
Cumbersome regulation and bureaucracy are other major challenges.
Without these fundamental issues being addressed, there's a risk that Indian AI companies will build shallow solutions that a next generation of founders will immediately make redundant, say experts.

"Someone like a Google will probably laugh if I tell them of my pilot. To make it sustainable and hard to replicate, it will have to be much more sophisticated," says Sen, displaying a self-awareness of where his product currently stands.

From a lack of experienced talent to the struggle to turn successful pilots into recurring government contracts to heavy dependence on expensive foreign technology, Indian founders are powering through many odds.
"We can still do it. We don't want protection, but propel us, give us the weapons to compete against the best," Mandava says, when asked what he wants from policymakers.
"To quote Jay-Z - I can't help the poor if I'm one of them," he adds.

articles.title: Father calls for apology after son target of racist taunts at Kitchener, Ont., hockey tournament
articles.summary: The father of a 16-year-old hockey player says he wants a public apology and cultural-competency training for the league after his son was the target of racist taunts at a tournament in Kitchener,…

image.caption: Ryder Doxtator of the Brantford 99ers and his dad Aaron Doxtator at Little NHL. (Submitted by Aaron Doxtator)

blocks.text: Indigenous

The father of a 16-year-old hockey player says he wants a public apology and cultural-competency training for the league after his son was the target of racist taunts at a tournament in Kitchener, Ont., on Nov. 8.
Kitchener Minor Hockey Association and ALLIANCE Hockey investigating
In a video provided to CBC Indigenous, a player on the Kitchener Jr. Rangers can be heard telling Brantford 99ers player Ryder Doxtator "Go back to the rez."

Aaron Doxtator, Ryder's father, from Oneida Nation of the Thames, was at his son's game Nov. 8. He said his son told him that he'd also been called a "dirty Indian" by the same player. Although Aaron Doxtator said he was unable to hear it from the stands, he said other players and staff on Ryder's team and parents told him they also heard the slur.
As a former athlete in hockey and lacrosse who experienced this type of racism throughout his playing career, Aaron Doxtator said he can't believe it's still happening.
Ryder Doxtator of the Brantford 99ers was told to 'go back to the rez' by a player on the Kitchener Jr. Rangers. (Submitted by Aaron Doxtator)

"It's always the same words, 'Go back to where you came from. Go back to the rez, you dirty Indian, or go back to your teepees.' Those are all different words I've heard growing up … My older son, happened to him all the way up," Aaron Doxtator said.
"You just get a gross feeling in your stomach when you hear those words."
He said despite being proud of his home, "They're making you feel like you're lower, 'Get out of here. You know you don't belong here.'"

Doxtator said there was a brawl just after Ryder scored a goal with one minute left in the game. The referees broke it up and Ryder was put in the penalty box along with two teammates and three Kitchener Jr. Rangers players.
Doxtator said they were arguing back and forth and a Brantford 99ers trainer went over to the box "to try to defuse the situation and tell our player to calm down."
He said she and a couple of the other parents heard the Kitchener players saying 'go back to the rez' and 'go back to where you came from.'
He was told by officials that the video was under review.
Doxtator said this isn't the first time his son's dealt with racist taunts from opponents.
"It angered him because he's heard that before and it's discriminatory … We should be equal with people," he said.
He said he's lodged formal complaints with leagues before, but they just get "brushed under the rug" and "nothing comes of it."
2 pending investigations into incident
The Kitchener Minor Hockey Association (KMHA) said it received several emails regarding the incident and there are two investigations looking into the incident.

Roland Cyr, general manager for KMHA, said in an emailed statement to CBC Indigenous that KMHA "is aware of allegations involving the use of a racial slur during a game conducted under the jurisdiction of the association."

The statement continued that KMHA is also aware that the matter was reported to the on-ice officials during the game, who documented the allegations and submitted the report to the Minor Hockey Alliance of Ontario (ALLIANCE Hockey) for review.
The statement said KMHA takes the allegations seriously "and is committed to ensuring a safe, respectful, and inclusive environment for all participants in our sport."
It said in accordance with its policies, KMHA will be undertaking a review of the incident and ALLIANCE Hockey, the governing body for both teams, will conduct its own investigation.
Brantford 99ers general manager Kevin Murray declined to comment as the investigation is ongoing.
ALLIANCE Hockey said in an emailed statement it is aware “of an alleged incident that occurred on Nov. 8 at the Kitchener Blueline Tournament" and is taking it seriously.
Previously in 2022, one of KMHA's U-13 Kitchener Lady Rangers players used a racial slur against an opponent and the team had to issue an apology and take part in diversity training.
Racial slurs pop out as they're 'still part of their lexicon,' says academic
Janelle Joseph, Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Racial Justice, Health and Sport at Brock University in St. Catharines, Ont., said incidents like this are sad but not surprising.
Joseph said there's been a lot of work around racial and gender justice in hockey which "continues to be run predominantly by that white majority."
"We are in the midst of a culture shift, but we're not on the other side of it," she said.
Joseph said players understand there are phrases they shouldn't say, "but if it's still part of their lexicon … when they get into the heat of a conflict, it spurts out."

Janelle Joseph is a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Racial Justice, Health and Sport at Brock University and associate professor. She's also the founder and director of Canada's first research laboratory devoted to issues of race and movement cultures, the Indigeneity, Diaspora, Equity and Anti-racism in Sport (IDEAS) Research Lab. (Submitted by Janelle Joseph)

"That means that it was just always there. They were learning ways to cover it up or ways to communicate that would be more socially acceptable. But the anti-Indigenous racism, anti-Black racism, anti-immigrant and xenophobia is underlying in many, many of our communities."
Beyond superficial anti-racism training, Joseph said all teams would benefit from open dialogue about history and "what those expressions mean."
"When someone says 'go back to the rez,' what are they really saying there?" she said.
"I think we need to surface those kinds of conversations across every locker room, every team, so that we can start to make racism not something that happens over there, with those other people."
She said then we can start to see how some of those ideologies and understandings about who belongs and who doesn't are part of the dominant culture.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Candace Maracle is Kanien'kehá:ka, Wolf Clan from Tyendinaga Mohawk Territory. She has a master’s degree in journalism from Toronto Metropolitan University. Her latest short film, Tsi ní:yoht yonkwayentá:’on ne óhses (How We Got Maple Syrup) is completely in the Kanien’kéha language.

articles.title: The U.K. is granting pardons to women for past abortion convictions
articles.summary: The U.K. government says it will grant automatic pardons to all women convicted of having illegal abortions over the last 165 years.

image.caption: Pro-choice protesters gather near U.K. Parliament during a vote to decriminalize abortion in June 2025. (Alishia Abodunde/Getty Images)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New
The U.K. government says it will grant automatic pardons to all women convicted of having illegal abortions over the last 165 years.
'Today is a historic day,' says a friend of a woman charged in 2020
The U.K. government is granting automatic pardons to all women convicted of having illegal abortions over the last 165 years.

What's more, it says it will expunge the records of those who have been investigated for abortion offences related to their own pregnancies, regardless of whether they were ultimately arrested or charged.

U.K. Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who successfully fought to decriminalize abortion last year, says these clean records will bring justice to women who were "dragged from hospital beds to police cells."

"This trauma cannot be erased," Antoniazzi said. "I hope that this offers some alleviation of the pain these women have endured, enabling them to participate fully in society again, living their lives to the full, working the jobs they've always wanted to."
It started with decriminalization
The U.K.'s Abortion Act of 1967 allows legal abortions up to 24 weeks, under a specific set of criteria agreed upon by two doctors.

Until last year, women in England and Wales could be charged for procuring abortions outside that framework under a Victorian-era abortion ban, which is still on the books and carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment.

But in April 2025, U.K. Parliament voted to amend its Crime and Policing Bill so that people could not be prosecuted for "an abortion offence relating to their own pregnancy." It recieved royal assent in April of this year, and those amendments came into force on Monday.
The measure was opposed by anti-abortion groups that argued it would open the door to abortion on demand at any stage of pregnancy.
But advocates cited what they described as an alarming increase in women being investigated for abortion-related offences, including several high-profile cases.

Nicola Packer, left, and her friend Helle Tumbridge. Packer was criminally charged in 2020 after she took legally prescribed abortion pills at home, not realizing she was past the legal threshold of 24 weeks. (Submitted by Helle Tumbridge)
Among them was Nicola Packer, who was criminally charged after she took legally prescribed abortion pills during the COVID-19 lockdown in 2020.
Packer, who argued she didn't know she was past the 24-week threshold for legal abortion, was cleared in a jury trial last year.
"It's a bittersweet day for her," Packer's friend and spokesperson, Helle Tumbridge, told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.
"She is, of course, pleased that this has happened … but, for her, this really never should have happened in the first place. And she will live with the trauma for the rest of her life."
LISTEN | Interview with Helle Tumbridge:
As It Happens6:36U.K. grants pardons to women convicted of having abortions. One advocate calls it a 'historic,' but 'bittersweet day'
Tumbridge says Packer experienced what's known as a cryptic pregnancy, which means that she didn't experience the tell-tale signs she was expecting.

As a result, she believed she was only a few weeks pregnant when she procured an over-the-phone prescription for mifepristone and misoprostol. It turned out, however, that she was 26 weeks pregnant, and the medication induced a stillbirth.
She required emergency surgery in hospital and, when she awoke, two police officers were waiting for her in the recovery room.
"Then, when she'd barely recovered, they took her off to the police station, where she was subjected to questioning and appalling treatment for a length of time," Tumbridge said.
"It took five years for her case to come to trial, so she was living all that time with this horrible trauma and stress, her life was on hold. And it was incredibly hard."
Tumbridge says her friend suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder and has authorized her to act as her voice in media interviews so she doesn't have to relive her experiences.
"While today is a historic day, it's an amazing day, and all campaigners and women everywhere are celebrating, I think for Nicola and the women involved, it is also a very difficult day," she said.
Doctors and abortion providers hail decision
The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) welcomed the decision in a joint letter with several reproductive rights organizations.

"Today's pardons are an important next step," said Dr. Alison Wright, RCOG's president. "They recognize the injustice of historical convictions and mean women no longer have to live with the consequences of a criminal record for something that should never have been treated as a crime."
The British Pregnancy Advisory Service, a U.K. charity and abortion provider, also welcomed the news.
"For too long, women have faced the devastating consequences of outdated abortion laws," said Heidi Stewart, the organization's chief executive.

The Society for the Protection of Unborn Children (SPUC), a U.K. anti-abortion group that opposed decriminalization, called the pardons an attempt to impose a "barbaric ideology on a past that showed more respect for human life."
In a written statement, SPUC spokesperson Alithea Williams decried the measure as "performative virtue signalling."
The Society for the Protection of Unborn Children organized a rally against the U.K.'s decriminalization measure in March 2026. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)
The government has not said how many women will receive pardons or have their records cleared.
But Antoniazzi estimates that more than 100 women were investigated for abortion-related offences in the five years preceding last year's decriminalization vote.
According to the Guardian newspaper, those investigations include women, and at least one teenager, who were later determined to have had natural stillbirths and miscarriages.

items: Conservatives lose candidate for Pontiac after reporting on anti-abortion, 2SLGBTQ+ remarks
How Gloria Steinem and her colleagues set out to 'change the world' with Ms. Magazine

blocks.text: The U.K. government says the pardons and record wipings will be automatic, and those affected don't need to take any actions.
Tumbridge, meanwhile, says Packer is calling for an official apology from the government, the police and the Crown Prosecution Service.
"We've had women doing jail time. It's really shocking," she said. "These cases should never have been brought to trial."
With files from The Associated Press. Interview with Helle Tumbridge produced by Nishat Chowhury

articles.title: Baby sea turtles swim out to sea after historic California nesting
articles.summary:
Hatchlings emerge after discovery in September of first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on US west coast

Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have…

blocks.text: Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific.

The eggs incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach after the historic discovery of two separate nests in September at southern California beaches, a shift likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions.

On Saturday, the Aquarium of the Pacific announced the turtles’ first emergence in a social media post: “The hatchlings are here! We are excited to share that some of the olive ridley sea turtle eggs from Seal Beach successfully hatched after a 58-day incubation period. Working with our partners, we carefully released them from the beach in the dark early hours of this morning.”

A day later, the Aquarium added: “Even more egg-citing news! A second group of olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings, this time from the Huntington Beach nest, was released into the ocean early Sunday morning.”

blocks.caption: Olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings are released in Huntington Beach, California. Photograph: Robin Riggs/Aquarium of the Pacific

blocks.text: In total, 54 turtles were released from the Seal Beach nest and 21 from the Huntington Beach nest.

On September 16, an olive ridley sea turtle was observed digging a nest and laying eggs on Seal Beach in the first-recorded instance of any sea turtle nesting on the west coast. Three days later, a second turtle was spotted nesting on Huntington Beach.
Typically a tropical species, the olive ridley sea turtle normally resides in the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans, but has been known to nest on the southern tip of Baja California.

“It is not known why these turtles chose southern California beaches as nesting sites, but it indicates an important historical change that could have long-term implications for the species and for local sea turtle management and protection,” the Aquarium of the Pacific said in a social media post.

“The behavior of these turtles was probably influenced, at least in part, by the incoming El Niño, along with, the recent tropical storm, range expansion, or perhaps navigational mistakes. The species is also known for its behavioral flexibility.”

As Hurricane Polo began to form in late September, researchers with the aquarium and its federal and local partners relocated the 204 eggs from the two nests to incubate in the safety of the aquarium’s animal care facility.

“As animals adapt in unexpected ways to changes in their natural world, humans will need to adapt and make space to ensure endangered and threatened species are given a fighting chance,” said Jeff Flocken, president and CEO of the Aquarium of the Pacific.

“If they successfully hatch, these baby turtles will likely one day return to nest to carry on future generations on these very same beaches, giving us a remarkable opportunity to help a species expand its range and thrive.”

Even as the Huntington Beach and Seal Beach turtles have begun hatching and returned to the ocean, researchers are continuing to advise the public to be on the lookout for more nests. On 1 November, a third nest was recorded in Ventura county although those eggs were swept away by unusually high tides – likely also caused by El Niño.

articles.title: Military's No. 2 defends GlobalEye surveillance jets despite capability concerns
articles.summary: Canada's second-in-command is standing behind the proposed purchase of six Saab GlobalEye surveillance jets despite air force concerns about their capabilities. Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee told MPs…

image.caption: Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee is seen at a conference in Ottawa in March. He told MPs on Monday that he's satisfied with the program to purchase Saab's GlobalEye. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Canada's second-in-command is standing behind the proposed purchase of six Saab GlobalEye surveillance jets despite air force concerns about their capabilities. Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee told MPs he's satisfied with the procurement process, arguing the aircraft will contribute to an integrated continental defence network alongside satellites and ground-based radar systems.
Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee tells committee he's satisfied with program
The second in command of the Canadian military told parliamentarians on Monday that he's satisfied with the way the program to buy airborne early warning planes is unfolding.

Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee made the comments in testimony before the House of Commons defence committee, which is studying Bill C-40, legislation intended to turn the Defence Investment Agency (DIA) into a Crown corporation.

Earlier this year, Prime Minister Mark Carney surprised many in the defence community by announcing Canada opened negotiations with Swedish defence giant Saab to purchase six of their GlobalEye surveillance jets — aircraft that would be militarized in Canada based upon a Bombardier 6500 airframe.
The federal government and the company have since agreed on a term sheet, a non-binding document that sets the stage for an eventual contract.

items: Feds sign preliminary deal with Saab for 6 GlobalEye aircraft
Ottawa chose surveillance plane without knowing it met military needs

blocks.text: In early September, multiple sources told CBC News that the air force was concerned the GlobalEye meets only a handful of the military's requirements.

On Monday, federal Conservatives pressed Topshee, the vice-chief of the defence staff, for assurances that military requirements would not be sacrificed for the sake of building up the country's defence industrial base.
"I am comfortable with the path we're proceeding down," Topshee told the three-party committee, referring to the GlobalEye program.

He said the airborne surveillance capability is crucial for the defence of North America and ties into an integrated air and missile defence system with the United States — a program U.S. President Donald Trump has nicknamed the Golden Dome.
Canada chose GlobalEye spy plane without knowing military's needs: sources
Topshee defended the choice of the GlobalEye, saying that NATO also plans to acquire it.
The air force, however, is concerned that the plane, under its current design and configuration, doesn't have 360-degree radar coverage and that blind spots are created during turns.
There are also concerns about the range and frequency of the radar.
Saab has proposed modifications, putting additional radar sets in the nose and tail.

The air force also has concerns about the number of crew stations and connectivity equipment to plug the plane into the NORAD network, which would limit the GlobalEye's ability to offer a "control" function during operations that involve a series of military assets.

items: Canada receives first F-35 jets from U.S., as full order remains under review

blocks.text: The military is also seeking a radar plane that can be refuelled in flight to cover the vast expanses of the Arctic, a feature that is not currently included on the GlobalEye.
"Every platform has advantages and disadvantages," Topshee said.
He also testified that the modern battlespace is changing rapidly with the introduction of drones and autonomous systems.
To maintain surveillance, the military, Topshee said, would rely on not only the GlobalEye, but also ground-based radar and satellites to get "the full picture."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

articles.title: United Airlines resolves tech outage that delayed flights
articles.summary: Hundreds of departing flights were delayed. The issue comes just days after an air traffic control outage caused major disruption to US airlines.

image.caption: The latest outage underscores airlines' reliance on computer systemsImage: Charly Triballeau/AFP

blocks.text: United Airlines said a temporary widespread technology outage affected hundreds of departing flights on Monday.
Flight tracker FlightAware said 418 United flights were delayed on Monday afternoon.
The issue comes three days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network grounded flights across the US on Friday.
What did United Airlines say about Monday's tech issues?
United Airlines said there was "no indication" that Monday's outage was the result of a cyberattack.
There was also no indication that the issues affecting United Airlines on Monday were related to Friday's nationwide shutdown.
US lifts nationwide air travel ground stop, but disruptions continue
United Airlines said later on Monday that it had "resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures."
The airline added that airborne flights, as well as those operated by its regional brand United Express, were not affected.
The disruption on Friday and Monday highlights how vulnerable air travel is to tech failures.
Disruption follows other recent major tech meltdowns
United Airlines' computer problem comes amid other recent similar high-profile technology meltdowns, including Friday's nationwide grounding.
Thousands of people in the US said they were unable to access their online banking accounts at several large US banks, after JPMorgan Chase reported a technical issue.
On Thursday, Microsoft saw a major disruption to its services, including its Outlook email and Teams messenger.
The tech company said Saturday that its services had been fully restored.
Worldwide Microsoft outage causes widespread disruption

articles.title: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
articles.summary: Attorney General Rob Bonta alleges OpenAI misled and endangered the public

blocks.text: Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.
The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.
Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.

"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.
OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.

"We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said.
The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents.
Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about".
"OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said.

articles.title: Taking Korea's toughest exam from behind bars
articles.summary: Eleven convicts at the Mandela Boys' School will be among the thousands of young Koreans taking the country's hardest exam, the Suneung.

blocks.text: Students intently focus on maths formulas written on a board before lowering their heads and taking notes as the teacher works through a sum.
The teacher's voice and the scratch of pens fill the room.
At first glance, this could be any classroom in South Korea.
But thick metal bars cover the windows and the students are wearing blue prison uniforms and rubber shoes emblazoned with the words "Korea Correctional Service".

This is Mandela Boys' School, an education facility for young prisoners inside the Seoul Southern Correctional Institution in Guro, south-west Seoul. In South Korea, young people who are sentenced to imprisonment by a criminal court must serve their time in prison.

"The boys here have committed serious offences and received criminal sentences," Jeong Yeo-gyeong, a correctional officer in the Korea Correctional Service's social reintegration division, told the BBC.
"As well as theft, there is a high proportion of serious offences, including violence, bodily injury, sexual violence and robbery."
But by opening educational institutes like Mandela, authorities are hoping to give these young offenders a chance to better their lives after they serve out their sentences.

Opened by the justice ministry in March 2023, it allows boys who were aged 17 and under when their sentences became final to prepare for school equivalency exams as well as the Suneung - the country's notoriously difficult university entrance examination - while still serving their sentences.
Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.
Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.
The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.
A total of 551,864 people have applied to take this year's Suneung on 19 November.
Around 30 prisoners are enrolled in the Suneung preparation class at Mandela Boys' School, and 11 of them have applied to take this year's exam.
Park Soo-young (not his real name), a 17-year-old inmate, has been at the Mandela Boys' Suneung preparation class for two months and hopes to study social welfare.
He tells the BBC that he had dreams of becoming a police officer before committing the crime that landed him behind bars.
He says he could not bring himself to look properly at his mother during his trial. When he turned towards her after his sentence was announced, she was crying.

"Seeing her like that, I broke down too. I wondered how I was going to live from then on, and how I could look after my mother, who was on her own. I think I kept crying for about a week while I was in the detention centre."

Looking back on his offence, he says he feels "very ashamed that I couldn't control that impulse". If he could meet his younger self, he would tell him: "Control that impulse. If you do, everything will be different."
"I'd grab myself by the collar and shake myself as I said it."
He hopes the Suneung and university will offer him a chance to start again.

"Once I'm out, I need to cut ties with the friends and people I used to know and start a new life. I think university is the only way to do that. Going to university would let me leave the area where I used to live, move somewhere else and start something new. That's why I began studying again."
But he describes beginning Suneung preparation as "a struggle every day".
"But the teachers don't let anything slip past. They keep helping us until we understand. If I don't understand something, I put my hand up and they come over and explain it.
Sometimes, if I've missed something, I keep working at it on my own. If I still can't get it, I ask the students next to me to explain," he said.
Park's day begins at 06:30 with a morning check by prison officers. He starts memorising English vocabulary and working through Korean reading passages early in the morning.

"I learn English words whenever I can, even before breakfast. From 07:00, I work through a Korean passage, something like literature or speech. We have to come down to the classroom at 08:00, so we have another check and then come down for lessons."

During breaks, students make calls to their families or leave the classroom for scheduled visits. In the evening, they return for supervised study. Once the day's activities are over, they must go back to their cells together.
Park says he studies until 22:00 before finishing for the day. If he wants to study longer hours, he needs permission from a prison officer.

But even if gets a good result this year, Park will not be allowed to leave prison and attend university straight away. He is only due to be released in 2028, but plans to use this exam as experience and continue studying next year.
"This time, I want to experience how the Suneung works and how competitive it is. Then, next year, I'll work hard from the start so I can get in the year after that."
Some former students from Mandela Boys' School have managed to get into university, according to the justice ministry.
Others have continued their studies after leaving prison, including by enrolling in residential exam preparation academies.
The inmates are taught by a team of seven prison officers, all of whom hold teaching certificates. Each is responsible for a subject.
Visiting instructors provide classes in the humanities, arts and sport, while university student volunteers help with learning. Professional psychological counselling is also available.
Park Min-yong, who applied to work here in 2023, teaches science. And alongside Suneung lessons, he works with the students' to change their habits and behaviour.
One thing he often tells them is that they need to "learn how to become adults".

He believes that while studying in itself does not necessarily turn inmates away from a life of crime, the experience of having worked hard at something: staying with a concept that makes little sense, revisiting a wrong answer and continuing even when grades do not improve straight away, is valuable in itself.
"Studying properly means pushing yourself to your limits, and that takes considerable stamina and patience," he says.
"Whether they chose to do it or not, the experience of persevering, enduring and not giving up easily may help them to some extent when they face the difficulties of life after release."
He says the material they encounter while preparing for the Suneung also gives them new things to think about.

Korean reading passages cover literature, society, science and philosophy. Students have to consider a character's perspective, examine the evidence behind an argument and understand unfamiliar concepts. They also encounter explanations that differ from their own and have to reconsider what they think.
"They gradually learn that it's not just about their own personal view - that these concepts and relationships have been developed through a shared understanding among many people," Park said.
There are difficult moments too.
Park says students sometimes cheat in classroom tests even while he is watching.

"They cheat as if it's nothing. They give each other answers, even when I'm watching them. Some repeat it after being told off. There may be an element of doing it deliberately, but often they haven't thought it through. They don't think about the impact their actions or words could have on others."
The boys also have a strong desire for recognition, he says.
"It's all the time. 'Look how much I've done. Look how much my grades have improved. I've done this much - haven't I done well?' They're always like that. They're hungry for it."
Not everyone agrees with this initiative though.

One criticism is that young people who have not committed crimes also face fierce competition for university places: so there is some anger that the state provides offenders with separate education and opportunities to prepare for this exam.
Father Jeong Min-ha, of the Archdiocese of Seoul's correctional ministry committee, worked with Seoul Southern Correctional Institution from September 2023 until last year.
He acknowledges these criticisms.
"Studying gives them a sense of achievement and time to look seriously at their own lives. That's why I think it matters. I think that is the most important part of rehabilitation."
Of course, there is no guarantee.
Park recalls a student who had done well at the school but later returned to prison.
"He was doing well when he left, but in the end he came back. So something went wrong. I'd hoped he would carry on with what he'd been doing here, but he couldn't. That's disappointing."

According to the justice ministry's 2026 corrections statistical yearbook, 35.5% of prisoners aged under 20 who were released in 2021 were imprisoned again within three years. That was about 1.7 times the overall rate of 21.2%, and the highest of any age group.
But Park hopes the students will continue learning after they leave prison. "We don't know what the outcome will be," he says.

"They say the way to clear a glass of dirty water is to keep pouring clean water into it, rather than trying to remove each bit of dirt. I hope they fill their minds with good things, learn to use their energy and intellect in the right way, and put that learning into practice at the right time and place."
Additional reporting by Hosu Lee.

articles.title: China is hosting the world's leaders in its AI wonderland. Here's what they won't see
articles.summary: Leave Shenzhen's tech-flecked city skyline and you run into the challenges confronting Xi's China.

blocks.text: Watch: The two sides of daily life in Shenzhen
ByLaura Bicker
China correspondent Reporting fromShenzhen
At 27, Huang Shihua is living the Chinese Dream.

He works as an engineer for a leading humanoid robot company in Shenzhen. The sprawling south-eastern metropolis is touted by China as the origin story for a high-tech future powered by artificial intelligence, robotics and home-grown innovation.

Drones soar across the sky to deliver your dinner, driverless taxis play relaxing music as you journey to your destination, and robots don't just hand you a cappuccino - they explain the origin of your coffee beans.

"We have created a miracle in Shenzhen," Huang says, surrounded by humanoid robots making coffee and playing chess. "Many young people from across China, full of passion and dreams, have flocked here."
Now they all spend their days figuring out ways to make robots smarter.
Image source, Getty Images
Shenzhen, China's AI-powered "city of dreams", has long been a place of opportunity
The Chinese call Shenzhen the "city of dreams". The moniker suits it: one of China's wealthiest, it is close to Hong Kong and the place where the country's explosive growth took off decades ago.

Its manufacturing inventory mirrors China's rise: cabbage patch dolls, then TVs, later iPhones, electric vehicles, drones and now the robots, which are drawing Huang and a new generation of Chinese ambition.

The "miracles" these young engineers are chasing are central to Xi Jinping's bold vision for China. So where better to show it off than Shenzhen, which will be centre-stage when US President Donald Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and others arrive for a global economic summit this week.

And yet there is another side to this flashy, coastal city, a side that they will not get to see. Drive away from towering skyscrapers towards Shajing and Songgang, once the source of much of the world's electronics, and you will run into the challenges confronting Xi's China.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Young, ambitious developers  have turned Shenzhen into a "miracle", Huang says

blocks.text: Young, ambitious developers have turned Shenzhen into a "miracle", Huang says
"Everyone feels life is hard," one construction worker tells us. "Lots of factories have relocated and workers lost their jobs."

China remains exceptionally good at making things - and Shenzhen is proof of that. But the city also holds the evidence for what ails the world's second-largest economy. The property crisis is not over, denting confidence in the future. This is one of China's most expensive cities but even here, our taxi driver tells us, his house is now only worth a third of its original price.

A weak property market and sluggish consumer spending mean many households are buying less. Factories are increasingly relying on exports while many manufacturers have cut production, downsized, automated or moved elsewhere in search of cheaper labour.
The result is a growing number of workers turning to temporary jobs in the gig economy, often with lower pay and fewer benefits.
"Shenzhen is not a magic place," says one delivery driver in his 40s, unwilling to give his name.
"Some say there is gold everywhere in Shenzhen, but it's not like that anymore. It's not a city where you can come and thrive. If you don't work hard, you won't have anything."

The BBC spent several days in Shenzhen exploring these two very different sides of China's progress: on the one hand is the dazzling promise of AI, and on the other are the anxieties of workers who worry if there will be room for them in the future it creates.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Delivery drones in Shenzhen have become a tourist attraction

blocks.text: Delivery drones in Shenzhen have become a tourist attraction
Wednesday is sandwich and bubble tea day in the offices of DexForce Technologies.

The elevator is packed with young engineers and developers headed to the right floor for the free carbs and sugar that will fuel their afternoon. They jostle past their creations en route: human-sized, yellow robots whose limbs fill every available corner.

"I believe that in a decade, robots will be able to better serve humanity by taking on highly repetitive or even dangerous tasks," Huang says. That could be anything from serving coffee to working in mines, and they are being trained for all of that in this laboratory for the future, where machines flail, jerk or lurch into motion as they learn to behave.
To him, "Shenzhen is another 'America'. Because, much like in the US, many young people have been able to realise their dreams and earn the wealth they desire."

This is what Xi wants to hear as he pushes China to lead the world in advanced tech. Shenzhen has indeed long been a place for seeking opportunity but Huang and his colleagues want to do much more. They don't simply want to continue China's manfuacturing supremacy. They want to transform it.

blocks.caption: Image caption, DexForce Technologies is brimming with robots - and faith in a tech-charged future

blocks.text: DexForce Technologies is brimming with robots - and faith in a tech-charged future

Beyond making "our lives more convenient and comfortable", Huang sees AI as helping "the entire world become one family - a global village. AI has the potential to foster equality and the prospect of AI-driven equality is, to me, the most exciting possibility of all."
Smiling enthusiastically, he explains how he hopes that robots can help emerging economies across Africa and South East Asia catch up by reshaping their production lines too.

This tech-charged optimism, which is everywhere in the building, jars with the uncertainty elsewhere in Shenzhen, where robots are nowhere to be found. Yet. But that's just the first of the differences.
In Huang's side of the city, tech and finance workers stroll to the office after a morning workout, sipping coffee that probably cost more than 30 yuan ($4.50; £3.40).
On the other side, scooters whizz through streets piled high with goods being shuttled between factories as vendors sell whole breakfast plates of spicy noodles for under 3 yuan.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The two sides of Shenzhen are a contrast in more ways than one

blocks.text: The two sides of Shenzhen are a contrast in more ways than one
Outside one of the city's tallest skyscrapers, 50-year-old Ms Lu has a phone to her ear and a pen in her right hand while grabbing a bag with her left from a delivery driver.
She shouts four key numbers at her co-worker: instructions for another Chinese woman who is waiting to take the delivery up the elevator to someone sitting at their desk.

This is the lunchtime rush outside SEG plaza, home to 70 storeys of thousands of tenants. Lu used to be one of them. "I ran a small business on the second floor. I sold circuit boards," she says. "But it's getting so hard to do business these days and the rental fees got higher."

Often likened to China's Silicon Valley, Shenzhen has seen rents soar with the influx of new capital, squeezing out smaller, more traditional businesses. At 50, Ms Lu couldn't find another job until the delivery drivers came to her with a plan.
The wait for the elevator can take half an hour – wasted money for a driver trying to fill as many orders as possible. So Ms Lu became a new layer in the ever-evolving gig economy.

"The delivery drivers bring food here to the building entrance. We pick it up and take it upstairs. The drivers pay us 2 yuan per order," she explains, always on the move. Delivery drivers earn between four to eight yuan per order, so Ms Lu gets a decent cut of their earnings.

"The lunch peak time only lasts two or three hours… if they use our service, they can get more orders done, and we can earn some money as well. But the market is bad. These days I only earn around 200 yuan per day."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ms Lu, standing in the middle, joined the delivery business after losing her job

blocks.text: Ms Lu, standing in the middle, joined the delivery business after losing her job

An estimated 200 million Chinese workers, roughly 40% of the urban labour force, now depend on some form of gig work. Many delivery drivers in Shenzhen tell us they chose temporary work because there are fewer opportunities at factories than before.

"We need to adapt to the situation we find ourselves in," one driver told us, "rather than waiting for it to adapt to our needs." A group of them are waiting outside the gates of an e-cigarette factory to make industrial deliveries.
Others nod in agreement. Another driver says he has little choice: "I have two children to raise and I can't stop working. I don't have time to think about anything else."
Permanent jobs often require contributions to social security and pension, which reduces take-home pay. But gig work means more cash in hand and flexibile hours.

"Most workers prefer jobs with a fixed, shorter-term duration. It allows them the flexibility to resign and leave whenever they choose; they have no desire to become permanent employees," says job agent Li Xiaohe.
Increasingly, he puts up boards on pavements advertising temporary factory jobs that pay around 22 yuan an hour for assembling small electronics.
Although agents also appear to be in a shrinking pool, with several former shop fronts shuttered: yet another sign of the downturn in traditional manufacturing.
"Our business is perhaps not as optimistic as it once was," Li admits. "We can feel the effects of Shenzhen going through a transformation."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Li, a labour agent who advertises temorary jobs, says his own business has been struggling

blocks.text: Li, a labour agent who advertises temorary jobs, says his own business has been struggling
That transformation is hard to miss.

Drones buzz above the lush grounds of a purpose built "talent park" along the city's waterfront, dipping and darting as they deliver meals to a dedicated platform. Phones held high, tourists capture them landing with their lunch.

"This is amazing. The technology is just great. I wish we had this back at home," exclaims one Canadian tourist. Our coffee order - for a five-yuan delivery - arrives in just over 15 minutes, the drone landing seamlessly so I can pick up my order.

"I heard that many years ago, Shenzhen was a fishing village," says Anle, who is visiting from Vietnam. "Ha – no more fishing village," he laughs as he orders milk tea to be delivered by drone for him and his wife.

For all the ingenuity on display, it feels more like a demonstration of what is possible rather than a mundane reality. The deliveries, which are only possible in certain locations, stop at 20:00 local time. The driverless cars, which need a separate app to order, are also a novelty – they even offer you a massage when you are on your way.
At night, in the glow of a thousand dancing lights, the drones take on a different role. They fly above the park warning people to behave and not cause trouble.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Shenzhen still draws millions of migrant workers from across China

blocks.text: Shenzhen still draws millions of migrant workers from across China
Far from the glittering skyline, workers gather around plastic tables outside restaurants serving cheap hotpot and seafood skewers.
There are more expensive restaurants along the street, but they too have taken a hit. One owner told us business is down by more than 70% as workers are hesitant to splurge on dinner.
Many of them have spent decades here, including 58-year-old construction worker Mr Wu. He arrived in Shenzhen from Sichuan in the 1990s not long after China opened the city up to foreign businesses.
He was among millions of migrants from poorer provinces who came to work on production lines or build skyscrapers. They are still coming.

All the people we spoke to came from elsewhere. They often labour up to 14 hours a day and live in shared dormitories, sustained by the prospect of stable work and decent pay to send home to their families.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dormitories like these have houses workers over the decades

blocks.text: Dormitories like these have houses workers over the decades
For these workers, the Covid pandemic, when Chinese manufacturing hit a record low, appears to have been the first turning point.
"After Covid, our salary dropped by at least a third," Mr Wu recalls, after which wages never fully recovered.

"I will continue to work," he adds. "As long as you keep working, you will have an income. More salary or not? It doesn't matter. As long as you keep working, you will have an income. If the economy slows down, we all slow down. If it grows, we all get better."
For all these decades, Shenzhen lived up to its bargain: work hard and your life would improve.
But now, in a city that is being redefined by automation and AI, that old promise feels less secure.
